News.title: UK power plant 'shut down for four days' after major Iran-linked cyber attack
News.content:
UK power plant 'shut down for four days' after major Iran-linked cyber attack

The incident took place in July, at the same time as a series of attacks on US water infrastructure which sparked worry in the White House and affected 12 states

View 2 Images A file image of a power station in the UK (Image: PA)

A power plant in Great Britain was forced to close for four days after a cyber attack by Iran-linked hackers, it has been revealed.

‌



According to reports, the facility was disabled "while staff fought to bring it back online" after the attack last month - the exact location of the site has not been revealed due to security reasons.

‌



It is, however, understood that the plant affected was not one of the biggest sites in the country, according to the Telegraph. Due to the relatively small nature of the plant, the outage had no impact on the UK’s wider power supply or energy generation. This has been confirmed by the Government, which has described the UK's energy system as 'highly resilient.

‌



The incident took place in July, at the same time as a series of attacks on US water infrastructure - those attacks affected 12 states and caused concern in the White House.

View 2 Images The plant involved has been described as a 'small scale site' (Image: Getty Images)

‌



In response, the Government briefed the chief executives of power companies and wrote to businesses with advice, direction and next steps.

A Government source told the Telegraph: “We have thresholds for important generators to legally notify us of cyber activity, and this site is nowhere near. It’s a very small scale site, less than a rounding error compared to grid capacity.”

A Government spokesman said: “The UK has a highly resilient energy system. We work closely with the energy sector to protect infrastructure and ensure the highest security standards.

Article continues below

“This story refers to an incident impacting a small-scale energy generator, and at no point was there a risk to the wider energy system.”

News.title: Ed Miliband vows bond between Britain and Ukraine 'unbreakable and built to last'
News.content:
Ed Miliband vows bond between Britain and Ukraine 'unbreakable and built to last'

EXCLUSIVE: Speaking as Kyiv marked the 35th anniversary of Ukrainian independence, the Foreign Secretary Ed Milband also praised the solidarity shown by the British people

View 2 Images Ed Miliband said the bond between Britain and Ukraine was 'unbreakable' (Image: Getty Images)

Ed Miliband has vowed the bond between Britain and Ukraine is “unbreakable and built to last”.

‌



Speaking as Kyiv marked the 35th anniversary of Ukrainian independence, the Foreign Secretary also praised the solidarity shown by the British people.

‌



Speaking to this newspaper, Mr Miliband also issued a reminder that Ukrainians were fighting for the security not just of their own country, but for Europe. He said: Mr Miliband said: “Tomorrow, as Ukraine marks the 35th anniversary of its independence, celebrating its sovereignty, identity and culture, the United Kingdom stands proudly alongside the Ukrainian people.

‌



"This day serves as a powerful reminder of the extraordinary strength Ukrainians have shown in defending their country in the face of Russian attack. I pay tribute to their immense and enduring courage.

At least 15 killed and 130 injured in Russian drone strike on Ukrainian shopping mall READ MORE :

Andrew Tate and his brother reported to counter-terror cops after Russia trip READ MORE :

View 2 Images Andy Burnham has vowed to continue to “support Ukraine 100%” after Russia threatened the UK over drone strikes (Image: POOL/AFP via Getty Images)

“Ukraine’s defence of its freedom and self-determination matters to us all because of the values they are fighting for and because of what this conflict means for our security in Europe. British people have time and again shown their solidarity with the people of Ukraine during this conflict.

‌



"We will continue to help Ukraine strengthen its security, and work with international partners to ensure Russia faces accountability for its aggression. Our bond is unbreakable and built to last.”

Defence Secretary Wes Streeting will attend a candle-lighting ceremony at the Ukrainian Cathedral of the Holy Family in London to mark the anniversary, where he will pay tribute to Ukraine's resolve, while the PM will co-chair a call of the Coalition of the Willing on Monday.

Earlier this week Andy Burnham warned Vladimir Putin that Britain will continue to “support Ukraine 100%” after Russia threatened the UK over drone strikes.

‌



Mr Streeting said: "Thirty-five years ago, Ukrainians chose independence. Over more than a decade, Putin’s illegal and barbaric war has tried and failed to destroy Ukraine’s freedom and way of life.

“We stand proudly with Ukraine and our support will not waver. They are fighting for freedom everywhere, and we will stand by them until they win.”

It comes as the Ministry of Defence hosts a photographic exhibition and panel discussion at the National Army Museum, showcasing the UK's training effort for Ukraine's Armed Forces through Operation Interflex. Launched in June 2022, it has now trained more than 67,000 Ukrainian defenders.

Article continues below

Selected images from the exhibition are expected to travel to Kyiv in October, marking Ukrainian Defenders Day.

News.title: Two men bailed after being arrested on suspicion of manslaughter of 22-year-old soldier
News.content:
Two men bailed after being arrested on suspicion of manslaughter of 22-year-old soldier

Two men, aged 22 and 23, arrested on suspicion of manslaughter in connection with the death of 22-year-old soldier Liam Potts have been released on bail

View 3 Images Liam Potts was the 'heart and soul of any room', his family said (Image: Northumbria Police)

Two men arrested on suspicion of manslaughter after the death of a 22-year-old soldier have been released on bail.

The men, aged 22 and 23, were arrested on Saturday after the body of Liam Potts was found in the River Tyne on Tuesday (August 18), three days after he disappeared during a night out. Northumbria Police confirmed on Saturday evening that the two men had been released on bail.

Mr Potts, who served with the Coldstream Guards, was last seen heading towards Wylam in Northumberland at around 12.20am last Saturday (August 15).

His body was found a short distance away from Wylam Bridge following a major search by police, HM Coastguard, North of Tyne Mountain and Northumberland National Park Mountain Rescue teams.

Prior to his disappearance, Northumbria Police had received a report of a disturbance and subsequent collision involving a vehicle and a group of pedestrians on the bridge.

View 3 Images Tributes left on Wylam Bridge in memory of Liam Potts (Image: Chronicle Live)

On Monday, the force said two men were arrested in connection with the report and subsequently released on bail. They were re-arrested on suspicion of manslaughter on Saturday as detectives investigated whether the two incidents directly led to Mr Potts entering the water, police said.

Mr Potts was not in the vehicle involved in the collision, nor was he struck by it, police said.

The force said that when officers found Mr Potts’s body, they did not believe there to be any third-party involvement, but further inquiries led to the manslaughter arrests.

A man and a woman, both in their 20s, suffered serious injuries in the collision. The woman has been discharged while the man remains in hospital for further treatment.

In a tribute, Mr Potts' family said he was the "heart and soul of any room".

They said: "To our Liam. You may no longer be here beside us, but your presence will never be forgotten. Your family, friends and colleagues have all said the same thing: 'Once you met Pottsy, you could never forget him.'

"You really were the heart and soul of any room. We are going to miss your smile, your laugh and the little things that made you who you are. Though time may pass, the love we have for you will never fade.

"You will always be remembered, and forever loved. Rest peacefully, knowing that your memory lives on in all those whose lives you touched."

They continued: "To everyone who reached out with kind messages, calls, visits, flowers and thoughtful gestures; please know how deeply grateful we are.

"Your love and support bring us comfort when we need it most; it really has been extremely overwhelming the amount of support we have been receiving. It’s clear to see how loved Liam was.

"Thank you to everyone who tirelessly supported in the search for Liam, including all the members of the public. As you will have hopefully already seen, a GoFundMe page has been created to donate to all the amazing volunteers of the Mountain Rescue Teams.

"However, beyond this, we would like to extend our appreciation to Northumbria Police, particularly the diving team that were able to successfully bring our boy home."

View 3 Images 'Once you met Pottsy, you could never forget him,' Liam's loved ones said (Image: Jam Press)

Detective Inspector Rachael Rutherford, of Northumbria Police, said: "Our thoughts remain with Liam’s family during this difficult time. The facts remain the same, that Liam was on the bridge at the time of the collision, but he was not an occupant of the vehicle and was not struck by the vehicle.

"Inquiries have revealed that Liam, for reasons yet to be established, entered the water within minutes of the collision. We have therefore made the further re-arrests as we are looking to establish whether there is any link between the collision and Liam entering the water."

Article continues below

Det Insp Rutherford added: "We know there has been a lot of confusion and speculation in the community. It’s clear that Liam was a very popular young man. We are committed to finding answers for Liam’s family and we will continue to provide updates on our investigation.

"We would remind people to avoid speculation both online and in our communities as this could impact the ongoing investigation. We would continue to ask that people respect the family’s privacy at this tragic time."

Anyone with information that could help is asked to send Northumbria Police a direct message on social media, use the live chat and report forms on the force’s website, or call 101, quoting reference number NP-20260814-0016.

News.title: Miracle boy defies doctors — years after parents were told he wouldn't survive birth
News.content:
Miracle boy defies doctors — years after parents were told he wouldn't survive birth

Jude Bedingfield, who doctors feared might not survive birth, is now nearing his third birthday after defying expectations while living with three rare genetic conditions

View 4 Images Jude with his mum Heidi, who was warned he may only survive for hours or days (Image: Cover Images)

A little boy is preparing to celebrate his third birthday after doctors warned his parents he might not survive being born.

‌



Jude Bedingfield was diagnosed with three life-limiting conditions while he was still in the womb. Parents Heidi Knight and Ryan Bedingfield were told their baby’s prognosis was poor, and were warned he could survive for only hours or days - if he made it through birth.

‌



The couple had gone into their 22-week scan excited to find out their baby’s gender when doctors instead detected a number of abnormalities. Heidi said: "They told us that they’d found some problems with the baby and took us into a side room, it was such an out-of-body experience. They said he had lots of small different abnormalities which all added up and became a big problem."

‌



View 4 Images The couple recently welcomed a baby girl (Image: Cover Images)

Further tests revealed Jude had three rare genetic conditions - partial trisomy 13, Cri du chat syndrome and Pontocerebellar Hypoplasia (PH) - which come with lifelong disabilities. While doctors could not predict exactly how the combination would affect him, they warned the family he may not survive birth. Heidi and Ryan were also advised several times that termination was an option.

She said: “I’ll never forget one of the consultants sat us down and said it’s as bad as it can get and that our baby was not going to make it. They genuinely thought it was 50/50 if he’d breathe or not.

‌



“All I wanted to do was give him a cuddle. I wanted to meet him alive and have a cuddle, that’s all I thought I was ever going to get.”

Heidi was closely monitored throughout the rest of her pregnancy before Jude was delivered by Caesarean section on September 11, 2023.

Heidi, who is a beauty therapist, explained: “It was such a rush, I’ve never been so terrified in my life. I was about to find out if my baby was going to survive or not. When he was born, he let out this little cry; the only way to describe it is he sounded like a baby kitten. He was then taken away as he needed help breathing.

‌



View 4 Images Minutes after his birth, his parents had the first sign he would survive (Image: Cover Images)

“Before he was born, doctors told us they could use pulmonary surfactant, which can help babies clear their lungs - but we weren’t offered it in there. Ryan suggested it, and after he had it Jude started breathing on his own, and he was able to come over and have skin-to-skin with me, which was the thing I really wanted.

“He wasn’t on oxygen for seven minutes which was the first sign that he was going to be okay.”

‌



Jude was then taken to neonatal intensive care, where his progress quickly began exceeding doctors’ expectations.

Days later, Heidi and Ryan met with his medical and palliative care teams and were told he was doing remarkably well. After 15 days at the Oliver Fisher Intensive Care Unit at the Medway Maritime Hospital in Kent, he was able to go home. Nearly almost three years later, Jude is “thriving” compared with those initial predictions, although he continues to face significant challenges and is not independently mobile.

He is fed through a Mic-Key button in his stomach and has hypotonia, meaning he has low muscle tone and needs support to sit and stand. Heidi describes him as being “like a big baby”. Jude began NHS physiotherapy when he was just a few months old, before his parents decided to also pursue private sessions in the hope of helping his development.

‌



View 4 Images An anonymous £10,000 donation last year allowed Jude to attend his first two-week course of intensive physiotherapy (Image: Cover Images)

The family has since grown, with Heidi and Ryan welcoming seven-month-old daughter Scarlett. Around 18 months ago, they also began fundraising through children’s charity Tree of Hope to pay for intensive physiotherapy.

An anonymous £10,000 donation last year allowed Jude to attend his first two-week course at Ability Therapies in Essex - with his family saying the sessions made a major difference.

‌



Heidi said: “During that two-week intensive course, he learnt to pivot on the floor and change his direction, which seems like such a simple thing, but it’s made a huge difference. It has been absolutely life-changing for him.”

Heidi now hopes Jude’s story can offer hope to other families facing difficult diagnoses after she found support herself through families sharing their experiences online.

She said: “The outcome sounded bleak and we had discussions that no one should have. You think you’re going to have to plan a funeral; it’s horrible. I was adamant that I wasn’t coming home with a baby, and I now have an almost three-year-old - he has exceeded all expectations.

‌



“He is a happy, bright and determined little boy. We totally understand that Jude may be a rarity, but there’s a chance. He’s a happy and determined little boy who loves playing with his toys. We don’t know exactly what the future holds for him, but we want to enable him to live the best life possible.”

The family is continuing to raise money towards physiotherapy and other support Jude may need as he grows.

They are holding a family fun day at The White Horse pub in Sittingbourne, Kent, on Saturday, August 29.

Article continues below

News.title: Mum of Brit woman shot dead by dad in Texas to travel to US in bid to reopen probe
News.content:
Mum of Brit woman shot dead by dad in Texas to travel to US in bid to reopen probe

The mum of 23-year-old British woman Lucy Harrison is preparing to travel to the US in a bid to persuade prosecutors to reopen the probe into her daughter's death

View 4 Images Jane Coates is campaigning for the US investigation into the death of her 23-year-old daughter, Lucy Harrison, to be reopened

The mum of a British woman who was shot dead by her dad in Texas is preparing to travel to the US in a bid to persuade prosecutors to reopen the investigation into her daughter's death.

Lucy Harrison, 23, from Warrington, Cheshire, was shot in the chest by her father, Kris Harrison, while they were alone in a room at his home in Prosper, Texas, on January 10, 2025.

A grand jury in Collin County decided there was insufficient evidence to bring criminal charges after Mr Harrison claimed the Glock handgun discharged accidentally while he was showing it to his daughter. However, in February this year, a coroner in England ruled that Lucy had been unlawfully killed, finding that her father's actions amounted to gross negligence manslaughter under UK law.

View 4 Images Lucy Harrison, 23, was from Warrington, Cheshire (Image: PA)

Speaking to the Press Association more than 19 months after her daughter's death, Jane Coates said she has felt "incredibly alone" and "deserted by the British authorities" throughout her campaign for justice for Lucy, and has urged the Government to give her its full backing.

Ms Coates said she hopes to meet the Collin County District Attorney and campaign for a fresh investigation.

In February, senior coroner for Cheshire Jacqueline Devonish concluded that the gun could only have been fired after it was pointed at Lucy and the trigger was pulled.

The inquest heard that Mr Harrison had been drinking wine before removing a loaded Glock pistol from his bedside cabinet, and that police officers in Texas did not carry out an alcohol test despite smelling alcohol on his breath.

Ms Coates has now sought the help of Radd Seiger, who previously advised the family of Harry Dunn in their campaign for justice after the teenager was killed by a US citizen in a road crash in Northamptonshire.

Commenting on why she has felt "alone" during her campaign, Ms Coates told PA: "I think it’s not being heard - just raising all of our concerns and nothing being acted upon, and feeling like we’ve just been deserted by the British authorities.

"I think, save Sarah Hall, my MP, who has done everything in her capacity to raise and escalate Lucy’s case, it's just felt like there’s been doors shut at every single opportunity, and people haven’t been there for us."

Ms Coates said she had expected the unlawful killing conclusion to become a turning point in her campaign for justice.

View 4 Images Lucy Harrison's mum Jane Coates (centre), her friend Ella Gowing (left) and her boyfriend Sam Littler outside Cheshire Coroner's Court following her inquest (Image: PA)

She continued: "We had to wait until February 2026 before we felt that we could freely speak about what we felt had happened to Lucy and how let down we felt.

"Receiving the unlawful killing outcome was a day full of complete mixed emotions, but one where finally Lucy’s truth and voice has been heard in some capacity.

"But from then it still hasn’t moved things forward in terms of my request for a reopening of the investigation in Texas."

Ms Coates said she and Mr Seiger are now planning to travel to Texas in the hope of persuading the Collin County District Attorney's office to reconsider the case in light of the coroner’s findings.

Asked what a successful trip to the US would look like, Ms Coates said: "It would be that they do accept the outcome from the coroner in terms of the unlawful killing.

"Although I know that it’s a completely different jurisdiction, a completely different law, so it’s about appealing to them in terms of our real concerns with the US investigation, with the Texas investigation, and that they do agree to reopen Lucy’s case and give it new consideration. That’s the ultimate goal."

Ms Coates said she was not asking the Foreign Office to interfere in the American justice system, but wanted ministers to publicly support her family.

View 4 Images Kris Harrison (Image: Liverpool Echo)

‌



"Surely, having an unlawful killing conclusion in a coroner’s court should then mean something, and I definitely thought that it would have been escalated in the Foreign Office," she said.

"I’m not calling for the Foreign Office to interfere in jurisdiction abroad… but to be a voice for Lucy and for our family - to know that we are supported by the British Government, to be able to campaign for the case to be reopened."

The family have requested a meeting with Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband and other senior officials.

‌



Asked what she would say directly to the Foreign Secretary, Ms Coates said: "I would say I am a bereaved mum who wants to do everything I possibly can to ensure justice for my daughter and to do the right thing by her and for her, and I really do want the full support of the British Government behind me, so that I no longer feel alone."

Mr Seiger said Lucy's case was exactly the type of complex international case that Dame Anne Owers' review into the Government’s handling of the Dunn case envisaged would receive senior-level support.

He said the family wanted the case lifted beyond routine consular handling and said he planned to travel to the United States with Ms Coates to meet the district attorney and seek a fresh investigation.

Article continues below

A Foreign Office spokesperson said: "Our thoughts remain with Jane and her family for the tragic loss they have suffered. We were in contact with the family and provided consular support. We will always look to learn lessons to improve the consular support we offer to other families in the future."

It is understood Foreign Office officials are reviewing recent correspondence from Lucy's family and intend to respond.

News.title: Reckless thrillseekers ignore police warnings to plunge into sea from children’s charity roof
News.content:
Reckless thrillseekers ignore police warnings to plunge into sea from children’s charity roof

The Harriet Davis Seaside Holiday Trust in Tenby, Pembrokeshire, has warned someone could be seriously injured or killed as groups of young children climb onto its roof

View 4 Images Youngsters have been "tombstoning" from the charity's roof into the harbour below (Image: WALES NEWS SERVICE)

Thrillseekers have been jumping into the sea from the roof of a charity building used by seriously ill and disabled children.

‌



Groups of youngsters have repeatedly climbed onto the Harriet Davis Seaside Holiday Trust building in Tenby, Pembrokeshire, before “tombstoning” into the water below. The charity says the problem has escalated dramatically in recent weeks, with as many as 24 people accessing the roof around high tide and causing damage as they climb up and down the building.

‌



Footage of the dangerous jumps has also been shared on social media with the caption: “Got to keep the Tenby tradition going!”

‌



The trust, which provides specialist holiday accommodation for families caring for children with disabilities, complex medical needs and life-limiting conditions, fears somebody could be seriously injured or killed.

Tourist pulls off extraordinary escape after plunging 180ft down cliff face READ MORE :

View 4 Images The problem has worsened in recent weeks, the charity said (Image: WALES NEWS SERVICE)

'Extremely serious danger to life'

Senior Administrator, Carol Lincoln, said: “The activity presents an extremely serious danger to life - both to the young people jumping from the roof, and to fishing and other boats which may unfortunately be in the water below them.”

‌



She added: “The situation has now escalated significantly. This last month, as many as 24 young people on every high tide have been on our roof, jumping from the adjacent property into the sea and, in the process, causing continued and deliberate damage to the fabric of the building.

“We are now also experiencing youths hammering on our doors and windows as they climb onto and descend from the roof. This is understandably terrifying for the vulnerable families staying inside the property.”

The charity has repeatedly tried to make the building harder to access, including using anti-climb paint and fitting plastic spikes across the roof and three access points and thousands of pounds has also reportedly been spent repairing damage.

‌



View 4 Images Police did not attend on every occasion families called (Image: WALES NEWS SERVICE)

Acts of criminal damage

The charity said families staying at the property had contacted police about the youngsters but were told on some occasions that officers would not attend. When officers did visit, she said the charity was advised to remove bins which had been used to help people climb onto the roof. But this did not deter the children from acessing the roof.

‌



Carol said: “Instead, the youths simply stole fuel bins from the harbour and used those instead. We have followed the advice given to us and have taken every reasonable step within our means to prevent access to the roof.

“This has included installing anti-climb paint and rows of plastic anti-climb spikes across the whole roof and three access points. We have also spent thousands of pounds repairing damage to the roof. Despite this, the problem has continued and is now escalating.

“The young people are deliberately smearing the anti-climb paint over our external walls and are progressively ripping the plastic spikes from the roof. This is causing serious and continuing damage to the fabric of the building.”

‌



The Trust says its biggest concern is the impact on families who use the accommodation for what can be a rare opportunity to enjoy a holiday together. She added: “Our visitors are not tourists coming to the town for entertainment. Most of our visiting families come from Wales, and some are local families.

View 4 Images The charity's building is near the harbour in Tenby (Image: WALES NEWS SERVICE)

‌



'Charity is being let down'

“They are parents and carers looking after children and young people who may have profound disabilities, complex medical needs or life-limiting conditions. Many families are only able to have a holiday because our properties provide the specialist equipment and facilities they require.

“For many of them, this is an extremely precious opportunity to spend time together and create positive family memories in circumstances where ordinary holidays are simply not possible. Instead, they are increasingly finding themselves frightened and distressed by young people climbing onto the roof, banging on doors and windows and shouting as they gain access to and descend from the building.

“This is completely unacceptable.”

‌



The charity has now called for stronger action from police, parents and council officials before the behaviour ends in tragedy. She said: "What was once an occasional problem has now developed into a significant and increasingly popular activity, with ever larger groups accessing our roof.

“The greater the number of people jumping or even simply accessing our roof, the greater the possibility of a fatality. This risk is now very real. We therefore feel that this situation has moved far beyond an issue of occasional antisocial behaviour.

“It is now a serious and escalating public safety issue involving criminal damage, deliberate trespass, risk to life and the welfare of vulnerable families staying within our properties. We cannot wait until somebody is seriously injured or killed before this is treated with the urgency it deserves.”

Article continues below

County Councillor Michael Williams has backed the Trust and written to police calling for action saying their is a genuine fear that there could be a fatality. He said: “In my opinion at the very least criminal damage is being caused by these youths and they are they are trespassing with intent, and I would ask that you consider taking action on these specific activities.

“This amazing charitable organisation provides a unique opportunity for families who often have to contend with some of the most distressing circumstances conceivable and they deserve the support of everyone concerned.

“The Trust and their guests are being let down by the inability or unwillingness of organisations they should be able to rely on to effectively address these activities.”

News.title: Natalie Harp: Backstory and trigger for executive assistant's devotion to Donald Trump
News.content:
Among the fascinating details in Donald Trump's weird Turkey plane swap caper was who he took with him on the secret jet out of Ankara.

You could pretty much understand Pete Hegseth being on Trump's plane during the sneaky escape - although the concept of being in an enclosed metal tube with him for several hours doesn't bear thinking about.

But also in this select entourage was a 35-year-old blonde woman named Natalie.

Also known as "the human printer", Natalie Harp is Donald Trump's executive assistant. She gained that nickname because of her tendency to print out papers for Trump - often flattering news stories - at any time of the day or night.

‌



View 3 Images Natalie is pictured at a bill signing in the Oval Office (Image: Getty Images)

During a rally in Atlanta over the weekend, Democrat Senator Jon Ossoff - whom many (including me) have tipped as a future presidential candidate - accused Trump of wanting to "travel with Natalie" rather than of of perform his Presidential duties. The rather pointed remark has ignited a flurry of interest in Harp, and what exactly her relationship with Trump is.

She's an exceptionally visible member of the administration despite not having a public-facing role - simply because she is almost always where Trump is. She's always somewhere in the background, often with an armful of A4 printouts, neatly paper clipped together and ready to deploy.

‌



She was previously a presenter for One America News Network, a right-wing propaganda outlet, where she would often end her show either with a bible verse ...or a quote from Trump, introducing his outbursts as if he were some kind of divine prophet: "Remember what Trump said..."

After coming on Trump's radar by praising him over legislation he championed that she said had allowed her to get experimental treatment for bone cancer, she joined his 2024 campaign as an aide. And from there she was hired by the administration as an executive assistant to the President.

The New York Times' Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan included fascinating nuggets about her character in their book Regime Change, which came out in June, and in an earlier article for the Times. They report that she left "intimate letters" to Trump during the campaign. "You are all that matters to me," she's said to have written.

"I don't ever want to let you down...I want to bring you joy."

‌



The Secret Service were, by all accounts, perturbed by the letters, left for him in his "personal spaces".

But beyond her obvious proximity to Trump, a lot of the most fascinating tales of her closeness with the President are the stuff of legend - and are mostly recounted second-hand or through unnamed sources.

There's the tale of her being so eager to be close to Trump that when his campaign team moved from Palm Beach to his golf club at Bedminster, New Jersey in 2023, and she was not given a room - she set up a bed in the the women's locker room and spent several months sleeping there.

There are varying claims about how much access she has to his social media accounts - and which of his more contentious posts she has been involved in.

‌



Moreover, there are claims that she has access to other of his communications - texts and emails.

And Trump, early in his second term, is said to have told his team Natalie was "the only one who loved him as much as his wife and his kids."

To get more stories, gossip and analysis like this in your inbox every week, 

View 3 Images

‌



Click here to sign up

Kim Jong chill

North Korea has 57 nukes, Trump declared on Wednesday, as he led journalists on a tour of the construction site that is the White House South Lawn.

Trump is having a helipad installed on the lawn because the new Marine Ones keep scorching the grass. When the installation was first underway, it followed the camber of the hill atop which is the White House. Trump didn't like that, it was reported at the time, because he wanted it level with the horizon. And during his tour of the site yesterday, he let slip that another reason he wanted it flat was so he could host cocktail parties on the landing pad.

He later proudly declared that the new grass to be laid on the lawn had been supplied for free by the Scotts Miracle Gro company, a donor to his campaign and Super PAC. Scotts also distributes Roundup, and has benefited from a Trump-signed executive order that declared such herbicides "critical to US national and economic security".

‌



Anyway, somewhere between admitting to a huge conflict of interest and declaring himself "really good at flagpoles", Trump put a number on Kim Jong-un's nuclear arsenal. Which he's almost certainly not supposed to say out loud in front of a bunch of contractors and journalists, and definitely when he's being beamed live to TVs and computers around the world.

Trump has been back on his "little Rocket Man" love-in this week. He posted a picture of him and Kim taken during his first term - back when a President alienating America's natural allies while cosying up to its enemies was a novel event.

Then on Sunday night he had a direct pop at South Korea, announcing he would be scaling back American involvement in a series of military drills alongside Seoul, and branding the plans "inappropriate and hostile". Trump later explained that his was partly out of revenge for South Korea refusing to help with the war on Iran. Which is not an unreasonable position for South Korea to take, given they get 60% of their oil through the Strait of Hormuz.

But there we have it - we have a President proudly, or at least absent-mindedly admitting to huge conflicts of interest, cosying up to one of the world's most reviled dictators and wanting to host cocktail parties on the White House helipad all on the same day. Now, what else has been going on...

‌



High steaks

Susie Wiles, Donald Trump's chief of staff, has been spotted meeting with a potential candidate to replace Karoline Leavitt as mouthpiece of the administration.

She reportedly sat down for a spot of dinner with Scott Jennings - which does not surprise me. He's a MAGA blowhard who mostly appears on CNN panel shows, and has an apparently limitless appetite for saying whatever the President might want him to say, no matter how preposterous or offensive it is.

No surprise he's being sounded out for the Press Secretary vacancy, then. What did surprise me was their choice of dinner venue.

Morton's is a longtime staple of Washington's steakhouse scene, but its main differentiator is the long outdoor terrace where people go to smoke cigars.

‌



Point is, there are many classier restaurants in the Capital, and eateries that are more MAGA friendly than catering to cigar-chomping lobbyists and congressmen.

Not to mention there are many more private places to eat. In fact, I'd argue Morton's is probably one of the more surveilled rooms in Washington DC - both by nosey senators, and in the 2019 case of Democrat Senator Bob Menendez, the FBI. (He'd taken to meeting Egyptian officials there, from whom he accepted bribes, a court later heard).

An odd choice of venue for a quiet chat.

News.title: Donald Trump's wild week as BBC lawsuit descends into farce and he faces ridicule over 'close aid'
News.content:
Donald Trump's wild week as BBC lawsuit descends into farce and he faces ridicule over 'close aid'

As well as trying to avoid talking about Natalie Harp, Trump has been threatening to bomb the bond markets, blaming Canada, begging the Supremes not to keep him hangin' on and cosying up to Little Rocket Man

View 2 Images Trump has been desperately trying to avoid talking about his Natalie (Image: Getty Images)

Donald Trump spent much of this week trying to avoid talking about Natalie Harp, the 'extremely close' executive assistant whose role in the White House sits somewhere between 'Oval Office gatekeeper' and 'weird security blanket'.

‌



Before we get to the rest of the week's bizarre moments, it's worth addressing why the Natalie Harp story is one that needs to be told. Some would say it's unfair to focus on a member of staff - even one employed by the most powerful and consequential man in the world.

‌



At their most innocuous, Natalie Harp's oddly close relationship with Donald Trump is the story of a young woman, perhaps a vulnerable one, whose enthusiasm and support for a political hero has turned into desperate obsession.

‌



But at worst, it illustrates the kind of messianic devotion with which Trump has surrounded himself in his second Presidency.

Not all of Trump's team are so enthusiastic in their outpourings of love for their President. But Natalie Harp is not the only one who thinks he's an unquestionable gift from god.

Meanwhile, Trump has been threatening to bomb the bond markets, blaming Canada, telling the Supremes not to keep him hangin' on and cosying up to Little Rocket Man.

‌



Here's everything you need to know.

Trump threatens to launch military strikes on the bond market

Donald Trump's Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent this week said he was going to double the Government's purchases of long-term US bonds in a bid to prevent a panic in the bond markets - wobbles in which have sent government borrowing costs skyrocketing.

But that's not what we're looking at today. We're looking at this truly bizarre moment where Trump, asked about the intervention, appeared to have some kind of brain episode and threatened to bomb the bond market.

‌



Content cannot be displayed without consent

They're not even a real country, anyway

Donald Trump has come up with a wizard new scheme for making life more expensive for regular Americans, just in time for the midterms. Blame Canada.

Well, strictly speaking, each side blamed the other for trade talks breaking down on Friday night - but the upshot is both sides have slapped 50% tariffs on the other's goods.

‌



President Donald Trump’s import taxes will hit about 5% of what Canada ships to the United States every year, ranging from hockey sticks to tongue depressors. Prime Minister Carney said Ottawa would respond with targeted tariff protection for industries exposed to the new US duties, including some steel products. He also mentioned the dairy, appliance, agricultural equipment, pulp and paper and electronics sectors.

No further talks were planned. Whatever the eventual outcome, a loss of trust seems one of the earliest casualties.

Carney accused Washington of using “economic integration as a weapon” and said “its signature was written in pencil.” Resorting to the language of battle, he said his country had been “attacked” by the new American tariffs. “You’re at war when you get attacked,” he said, adding that Canada had the reserves, resilience and plan to respond.

‌



Where's the beef?

American ranchers used to be among Trump's fiercest defenders. And why not? He promised them a utopian future during the campaign.

But he has, understandably, gone down in their estimation since it turned out he was perfectly willing to screw them in time for the midterms.

In his second intervention in the beef industry this year, Trump announced he'd struck a deal to allow 300,000 metric tonnes of beef mince to be imported to the States, tariff free, over the next three months.

‌



The importers, Trump said, had agreed to sell it at 25% off market rate - in a move he said would help to "rebuild the herd" of American cattle - which is at its lowest rate for decades due to drought and high working costs for farmers.

But it has the added advantage of making food a bit cheaper until shortly after America next goes to the polls.

Colin Woodall, of the National Cattlemen's Beef Association, told the New York Times that "flooding the market with government-subsidized, below-market beef is not the way to rebuild the American cattle herd".

‌



And let's not forget this is the second time Trump has screwed farmers this year - after promising to import 80,000 metric tonnes of beef from Argentina in a bid to shore-up Agrie President Javier Milei's struggling government.

Trump heckled by man in 'kill paedophiles' shirt

Trump gave another one of his pre-midterms rallies in South Carolina last night. The rally was in support of Darline Graham, who is running to replace her late brother Lindsey in the Senate seat - and is rapidly proving to be a liability.

But the most embarrassing thing that happened at the SC rally was the guy who stood up during Trump's speech and shouted something indecipherable, while wearing a tee shirt that read: "Kill your local paedophile."

‌



If what he was shouting was anything like as coherent as what was written on his shirt, Trump probably needn't be worried.

Content cannot be displayed without consent

She's running...

Photos revealed by the Mirror on Friday show Donald Trump aide Natalie Harp sprinting after his cart at his Scottish golf course - confirming just one of the many bizarre tales about the President's "Human Printer."

‌



It came after bizarre letters she sent him confessing her devotion to him were published.

Questions continue to be asked about the 35-year-old executive assistant's unusually close relationship with the US President. Harp is nicknamed the "human printer" because she frequently prints out and hands the President printouts of flattering news stories and cherry-picked poll numbers - acting as a "filter" for information reaching him.

View 2 Images She's running...after his golf cart

‌



You can - and should - read more about the frightening letters she is said to have written to the President here.

But many of the tales about Harp's behaviour are the stuff of legend, and reported, usually credited to anonymous sources, in books and longreads. Like the time she is said to have ridden in the boot of an SUV in order to stay close to Trump.

So it was a pleasure to be able to confirm one of the legends - that she sprinted around Trump's Turnberry golf course on foot in 2023 - as entirely true.

‌



Pictures published by the Mirror show this incident for the first time. Harp is shown running full-tilt uphill after Trump's cart on the first day of his trip to Turnberry on 2 May 2023.

Worried that she had upset Trump, Harp explained in a letter during or shortly after the trip: "The first day I was told there were no carts, and people walked, which is why I walked.

"The second day, I was specifically asked by, I forget who his name was, but one of the main people who worked there, if I could continue walking, and tell any other girls who would head out there to do the same to spare the Course any more Carts.

‌



"If there is anything else I have done to cause you trouble, please forgive me."

And it didn't end there...

Donald Trump on second golf holiday with Natalie Harp

We also revealed today that Trump left his wife at home for another golf holiday in Scotland last year - on which he was accompanied by Hart.

‌



Harp accompanied Trump to Turnberry last July for a second visit - where she followed him on the golf course and sat in on at least one meeting with a world leader.

You can read about that one here...

More shenanigans in Trump's BBC lawsuit

Donald Trump's lawyers have badly miscalculated the President's increasingly preposterous lawsuit against the BBC in many ways. There was the original lawsuit, which would have forced Trump to hand over his financial records - we talked about that in our weekly Youtube roundup here.

‌



There was the bit where they managed to get it written down in evidence that a maximum of 285 people watched the offending Panorama programme in the United States...we talked about that in this episode - and I strongly recommend you give that one a watch if you haven't, because it's super funny.

Anyway... perhaps Trump's biggest blunder was assuming the BBC was just like any other media company - and that they would fold under the threat of a 10 billion dollar lawsuit and settle out of court.

See, Trump sues a lot of people - but his lawsuits seldom end up in a courtroom. Particularly when it comes to media companies, it increasingly seems that a settlement is what he's actually after. It happened with ABC News - who agreed to pay fifteen million dollars after a presenter wrongly stated that Trump had been found liable for rape, when the jury found he'd technically been found liable for sexual assault - a distinction the judge put down to a quirk of New York law.

‌



Later, Paramount settled for sixteen million dollars over an entirely spurious lawsuit relating to the editing of an interview with Kamala Harris on an episode of 60 Minutes. The interview was entirely fine, but Trump decided had been edited to present Harris in a flattering light, and Paramount had a merger they wanted to get through the regulators.

So one can imagine Trump's team saw the Telegraph having a meltdown about the editing of the Panorama programme - which again, was broadly fine - and thought..."easy money."

But from the beginning the Beeb has said they would fight this lawsuit to the end. And their lawyers' assertive approach to the case certainly does not give the impression they're in any mood to tell Trump "oh I suppose you're right, here's a few million quid to go away."

‌



There's just very little incentive for them to do so. They don't have a parent company that needs to do business in America. And while they are technically allowed to settle out of court, the BBC is rarely sued, and has a real appetite for defending claims it thinks are weak - not least because any payment would be taken out of licence fee cash. And suddenly the British taxpayer is effectively paying money to the leader of a foreign country over a spurious lawsuit - and it becomes a diplomatic issue.

Meanwhile, Trump has been getting increasingly upset about the BBC doing entirely normal things to fight its case.

See, they've issued summonses to Donald Trump Jr, Ivanka Trump and her husband Jared Kushner to give evidence in the case.

‌



The BBC says all three have personal knowledge of Trump's state of mind on January 6th.

But they've been somewhat reluctant to allow themselves to be served with papers - something that usually has to be done in person in the states. And their secret service protection have declined to facilitate the process.

So the beeb have gone back to the judge to ask for help in making arrangements to get these witnesses to give evidence.

‌



And that's why, on Monday, a spokesperson for Trump's legal team issued a wild statement accusing the BBC of "seeking to harass him, his family, and supporters".

The beeb has now asked the court to allow service of papers to be done by email and certified mail.

What makes this interesting is that in pursuing what he thought would be an easy case of extracting cash from a broadcaster, Trump may have succeeded in prompting a full-scale relitigation of what happened on January 6th - an piece of history he's spent a lot of his second presidency trying to rewrite. This could turn out to be a genuinely massive story when it lands in court next year.

‌



Kim Jong Un

And if all that wasn't enough, Trump is cosying up to North Korean megadictator Kim Jong Un again.

The pair have been talking again. Trump posted a picture of him and Kim taken during his first term - back when a President alienating America's natural allies while cosying up to its enemies was a novel event.

Then on Sunday night he had a direct pop at South Korea, announcing he would be scaling back American involvement in a series of military drills alongside Seoul, and branding the plans "inappropriate and hostile". Trump later explained that his was partly out of revenge for South Korea refusing to help with the war on Iran. Which is not an unreasonable position for South Korea to take, given they get 60% of their oil through the Strait of Hormuz.

‌



And when he was asked about the gruesome twosome rekindling their situationship, Trump casually let slip that North Korea has "57 nukes". Which is something you don't really want to say out loud, especially in front of - as he was - the White House Press Corps and a load of contractors working on his new helipad.

Supremes won't stop Trump's ballroom. Not even in the name of love

Supreme Court Chief Justice John Roberts is allowing the White House to continue construction on President Donald Trump’s $400 million ballroom project for now. Roberts signed a temporary order on Friday allowing work to continue while the court considers an emergency appeal from the Trump administration. Lower courts had ordered a halt to the project, finding that it must have congressional approval.

Honestly, at this point the structure is like 60% built. Even if building it was illegal, what are they going to do? Order Trump to rebuild the East Wing brick by brick?

News.title: Two police officers among seven killed in wrong-way car crash
News.content:
Two police officers were among seven people killed when a car travelling the wrong way down a dual carriageway crashed into a force vehicle.

A Volkswagen Passat with five occupants said to be in their late teens struck an oncoming marked Cleveland Police vehicle on the A66 near Middlesbrough at about 03:39 BST.

The BBC understands a pursuit of the car had ended before the crash, with the police vehicle just happening to be in the South Bank area. The occupants of both cars were pronounced dead at the scene.

The officers have been named as PC Matthew Blades, 37, and PC Tom Clough, 38. Chief Constable Victoria Fuller said they were "brave officers protecting our communities".

She said it was an "incredibly sad day for Cleveland", adding: "No one should leave their home and not return safely.

"These were brave officers protecting our communities and serving our residents, who didn't return home to their families at the end of their shift."

News.title: Video appears to show police chase minutes before fatal A66 crash
News.content:
Security camera footage appears to show several police vehicles chasing a car just minutes before a fatal crash that killed seven people, including two police officers, near Middlesbrough.

The clip is thought to have been filmed on Lime Road at 03:36 BST on Saturday morning, around three minutes before a Volkswagen Passat travelling the wrong way on the A66 nearby collided into a marked police vehicle.

The BBC understands the police car involved in the crash was not part of the pursuit and that the chase had stopped before the collision.

Following a mandatory referral from Cleveland Police, the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) has opened an investigation into the circumstances of the crash.

News.title: Struggling households need more help with bills, energy industry says
News.content:
Higher energy bills this winter mean the government should step in to provide more help for households most in need, the body representing energy firms in the UK has said.

Stubbornly high prices over the last few years have left some people needing "emergency support" over and above the existing Â£150 Warm Home Discount, Energy UK said.

It added that bills were unaffordable for millions and a "better targeted and more agile" support scheme was needed.

On Wednesday, the energy price cap for October onwards will be announced by regulator Ofgem and is expected to hit a three-year high.

"Suppliers continue to do all they can to help their customers but as well as persistently high bills, record levels of debt show how the current system is failing to provide the right support to those in need," Energy UK chief executive Dhara Vyas said.

A new "social discount" scheme would result in "a system that works better for everyone", she added.

Ofgem reported at the end of last winter that customers who had fallen behind on their energy bills owed suppliers a record Â£4.7bn. Since then wholesale energy prices have risen, following the start of the Iran war in February.

Energy consultancy Cornwall Insight predicts Ofgem's cap on household price rises, which is set every three months, will go up by 4% when it is announced on Wednesday.

The rise will apply to household bills during the first half of the coming winter and follows a sharper 13% rise in July.

As well as the conflict in the Middle East, Cornwall Insight said prices had been affected by heatwaves across Europe that had increased demand for power generation to support air conditioning and other cooling.

The price rise would outweigh the impact of Prime Minister Andy Burnham's move to remove VAT on household electricity bills from October, it added.

Currently, people receiving means-tested benefits are entitled to the one-off Â£150 Warm Home Discount over the winter, something administered by the energy suppliers themselves. The rebate is paid for by a levy on all energy users that is collected and redistributed via bills.

Energy UK said the Warm Home Discount reached six million customers, but there were another 2.5 million who needed help because a medical condition or draughty home meant they consumed more energy.

It said if the government would allow the combining of information about customers' income, health and energy consumption, a discount scheme could offer targeted and adjustable support, and respond to changing needs and price levels.

The body said its proposed new scheme would cost Â£1.9bn - nearly double the cost of the current scheme - but could offer Â£450 in support to some households.

Energy UK suggested the new support scheme could continue to be part-funded through bills or shifted entirely onto the taxpayer, via government funding.

The last time the price cap reached a similar level was in July 2023, Cornwall Insight said, which was still below the peaks reached the previous year in the wake of Russia's invasion of Ukraine.

During that energy price spike the Conservative government committed a total of around Â£40bn , externalof government spending to support households with energy bills.

The challenge of combining sources of personal data, including income and health, and the proposal to find more taxpayer money to fund such a scheme are likely to raise questions.

However, Adam Scorer, chief executive of National Energy Action, said this was the sort of approach his charity was calling for, especially as the Warm Home Discount has risen by only Â£10 over the last decade.

"We desperately need a new approach," he said.

"There will be a lot of detail to get right, but if government genuinely wants to provide breathing space for people in fuel poverty, it needs to take this challenge on and work with energy companies and charities to design something truly fit for purpose."

News.title: Lucy Davis 'grateful' for support over cancer diagnosis
News.content:
It was the first time Davis had appeared at a public event since announcing on 11 August that she has stage four breast cancer.

She said in that announcement that it had "metastasised" to her bones following a diagnosis a year-and-half-ago, meaning it was "too late" for chemotherapy.

Davis signed autographs and posed for photographs before appearing on Saturday's panel.

Some fans posing questions told the actress "I love you so much", but she was not asked directly about her health.

The Shaun of the Dead director, Edgar Wright, and Simon Pegg, who played the film's lead role were also on the panel. Davis played Dianne, an aspiring actress who was one of the core group of survivors of the zombie apocalypse, in the cult British movie and helps Pegg's character Shaun fight off the legions of the undead.

Her favourite memories of filming, she said, were "when we all pretended to be zombies and walked across the square; it was like being naughty schoolkids.

"It was a fun time, we went a bit mad."

The actress, who played receptionist Dawn Tinsley in the BBC sitcom The Office and whose father is comedian Jasper Carrott, was also applauded when asked for advice about getting into the film industry.

She said: "We all grow up with a different life with a different world telling us we all have limitations.

"None of us do, our only limitations are things that we think are limiting. We can do anything, or be anybody, and don't apologise for that."

David had thanked fans for their "kindness and support" in another post two days after revealing she had cancer.

"OK, so the last two days have been utterly overwhelming, in that I had zero idea my cancer post would have the attention it did," she said.

"Truly, I am in shock. That said, thank you to everyone for the tremendous amount of kindness and support you have sent me. Good grief it was emotional."

News.title: The hotel booking mix-up that could free mushroom murderer
News.content:
Last July, hundreds descended on Australia's Gippsland region from around the country for the most exciting event on the annual table tennis calendar.

But as elite players vied for medals at the national championships, one of the biggest criminal cases in the nation's history - that of mushroom murderer Erin Patterson - was unfolding just a few kilometres away.

This tournament inadvertently became part of a perfect storm which the triple killer's lawyers are now arguing "fatally undermined" the fairness of her trial.

The jury which condemned Patterson to prison were supposed to be isolated - sheltered from the frenzy surrounding the case while they deliberated.

But accommodation shortages in the region, exacerbated by the table tennis competition, meant they shared a hotel with members of the prosecution, a key police witness, and journalists.

Now Patterson's legal team is trying to overturn her convictions on appeal.

"The only proper remedy is... the order for a re-trial," Patterson's barrister Richard Edney said.

News.title: How a new era of heatwaves could shake up the school calendar
News.content:
Over the past two weeks, the sound of children has returned to Scotland's school playgrounds. Their summer breaks began in late June or early July and ended in mid-August.

It's an academic year replicated in other European countries too.

In England, Wales and Northern Ireland, however, children will not return until early September. Their holidays are a similar length to Scotland's but England and Wales schools did not break up until late July, something that meant pupils were in school during the peak of the early summer heat.

Or at least they were meant to be in school. While it was 30C or more outside, inside many classrooms it felt far hotter. With no air conditioning and limited ventilation, the heat became stifling and more than 1,000 schools across the UK either closed or sent pupils home early before the hottest part of the afternoon. Conditions were particularly challenging for GCSE and Aâlevel students sitting exams during extreme heat.

Baroness Brown, chair of the UK's Climate Change Adaptation committee, has warned that "we know high temperatures can significantly impair concentration and performance" of children in schools.

Back in February 2026, Ofsted's chief inspector Sir Martyn Oliver said the timing of the school holidays should be reconsidered: "It's pretty hot usually in May, June and July, just at the point you're asking children to sit down and take an examâ¦ so I think there is a need to have a good old look at it [the school year]."

The recent hot weather has seen some parents join his call. Andrea Bigger, a parent in London, is "absolutely aware of the dangers" of extreme heat in classrooms. She says her daughter has previously suffered from heat exhaustion and was hospitalised after overheating at her primary school. She is "really concerned that the UK is not ready or prepared for this".

And this summer was not a one off. BBC analysis of temperature data shows a clear shift. In the 1960s, the first 30C day was occurring on average on 13 July. In the 2020s that figure has been 19 June.

News.title: Why we can't look away from hoarder home clean-ups
News.content:
Gordon says the main reason she posts online is to raise awareness, particularly about hoarding disorder and mental health.

According to the NHS, hoarding disorder is a mental health condition, external in which someone collects a lot of things and finds it difficult to get rid of them, even when they negatively affect their daily life.

"I think it's really easy to be quite judgmental," she says.

"People see footage of these homes online and in documentaries, and it's really easy to judge and think the person's lazy.

"There's a lot of stigma behind it and a lot of misunderstanding."

She says the stigma of being a hoarder can stop people from seeking help.

"This is real life. It's mental health. It's people who are finding themselves living in really unsafe, unsanitary conditions through no fault of their own.

"The more we can talk about it, the better. The less we judge, the more we can understand, [and that] is only going to be a good thing."

Gordon says many of her followers are hoarders themselves.

"I get a lot of messages in my inbox saying, 'Thank you so much for your content. That house that you did last week, mine's not dissimilar to that and you're making me feel like I'm not the only one that lives like this'.

"A lot of people have messaged me and said that, because they've seen my videos, they found the courage to ask for help or maybe hire a cleaner.

"So it is having a really positive effect."

Listen to highlights from Lincolnshire on BBC Sounds and Hull and East Yorkshire on BBC Sounds, and watch the latest episode of Look North.

News.title: Trump Mobile promoted a 'Made in the USA' phone - but the details kept changing
News.content:
When Trump Mobile was launched by US President Donald Trump's eldest sons in the summer of 2025, the company advertised that a "T1" smartphone would be built in the US and shipped to customers within months.

Over the last year, key details about the phone's manufacture, design and delivery date have changed, and some customers are still waiting for their phones - as Thomas Copeland explains.

News.title: Baby whose parents feared had just days to live is 'thriving' after life-saving heart operation
News.content:
A baby, whose parents feared had just days to live, is "thriving" after having life-saving operations on his heart.

Macs Green, a previously "completely healthy baby" suffered two cardiac arrests and was diagnosed with dilated cardiomyopathy - which can lead to heart failure.

After a struggle to find suitable hospital beds, he has now had device called a Berlin Heart, external fitted, which takes over the function of his heart.

But he still needs a transplant and doctors have told his parents Catrin and Dylan they do not know how long the wait will be before he gets one.

But, after his operation in Newcastle's Freeman Hospital, Dylan said Macs was already "completely different" from how he was before.

Before surgery he had been in a specialist unit in Bristol Royal Children's Hospital on an extracorporeal membrane oxygenation, external (Ecmo) machine, which helped pump oxygenated blood around his body.

News.title: Vigil held for family who died in sea off Shoreham
News.content:
Alden added: "The way everybody has come together and marked today with this minute's silence, and there were people who met with paddleboards and kayaks over at Kingston Beach as well this morning, it's been a really lovely way to pay to the very sad loss of these lives."

Wesley Horscroft attended on behalf of paddlers in the Kingston beach community.

He said he had originally planned to go out alone and "put some flowers on the water" to honour the family, before he decided to invite others.

"It's kind of grown and a lot of people wanted to turn up to do the same," he said.

He said Saja's death had added an "another layer" to the grief felt in the town.

News.title: Economic adviser O'Neill rules out government job but backs PM's devolution plans
News.content:
Economist Lord Jim O'Neill, who has been advising the prime minister, has said he will not be taking a job in Andy Burnham's government.

As first reported by, external the Financial Times, Lord O'Neill, a crossbench peer who was once a treasury minister under the Conservatives, said he did not want the constraints involved in taking on a formal role.

The former chief economist at Goldman Sachs had been tipped to become Burnham's chief economic adviser.

He said he was enjoying what he was currently doing too much and did not want to have to give up control of his business interests to comply with official rules.

He told BBC Radio 4's Today programme that he had "lots of other things that are going on that I very much enjoy" and, having been a minister before, he knew the job included "all the constraints that understandably go with it, like a blind trust and to abandon everything else you do, never mind the fact that it's 24/7".

In placing shares in blind trusts, ministers have no knowledge of how their investment is being handled, to avoid any potential conflict of interest.

He said he concluded he would rather be a voice to talk to and "get on with the rest of the things in my life".

He earlier told the Financial Times it was "not because of any policy disagreements", adding "I'm a massive fan of the focus on devolution and I hope Andy and his team will be bold on this and everything else."

He pointed to Greater Manchester as an example of economic growth and said if you could repeat that around populated areas, "then national economic performance will improve".

Asked by the BBC whether the new government in the upcoming October budget would need to raise taxes, Lord O'Neill said it was a choice for the prime minister and his team "based on the things they're saying they want to do more of - defence spending is obviously the one that catches the eye", among other things.

Pressed on whether the government could turn to something such as wealth taxes, Lord O'Neill said he was "not a fan of further increases in these kind of taxes, particularly as it relates to capital gains for genuine risk taking things like venture capital".

He noted that the country has boosted government spending "dramatically" in recent years and needed a "more sensible approach to welfare spending under genuine welfare reform".

From 2015-2016, Lord O'Neill was commercial secretary to the Treasury under the then-Chancellor, George Osborne.

The peer, who grew up in Greater Manchester, was a key figure in pushing the Conservatives' Northern Powerhouse agenda, which was aimed at boosting the economy of the North of England.

Lord O'Neill is also known as the economist who coined the term Bric in 2001 to describe leading developing or newly industrialised countries with potential for fast growth and, therefore, investment returns.

The original four nations - Brazil, Russia, India and China - later became the Brics when they were joined by South Africa.

News.title: Welsh county becomes global hotspot for carbon emissions after wildfires
News.content:
A county in Wales had one of the world's highest carbon emissions per square kilometre due to wildfires in July, according to a charity.

The fire above Blaenavon, Torfaen was described as "one of the largest and most challenging" in south Wales in recent years by the fire service.

Save the Children said it was concerned about possible health consequences after data, external published by the European Union's earth observation programme, Copernicus, showed Torfaen behind Malanje in Angola, Spain's Ãvila and Annaba in Algeria in terms of wildfire emissions in July.

Torfaen council said it was unaware of the EU data but its own air quality monitoring showed "elevated particulate concentrations".

A blaze the size of about 300 football pitches broke out on Mynydd Garnclochdy, between Abersychan and Blaenavon, with people reporting smelling smoke about 30 (48km) miles away in Cardiff.

Combined with others across the region it contributed to a major incident being declared, which eventually required assistance from the military.

Blaenavon councillor Janet Jones said the smoke had been "particularly bad" on 13 August - about three weeks after the fire first ignited.

"There was great concern about air quality and the impact on elderly people and those suffering with respiratory issues such as emphysema and COPD."

Jones said she had spoken with GP practice nurses two weeks ago and was not aware of any increase in patients complaining about respiratory problems, but added this "could change in the months ahead".

News.title: Third arrest in murder probe after cyclist punched
News.content:
A third person has been arrested as part of a murder investigation following the death of a "loving and loyal" man in Leicester.

George Glover, 27, was punched as he cycled along Narborough Road, close to the junction with Noel Street, at about 06:30 BST on Monday, Leicestershire Police said. He died in hospital on Thursday.

A 24-year-old man was arrested on suspicion of conspiracy to commit murder on Friday and remains in custody.

A 31-year-old man and 39-year-old woman, who were previously arrested on suspicion of robbery and conspiracy to commit murder, also remain in custody, the force said.

In a tribute released by police on Friday, Glover's family said they were "so proud of the young man he'd become".

They said: "George was a much-loved son and big brother to his three siblings. His loss is already felt so deeply."

Officers from the East Midlands Special Operations Unit are continuing to appeal for anyone who may be able to assist with their inquiries to get in touch.

Det Insp Kevin Hames said: "If you can help but haven't yet contacted us, please be assured it's not too late and anything you're able to provide â including any footage â could be vital to our investigation."

News.title: Hidden museum gallery to reopen after 83 years
News.content:
A gallery that has remained closed to the public since World War Two is to reopen at London's Natural History Museum next month.

The gallery, which has remained hidden from view since 1943, will reopen from 16 September, featuring 50 objects which show our evolving relationship with the natural world.

The exhibition, named Nature and Us, is part of a transformation project called NHM150, which aims to open a new or revamped showcase every year until the museum's 150th anniversary in 2031.

Dr Doug Gurr, director of the NHM, said: "For the first time in over 80 years, visitors will be able to step into this beautiful historic space and explore our changing relationship with the natural world."

News.title: Blue plaque unveiled at home of Paddington creator
News.content:
The unveiling of a blue plaque at the former Surrey home of Paddington Bear creator Michael Bond was a "lovely" occasion with an unexpected surprise, the organiser has said.

Bond, who died in 2017 at the age of 91, moved to Fairacre in Haslemere in 1968, where he spent the next 10 years writing several Paddington books alongside the scripts for the original television series.

The unveiling on Saturday took place with the permission of current owners, Steph and Neil Stephenson, and was attended by Bond's daughter, Karen Jankel, who presented them with a special gift.

"It was the [Paddington] Bear that was Karen's as a child," Haslemere Society chairman Chris Harrison said.

News.title: Two men re-arrested after death of soldier
News.content:
Two men have been re-arrested on suspicion of manslaughter after the body of a soldier was found in a river.

Northumbria Police recovered the body of Liam Potts, 22, who served with the Coldstream Guards, close to Wylam Bridge on 18 August.

Prior to his disappearance in the early hours of 15 August, the force said it received reports of a disturbance at The Boathouse pub and a subsequent collision at the bridge between a car and group of pedestrians. Police are investigating whether the incidents are linked to the soldier entering the water.

Two men, aged 22 and 23, have been re-arrested on suspicion of manslaughter and released on bail as inquiries continue.

A man and woman, both in their 20s, sustained serious but not life-threatening injuries in the collision.

The woman has since been discharged, while the man remains in hospital for further treatment.

Police said the soldier was on the bridge at the time of the collision, but was not in the car or hit by it, yet entered the water "within minutes" of it happening.

News.title: Karmelo Anthony’s bid for new trial is denied by judge in murder case of high school track star
News.content:

A Texas judge denied a new trial for Karmelo Anthony on Saturday in the stabbing death of a 17-year-old athlete at a high school track meet, a killing that drew national attention and led to harassment of the families.

Anthony, 19, was convicted of murder in June and sentenced to 35 years in prison for the April 2025 killing of Austin Metcalf, 17.

Judge Michael Chitty denied the retrial motion in a half-page order following a two-day hearing this week near Dallas, citing a review of the evidence and arguments. He did not elaborate.

Russell Wilson, Anthony's attorney, said the defense would appeal.

“Our commitment to our client has not changed,” Wilson said. “We will continue to advocate vigorously on his behalf through every lawful avenue available.”

A Texas judge denied a new trial for Karmelo Anthony on Saturday in the stabbing death of a 17-year-old athlete at a high school track meet, a killing that drew national attention and led to harassment of the families ( Texas Department of Criminal Justice )

Prosecutor Bill Wirskye defended the trial as fair this week.

“We respect, and expected, the court’s decision denying the motion for a new trial,” Collin County District Attorney Greg Willis said after the denial was announced. “The jury’s guilty verdict stands, and we remain confident in the process. Every defendant has the right to appeal, and our thoughts and prayers remain with the Metcalf family in the painful wake of last week’s hearing.”

Anthony’s attorneys also demanded a retrial because they said trial judge John Roach’s courtroom rules were so strict that they limited the public’s access to the proceedings. And in asking for Roach's recusal, they noted that he gave a posttrial interview with a Dallas TV station in which he said the jury “got it right.”

Roach said his rules were necessary for a fair trial, and prosecutors insisted he did nothing wrong.

The case attracted widespread attention in part because of a flood of social media posts that amplified the killing in racial terms. Anthony is Black; Metcalf was white. Lawyers on both sides, however, told jurors that the case had nothing to do with race.

Jurors rejected Anthony’s claims that he was defending himself during a confrontation with Metcalf in the bleachers of the track meet.
