World.title: Inside Gusau’s ‘rotten’ NFF, by Patrick Omorodion
World.content:
Patrick Omorodion

There is no story trending in Nigeria’s sports circle today that interests Nigerian football fans as the call on the leadership of the Nigeria Football Federation, NFF to either resign or not to bother to seek to return in the next election.

Mainstream and social media platforms are buzzing with stories on what has happened or about to happen to the outgoing board of the NFF headed by Ibrahim Musa Gusau.

Stakeholders like Chief Segun Odegbami, Dr. Danladi Bako, Barrister Godwin Dudu-orumen and Tony Ubani, editor of Sporting Vanguard are all of the opinion that Gusau and his clique have no moral right to seek reelection. Another strong voice that is singing the same song, London-based anti-corruption crusader in football, Osasu Obayiuwana has joined them.

Obayiuwana, a renowned former BBC sports correspondent, has worked closely with the NFF at committee levels and knows much about the shenanigans going on there.

In his reaction to an inquiry on the NFF brouhaha, Obayiuwana retorted, “I know you folks want me to give you chapter and verse on all that is happening.

But to be honest, I’m fed up of talking….”.

The crusader spirit in him however, didn’t allow him to “siddon look”, apologies late Chief Bola Ige, so he voiced his mind in these words:

”As a member of the NFF governance reform committee, between 2018 and 2020, I said all that needs to be said, about what must be done to put the filthy house of Nigerian football in order. The NFF during Pinnick Amaju’s time, of which Ibrahim Musa Gusau was also a board and congress member, threw our well thought out recommendations into the dustbin.

Seyi Akinwunmi, then NFF first VP and the chair of our committee, will testify that I asked the NFF secretariat, during one of our sessions, for its organogram, in order for me to analyse organisational flow and the general chain of command. Do you know that they could not give this to me for three months, despite repeated requests? And when they did, they sent me a pathetic scrap of paper that said nothing. That told me everything I needed to know about the quality of NFF governance.

At the laughable NFF fact-finding committee, headed by Fanny Amun, coach (Austin) Eguavoen and Justin Madugu have been spitting fire over the last few days, about their frustrations of working for the federation.

But Madugu has not helped himself by only talking about his challenges after the Super Falcons crashed out of the Wafcon. Why did he not speak in the months before the competition? I hear that he is also owed years of wages, since he joined the team as an assistant coach in 2022.

Eguavoen is also complaining about how he is not enabled to do his job as Technical Director, because he is not given the required material support. But did he let the Nigerian public know? And shouldn’t he have done? Did Nigerians not see how Paolo Maldini and Leonardo swiftly resigned from the FIGC (Italian Football Federation), when the president interfered and disrespected their work?

During the 2024 AFCON in Côte D’Ivoire, I had a conversation with Ibrahim Musa Gusau at Hotel Ivoire in Abidjan. He asked me why I criticise him in public and do not counsel him privately, over my misgivings about the management of Nigerian football.

I had to robustly remind him that as a journalist and governance analyst, it is my responsibility to report the issues for the public’s notice. And while I was happy to tell him some things privately, it is not in my job description to be anyone’s courtier or supplicant.

Nigeria has brilliant, world-class people that can run football properly. But until the country’s football institutions are restructured to enthrone merit, competence and integrity, its football will remain in the deep, dark night and will remain in the hands of mediocre people. I have been saying this for decades now. But do the people that really matter listen? You all know the answer to that.” Another stakeholder in the pen profession who believes enough is enough to end the corruption in the NFF, which to a large extent, has contributed to the decline of football is Sylvanus Ofekun.

He wrote, “On record, no NFF administration has enjoyed the kind of financial windfall that the Gusau board has enjoyed. Beyond the ₦17 billion released in January 2024, the federation has received multiple intervention funds from the Federal Government, FIFA Forward funds, CAF grants, and sponsorship monies running into several billions. Yet with all this inflow, there is little or nothing to show for it. Both the male and female national teams have failed to qualify for the World Cup.

Age-grade teams have been absent from major tournaments. Training camps are poorly organized, foreign-based players are owed, and domestic league clubs are struggling.

The Super Falcons are currently in the Court of Arbitration for Sport, CAS, with the NFF over unpaid bonuses and entitlements, an issue that has been deliberately blocked from entering mainstream media.”

Nigerians have forgotten that in 2005, Alhaji Ibrahim Galadima’s only sin was that the Super Eagles failed to qualify for the 2006 World Cup. He had no financial scandals hanging on his neck like the present administrators, yet he was booted out.

Twenty years after, and after missing two consecutive World Cup Finals, those who shouted “crucify Galadima” then, and are responsible for the embarrassing performance of all our national teams and are being investigated for financial misdeeds are telling Nigerians that they deserve another term in office.

And we ask, for what ? For destroying Nigeria’s football ? Or for the misapplication of a humongous N17 billion and other intervention funds the federal government made available for the various national teams?

World.title: The pluralistic relativism of critics and criticisms
World.content:
By Bobson Gbinije

“Criticism is a disinterested endeavor to learn/And propagate the best that is known and thought in the World.” Mathew Arnold (1822-1888) Essays in Criticism.

In his poem, The Volunteer Day, C. Lewis took an emotional and retrospective glance at the travails, trauma and tribulations of the volunteers of war for ancient England. “It was not fraud or foolishness, glory, revenge or pay! We came because our eyes could see no other way. There was no other way to keep man’s flickering truth alight; these stars will witness that our course burned briefer, not less brighter.” So also the altruistic zeitgeist of these patriots. They stood between Scylla and Charybdis, Critics and Kill –sports, but with dogged pertinacity, the punctiliousness of a Spaniard and Trojan perseverance, they were able to move mankind forward.But,critics were their best friends and their worst enemies in the journey.

Man is imperfect, perfection is nowhere within the purview of man – hence imperfection is a uniovular twin with man. Giving this state of imperfection –mistakes, defects, shortfalls, indispositions, and even death becomes a concomitant of man and his activities. Longfellow asserted that “No man is an Island unto himself.” In the light of this, social, political, cultural and educational engineering heightened a concatenation of events that gave rise to “The Society” and “The Social Contract.” In professions, men, women, students and critics contribute their quota towards ensuring a viable “social contract.” Ideally, the critic is the argo-eyed spectator who sees a better part of the game. He mirrors-in and mirrors-out activities through communication engineering, information technology and information management, seeing the world as a global village.

A critic should have a profound and all- embracing understanding of his profession and goings-on in society and the world, to enable him form informed opinions and views. A critic, say in “Architecture” must have and know the nuts and bolts of the architectural profession, the basics of “Architectonics” – construction, designs, planning, framework, and style and History of designs. He should have hindsight, cognate experience, formal and informal training. He should be master of situations and not situations mastering him.

Karl Popper, a foremost authority on criticism asserts in his book: The Open Society and its Enemies – chapters 22,23 and 24 and Conjectures and Refutations” chapter 10 [Rout ledge and kegan Paul, 1963] that “the institutionalisation of criticism is the basic precondition of improving social and political theories and society.” Popper recognises that politically, there are good and bad rulers and also good and bad critics, but that in any situation, criticism must be institutionalised. Which good critic will want to work under a bad or dictatorial ruler and vice-versa? The courage or foolhardiness of the critic is brought to the fore here.

A good critic must espouse the good course to enable society move forward. The Aristotelian concept of the pursuit of the greatest good for the largest number should be his diadem and garlands of honour with which he is festooned even unto death. Is there such a critic? “Few.” A critic is a human being and unless he is given the enabling environment, he cannot appropriately deliver. Though many have climbed to the pinnacle of martyrdom in it and they changed the world for the better.

No critic would have liked to work against Hitler during the slaughtering of the Jews, Idi Amin Ðada of Uganda, Hastings Kamuzu Banda, Stalin, Mobutu, Abacha and Tsars of Soviet Russia, etc.

Apart from dictatorship, another problem the critic faces is lack of tools to do his work and democracy. But he should not develop, in Marxian dialectics, “An inverted attitude to an inverted world.” The profession and every facet of life is literally closed because there is no mirroring-out. There is communication Erebus as there is no way to get information except from government propaganda machinery and literary hirelings. Nobody knows what is going on except what they want you to know. Wherever information is hoodwinked, teleguided and unnecessarily classified, it precipitates information imperialism, news autocracy and the messiah complex.

This first tool of a good critic, be it in philosophy, politics, Religion, Mathematics, the Arts and the sciences etc. is the “fact” yes the raw facts. Not deductive and speculative reasoning, researched and proven truth.

This is the one basis and inobliterable plinth on which the “Art” of Criticism” rotates. A critic must be an effervescence of information and not exiguous of it. He should not hide under the “capacious umbrella” of generalisation, social forces, livid analogy, kierkgard’s existentialist determinant, bias and subjectivity.

If he appears as a newspaper columnist, commentator, an arbiter, wine connoisseur, book reviewer, arts pundit, an expositor in a colloquium, seminar and symposia, an evaluator, a judge of formal standard, professional analyst and an authority on the subject, then he is a critic.

The Veiled Haunting Stench in criticism

I read, listen to your criticisms our leaders often tell us.But, continue to luxuriate in administrative lapses and inertia.A critic is therefore inextricably intertwined with society’s development as a watch dog and balancing pedestal.

But when a critic resorts to being a paid hack, pen-outrage, an animadversions, Bad press, brickbats, disparaging flak, querulous fault-finder, a detractor, Momus and stricture-possessed, then, there is paradigm shift and normative gap in the practice, he is a bad critic, but in a bad society, he is a “Heroic Critic” – the plural impasse.

The French philosopher, Rene Descartes asked himself “what is it that we know certainly? The answer is obvious. But he asked conclusively that hewas certain he could think and from that, he inferred his existence- cogito ergo sum [I think: therefore I exist]. So also do I wish to state with unmistakable exactitude that society has bad and good critics, but a pot-pouri of bad governments and the larger society made them what they are!

Since perfection is outside the reach of man, what is the middle of the road approach and personality of the “Dynamic critic” of the modern era that will be able to move society forward. It is an unacceptable over simplification to assert that he is either good or bad. No, that betrays uncompromising intransigence. He should be near-good or near bad not perfectly bad or perfectly good.

In his Ideology and Utopia, Professor K. Mannheim was greatly rebuffed by Dr. Bhikhu Parekh, lecturer, Department of Political Studies, University of Hull for his taking Sociology of Knowledge as his answer to Ideology and criticism.

He asserted”………….like moral ideals that cannot all be achieved these demands cannot all be met. In heightening up its concept or achieving comprehensiveness, a theory or criticism may lose in empirical richness. In trying to be “absolutely accurate” it might become as chaotic as the reality itself losing in coherence what it gains in suggestiveness.

As no criticism possess all the qualities one ideally expects in it, beyond a certain point, the choice between them is a matter of individual discretion. Objectivity or partiality, therefore is not the only or even always the highest virtue in criticism. If a discipline is dominated by a single body of assumptions that its professionally socialised practitioners unconsciously assume to be self-evidently true, there is much to be said for advancing or accepting an extreme criticism in order to stir them into critical self-re-examination and to encourage a radical reappraisal of the concepting tools of the discipline since objectivity and impartiality are achieved as a result of the clash of subjectivity and partiality , falsehood and extremism often make most worthwhile contributions to the discovery of “truth”.

Dennis J.O . Haan in his treatise “HASTY CONCLUSIONS” said “ A Persian King wanted to teach his four sons never to make rash judgment. So he told the eldest to go in winter to see a mango tree, the next to go in spring, the third in summer and the youngest in fall , after the last son had returned from his autumn visit, the king called them together to describe what they had observed. “It looks like a burnt old stump said the eldest”. No “said the second, “ it is lacy green”. The third described it as “beautiful as a rose., the youngest said, “No ,its fruit is like a pear”. Each is right, “said the king”, for each of you saw the tree in a different season “. This didactic jeremiad serves to caution the critic,that given the multi-dimensionality of thought we can only see a portion of the truth at any point in time and hence can not be “completely Right.

The “Dynamic critic” of the modern era should be able to develop a comprehensive basis of vision , a dynamic and synthetic viewpoint that encompasses, explaining and integrates conflicting perspectives with truth and the love of society as the signet of his actions. Critics have always been buffeted by parochialism in government. Religion and philosophical cycles etc Socrates, Plato, Aristotle ,Isaac Newton, Galileo,, Sigmund Freud, Hobbes, Locke, kant, Voltaire, Helvetius, Bentham and Adam Smith were Victims.

Why do men criticize? There are two schools of thought in this regards. One says men generally do what they do because of selfish interest and the other says for the general good.

In the psychological theory of human interest and action as initiated by Hobbes, refined by Locke , and perfected by the thinkers of the French Enlightenment. Man , it was argued, was essentially a practical being, to make the world a habitable place.

Reason, it was argued further, was set in motion by Human desires; indeed, it was created by desires, so that the more a man desired the greater the stimulus he had to think and therefore the greater his reason .As Voltaire in his “Treatise on Metaphysics” remarked “the passions are the wheels which make all these machines go round”. Vauvenargues reflected the same attitude in his “introduction to knowledge of Human mind”. When he concluded that the true Nature of man did not lie in reason but in passions. Helvetius observed in his “Treatise on man” that reason in itself was insert and was set in motion only by desire.

Bentham argued, further, that of all Human passions the concern for personal interest was the most powerful, most important, most uniform, most lasting and most general. Adam Smith corroborates this view in his belief that it is natural for man to prefer himself to mankind; indeed, he argued that this desire comes with us from the womb and never leaves until we die.

It is clear, that, man acts out of personal interest, but in some cases man acts out of a genuine desire to improve his kind and move the world forward.

In all, the critic’s endeavours,let him allow conscience, nurtured by truth to be his guiding light.The English Playwright William Shakespeare agrees thus, “To thine own self be true, and it must follow as the night the day. Thou canst not then be false to any man”, for it is only this that can salvage the critic from the “plural impasse” and lay bare the pluralistic relativism of criticisms and critics.

World.title: Delta 2027: Why Ogboru will disappoint critics
World.content:
Ogboru

By Benson Ndokwe

Come 2027 in Delta State, it will be liberation time for Deltans when Chief Great Ovedje Ogboru and his African Democratic Congress (ADC) win the governorship election. Many critics will be taken aback while others will be astounded for somebody who has been written off. And so shall it be as Ogboru is a game changer.

The hidden truths about Delta politics will be unveiled. He will set the motion for an accelerated growth of the state while expanding the scope and numbers of those benefiting from the so-called dividends of democracy.

Ultimately, it is Deltans that will benefit as the sole aim of Ogboru is to see a greater number of Deltans crossing the poverty index. Deltans must not follow the old and usual pattern of voting during the 2027 elections.

They must vote for change enmass, no matter the monetary inducement. Regardless of tribe or religion, Deltans must do the needful in ensuring that Ogboru wins the guber election.

It is only when this is done that the gains and benefits of democracy will accrue to the people. Deltans have suffered for too long a time despite its huge oil and gas deposits and also being one of the country’s greatest contributors to our Gross Domestic Product – GDP.

It is my fervent prayers that God should open the eyes of Deltans to collectively deviate from their business as usual and vote in Ogboru to kick-start the needed change in the politics of the state.

Ogboru knows what the state truly lacks. He knows the inadequacies bedeviling the affairs of the state. Hence, he will pilot the affairs of the state in a pivotal way to attract the much sought-after Foreign Direct Investments. The state shall become a hub of industrialization and manufacturing, which will mean the creation of jobs for our teeming jobless youths. This will, in turn, increase the economic profile of the state. Clusters of cottage industries would be established in all the nooks and crannies of the state. Deltans should come out en masse on election day to make this change possible.

It was PLATO who said, “One of the penalties for refusing to participate in politics is that you end up being governed by your inferiors.” Furthermore, Socrates said, “the wise who refuse to rule should prepare to suffer the rules of idiots.”

Those who write off Ogboru are doing so at their own peril. His popularity across the length and breadth of Delta state is spreading like a wild fire. This can only be likened to the Finger of God upon his life.

Women empowerment shall be given the necessary attention it deserves because of the motherly roles women play in society.

The 2027 elections in Delta State should be given a level playing ground for free and fair elections without intimidation and other negative vices as witnessed in past elections. Candidates should be free to canvass for votes from the electorates.

If this is done, then it will be goodbye to bad riddance while we welcome the peoples general to take his rightful position in the governance of the state.

•Ndokwe lives in Agbor, Delta State

World.title: Governance not guns will secure West Africa
World.content:
By Lawal Farouq

A recent West Africa Security Retreat has warned that lasting peace will come not from firepower but from accountable institutions, resilient governance, and the trust of citizens.

West Africa has been fighting insecurity for decades, yet the region remains trapped in a cycle of violence. Extremist groups regroup after defeats, criminal networks adapt faster than governments, and communities liberated by force relapse into instability.

The retreat, which was held in Ilisan-Remo, Ogun State, was not another ceremonial gathering. Convened by the Amandla Institute for Policy and Leadership Advancement in partnership with the Open Society Foundations, it was a sober reckoning.

The answer that emerged was both simple and profound. Military strength remains indispensable, but it cannot by itself deliver lasting stability. Peace will endure only when governments build institutions that citizens trust, deliver justice and opportunity, and restore confidence in the state. For too long, West Africa has approached insecurity primarily as a military challenge. Troops are deployed, defence budgets expanded and sophisticated weapons procured. These responses are necessary, but battlefield victories rarely translate into durable peace.

The discussions reinforced another reality that policymakers can no longer afford to ignore: insecurity flourishes where governance fails. Equally compelling was the argument that intelligence must evolve beyond reacting to attacks. Increasingly, success should be measured not by how effectively governments respond after violence occurs but by how consistently they prevent it.

West Africa is hardly lacking in institutions. ECOWAS has established early warning systems, peace frameworks, and collective response mechanisms over many years. The greater challenge has been inconsistent implementation, inadequate financing, and wavering political commitment.

The Dialogue also exposed another uncomfortable reality. The region’s strategic environment is changing rapidly. Terrorism, organised crime, and illicit trafficking recognise neither borders nor political disagreements.

Modern conflicts are fought not only on battlefields but also in the information space. Winning public trust, therefore, requires credible, transparent, and consistent communication. Perhaps the Dialogue’s greatest contribution was its insistence that security should ultimately be measured by human outcomes rather than military statistics. The Amandla Dialogue did not produce dramatic declarations. It reminded policymakers that armies may reclaim territory, but only effective institutions can secure peace.

West Africa cannot shoot its way to peace. It must govern its way there. Military strength will remain essential, but lasting stability will depend just as much on accountable governance, resilient institutions, economic opportunity, and the confidence citizens place in the state.

World.title: Inter-generational conversations, by Bisi Adeleye-Fayemi
World.content:
I recently held mentoring sessions with three separate groups of young feminists and women’s rights activists. There were some questions that came up in every session. I am sharing a brief summary here.

What personal values have remained constant for you, and how have they shapedthe way you lead, influence, and build movements?

I have always passionately believed in the right to equality of opportunity and non-discrimination in all spheres of life. Next is the right to a voice. You need a voice toraise concerns, advocate,and demand accountability. One of the first things you do to take away someone’s power is to deprive them of a voice. When someone lacks a voice, they have no personhood, dignity, or respect. They live in fear. To address marginalisation and exclusion, people need the right to space – to think, read, write, organise, share ideas, and build solidarity. We can complain all we like as individuals, but things do not change without joint action.

What does it truly mean to live Feminist values?

First, you need to be clear about what Feminism means. Feminism is a global struggle against all forms of patriarchal oppression. It is about affirming that women are complete human beings.Feminism is a movement against systems of oppression and injustice, not against individual men. You can have a wonderful father, husband, brother, but still suffer within an unjust system that deprives you of rights.

Second, be the change you want to see.I recently saw a video of a man who locked up his wife in his windowless shop. Fortunately, an onlooker had seen him do this, so when the woman started to bang on the door, the witness summoned help and broke the locks. An adult male locked up his wife in a public place. What he does to her in the privacy of their home can only be imagined. A feminist knows what women go through and what we need to change. We are abused, exploited, and minimised. We should therefore not be seen abusing, exploiting, and minimising others. We need to embody this on a daily basis. Examples are the way we bring up our children. We should not be the ones encouraging our sons to become entitled consumers of women’s labour and sacrifices. We should avoid teaching our daughters that abuse is normal. Since many of us balance personal and professional obligations, we rely on others such as nannies, maids, drivers, to ease our burdens. We need to treat them well, otherwise we are perpetuating the cycle of patriarchal oppression, the abused abusing others.

I also believe that women should build their own tables. Nigerian women are resilient, self-reliant, and value-adding. Do not be the woman who is asked, what do you bring to the table?You must build your own table, then nobody will have the audacity to ask you such a stupid question. You cannot challenge patriarchy if you are dependent on crumbs from a table. This is not about pride or being overbearing. It is about knowing your own value and worth. No man wants to be with a liability. Any man that stops you from working or improving yourself is a weapon fashioned against you. Learn financial literacy, invest in the things that matter, and let your goal be showing up not showing off.

One of the ways in which we can live feminist values is to work with others to bring about change. Advocacy for inclusion, protection, accountability, are examples. The more people you work with, the better your chances of success. Everywhere is an advocacy site for a feminist – the home, workplace, community, place of worship, sports, school.All the gains we celebrate today as women have been made possible by feminist analysis and activism, even when we do not get the credit. Also, work with men as allies when you can find them. Men are well placed to encourage other men to do things differently.

How can Feminist Leaders remain principled, accountable, and compassionate, while leading through complex and difficult spaces?

You need to know your context. What is going on in the country or community where you live? There is a simple strategic thinking and planning tool called PESTEL.This looks at the Political, Economic, Social, Technological, Environmental and Legal issues that affect your area of analysis. What is the political environment like? Is it a fledgling or mature democracy, military rule,or dictatorship? Is it a country in conflict or post-conflict?Is there an economic boom or is there a crisis that is pushing people into multi-dimensional poverty? What aresocial drivers? What is going on with technology, is it making life easier or more difficult? For example, digital technology and the rise in technology-facilitated violence against women or Artificial Intelligence and implications for the labour market. Concerning the environmental factors – is your community plagued with exploitation of your natural resources, is it responsible for conflict? What is the legal environment like, are there laws that protect the rights of women? is there access to justice for victims of abuse? Your leadership should be relevant to your context, and you need to know how to navigate accordingly. This will point you in the direction of relevant programs, partners,and allies.

You also need to learn how to use data to frame or challenge narratives.One of the numerous lies patriarchy tells feminists is that we do not know what we are talking about. It is all in our imagination. We are emotional and sentimental. Read widely, do your research, and have relevant data at your fingertips. For example, one in three Nigerian women suffers from one form of gender-based violence or the other. The national prevalence rate for Female Genital Mutilation in Nigeria is 15-20%. The national prevalence of HIV is 1.3-1.4%, that is 2 million people, one of the highest HIV burdens in the world. Nigerian women have 3% representation in the National Assembly, no Female Governors, and 14 States where there is no female in the State House of Assembly. There is nothing emotional about this data, these are the lived realities of women whose lives need to change before we can record any meaningful progress or development.

As a feminist leader, you have to play your role to make sure women and girls are safe. Women’s safety and bodily integrity is non-negotiable. Do not be used to compromise justice or the well-being of another woman. Never be one of those to ask, what was she wearing?Never find yourself colluding with predators and those who abuse their positions.

As a feminist leader, you should use your platformas effectively as possible. Whenever you have a platform, ask yourself, ‘What do I want to leave behind? How do I use this platform to make a difference?’

What are your thoughts about Feminism on social media?

Feminism did not start on social media, and it will not die on social media. Feminists have used digital technology for movement building, rapid response, learning and skills, entrepreneurship, mentoring, coaching, philanthropy, and other endeavours. Social media platforms have created employment and wealth. We need to build on all these positive online practices. We, however,need to combat misogyny, digital violence, and cyber-bullying. The most painful part of all this is seeing women bullying other women online, as if the online violence and intimidation from men is not enough. If this persists, we are going to raise a generation of young people who have no compassion or empathy. We also need to note that Misandry (hatred of men) is not a Feminist agenda, although it is not hard to see why men are hated. I am opposed to misandry the same way I am opposed to misogyny (hatred of women) and internalised misogyny (women projecting misogynist behaviour on toother women). I want to see a world that is free, equal, and fair.

What other leadership lessons would you like to share with us as young people?

Leadership is a journey thatlasts a lifetime. There are many skills, capacities, and aptitudes you will pick up along the way. You will succeed and you might fail. You might fall, but you will get up. You will encounter many friends, enemies, and frenemies. You have to be prepared to give your best and have the resilience to handle the worst. Remember that even though some exhibit leadership capacities from an early age, leaders are mostly nurtured, building on strengths and minimising weaknesses. To be a successful leader today, your skills, qualifications and experience might get you through the door, but it is Emotional Intelligence that will keep you in the room. How you treat others, show compassion, respect and build bridges will stand you in good stead.If you are a person of faith, hold on to it. It will give you hope, a compass, and bring you peace. However, do not fall into the hands of those I call ‘spiritual merchants’. They can ruin your life.

Inter-generational conversations are a critical part of movement-building, and it is important for us to learn, teach and share across generations. No one knows everything, we all need each other.

World.title: Parents who think their children are the greatest!
World.content:
By Bunmi Sofola

RECENTLY, Frieda, the head of a leading private school, lamented that modern parents are praising their children to the hilt and bringing up their daughters as if they can do no wrong. She argued that being showered with too much praise and too many presents is not a good thing for a child creating an inability to take risks because of the fear of failure. As a result, she said, girls are turning into little princesses, who lack the resilience to handle criticism or take life’s natural knocks.

Joke, in her 30s and a lawyer, said as someone who grew up with an adoring mother, she was inclined to agree with friends. “My mother doted on me,” she said.

“She was warm, affectionate, supportive and loving and I became full of myself. Even today, in my 30s, the messages of those early years – and that lover-inflated opinion I had of myself – still resonate. My mother’s constant assurances that I was brilliant led me to stumble early on in my law career through naive overconfidence, and her insistence that I was beautiful did not tally with my fat and big-bum reality. As a consequence, I have been left with life-long issues about my body.

‘My mother, a quite’ successful lawyer herself hated leaving me with the house-helps. Luckily, her job was flexible and she often took me with her along with a maid. She often felt guilty about working long hours and her divorce from my father when I was five meant she suffered a high dose of guilt. She wanted to play the role of both parents. This, combined with her unconditional love made for a potent mix, and I was more buoyed up by my mother than I deserved to be.

“My father used to complain she spoilt me, and to compensate he was harsh bothering on being cruel. By the time my parents divorced I already suspected I wasn’t as marvellous as my mum had led me to believe. It was probably lucky that my father had always been less dazzled by me than she was, otherwise, I might have become insufferable. I was convinced by then that I was neither thin nor beautiful. My mother always told me I had great legs, but I knew I didn’t. My thighs have always been closer together because of my weight, so I became fixated on my appearance, always on one crazy diet or the other. Through it all, I never blamed my mother. She believed I was beautiful and thought that telling me so was a kind thing to do an ego booster for me.

Was it a good thing or a bad thing my mother’s encouragement? Who knows? It was certainly given in the spirit of love and belief. As a parent, it is hard to strike the right balance as I’m now discovering with my own four children. We are told that children’s confidence and self-esteem are largely down to their parents, especially in the early years, but these characteristics are increasingly fragile and rare. To help our children develop them, we must praise them. But for praise to work, it must be the right kind, at the right time.

“I know I forget to praise my children enough when they deserve or need it. I praise them on automatic pilot when I do remember, or I do it in a way that is overbearing and embarrassing.

“My biggest fear is that my children become spoilt as I in those early years of my life when I was a little princess. I know I don’t always succeed in pitching my praise perfectly, but I’m improving. The ideal way of praising my children remains a work in progress, but I’m hoping I will get it right enough to prevent them becoming little brats”.

Looking After Your Bones Isn’t Only For The Elderly

During the first 25 to 30 years of life, your bones build up to their peak strength. They then ‘draw’ on this strength as you get older. Look after your bones by steering clear of these common bone breakers.

DODGY DIETS: Statistics show being underweight is a common cause of bone deterioration in women in their 20s. To build stronger bones you need a diet that gives you sufficient calcium, which is essential for bone development, and vitamin D, which is necessary for the intestinal absorption of calcium. Excessive dieting denies your body of many good-for-you fats. It can also lead to missing periods, which causes a decline in the levels of oestrogen and other hormones produced by the ovaries – all of which are vital for the maintenance of bone density. Eat a healthy, balanced diet that includes good sources of calcium, such as low-fat dairy products (skimmed milk, yoghurt and cheese), dark-green and leafy vegetables such as broccoli and spinach, and foods that are fortified with calcium, such as All Bran Flakes.

FIZZY DRINKS: Carbonated drinks contain phosphoric acid, which can weaken bones by removing calcium. Plus, each time you choose a fizzy drink, you miss out on the benefits of healthier alternatives. Steer clear of caffeine-based fizzy drinks, too, as excessive caffeine hinders calcium absorption. Rather choose bone-friendly drinks such as low-fat milk, soya milk, smoothies or orange juice.

PROTEIN OVERLOAD: Protein is essential for the growth and repair of body tissue, but too much protein – particularly animal protein causes your body to ‘steal’ calcium from your bones to neutralise that acid. Health guru and author of The New Joy of Beauty (Random House), Leslie Kenton, says protein-heavy diets plays strong role in the genesis of osteoporosis. So, eat more fruit and vegetables – they do contain some acid, but they also have buffers that neutralise acid.

SMOKING AND DRINKING: Need another reason to quit? Smoking accelerates bone loss as it contributes to less efficient calcium absorption and lowers oestrogen levels. Nicotine’s the main culprit as it interferes with oxygen supply to bones and has a toxic effect on bone cells. It also slows the production of new bone-forming cells (osteoblasts) and impedes bone metabolism. Studies show that the bones of smokers have inferior biochemical properties to those of non-smokers and are therefore more likely to break. Quitting smoking will increase the level of oxygen in the blood and reduce the level of toxins, giving your bones the chance to build up strength. You may want to curb your drinking too – more than two glasses of wine a day can increase your chances of having weaker bones.

A STRESSFUL LIFE-STYLE: To cope with stress, your body requires extra energy in the form of glucose, so it releases a hormone called cortisol. ‘Cortisol causes your muscles to release protein so that glucose can be made’, says Dr. Michael Elstein, author of Eternal Health (Struik). ‘This leads to the gradual disappearance of muscle bulk and causes bones to lose mineral content.’ It is therefore important to reduce your stress levels. Exercising will do this – and it’ll help strengthen your bones. Weight-bearing exercise such as tennis, kick boxing and running is especially good for your bones.

CERTAIN MEDICATIONS: Some prescription drugs interfere with calcium absorption. These include diuretics, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, steroid-containing asthma medications and various antibiotics. Before taking new medication, find out whether it could interfere with calcium absorption. If it does, and you must take it, ask a doctor how best you can compensate for this.

World.title: Cross River: Who is bullying who? By Tonnie Iredia
World.content:
The public perception in Nigeria that the federal government is intimidating all the opposition political parties is well amplified. Indeed, many people believe that the goal is to turn the country into a one-party state-a battle that has been made to look like a federal project as if not much of it is happening in the states. In reality however, it is in the states that political intimidation is more active and patently visible. Beyond skirmishes at political rallies where official thugs can successfully disrupt political events by opposition parties, law enforcement agencies are used at will to silence opposition activists and critics. In some states, no one dares to say anything negative about a governor.

Only last week, the nation woke up to the harassment of citizen Denis Odama, a public commentator of Cross River origin who constantly calls on government to be accountable to the people. Odama was reportedly arrested by the Police in Lagos on Sunday, August 9, 2026 for allegedly using the social media to bully Governor Bassey Otu of Cross River State. According to the media, the accused was detained in Lagos for about 4 days before being forcefully taken to Calabar for prosecution. What appears to have amounted to the bullying of Otu, was a post in Odama’s social media page drawing attention to the governor’s failure to restore light to the Bekwarra community in Cross river state which the governor had promised 2 years earlier.

While awaiting trial, the prosecution secured a court order for Odama to be remanded in jail. But then as is usual in our clime in matters of political intimidation, no charge was ready on the adjourned date. Instead, the case was withdrawn on the grounds that the governor had ordered the release of the accused person. To some people, the government was not really interested in prosecuting the case; instead, the period of incarceration was all the punishment that those in power wanted the citizen to undergo for criticising the governor. But if to be held accountable to the people is the hallmark of democracy, why do Nigerian politicians who abhor accountability seek elective offices?

Odama’s case clearly reopens several political posers in Nigeria’s democratic landscape. First, we appear to have returned to the colonial era when a law of sedition was designed simply to silence anyone who criticised the colonial government. In present day Nigeria, that obnoxious law now has a version included in the Cybercrimes Act. Those arrested under the law are deemed to have committed huge offences such as treasonable felony, terrorism, and cybercrime. Second, the prosecution is entirely opaque which explains why instead of inviting Odama to the police station for interrogation, he was virtually abducted and incarcerated without knowing his exact offence.

There is also the culture of keeping the accused in detention for longer than the law prescribes by getting a ‘friendly’ magistrate to sign a remand order so as to have ample time to concoct charges for prosecution. But because no real offence was committed, such cases are usually withdrawn at the end as has just happened in the case of Odama that was reported to have been released on the orders of the allegedly bullied Governor Otu. It would therefore appear that the governor was magnanimous but which law gave him the power to personally stop a case and order the discharge of the accused? If the scenario was in the form of a drama series, perhaps Otu would have secured the power to also serve as an appellate court.

Luckily, the same social media that many detest came handy in letting us into much information concerning the subject. For example, no one would have known the complainant. We would have thought it was Governor Otu himself, but it is not exactly so. What was reported was that it was two of his aides, namely: Akiba Ekpenyong and Pius Ankpo who did so on behalf of their principal. In other words, they were the nominal complainant in the case. Interestingly, at the point of withdrawal of the case, the prosecution claimed among other things that “the nominal complainant had forgiven the defendant.”

A criminal offence is not just against a complainant or an interested party but against the entire society. As a result, no one should have the power of forgiveness over a criminal offence. If the complainant wanted to have a civil case where they can decide to forgive at a point, a simple case of defamation would have been a better option. It is clear however that those involved in the case were at home with impunity hence they converted a simple criticism into a cybercrime to achieve not justice but harassment of a citizen who wanted to hold government accountable to the people as is done in liberal democracies.

Governor Otu’s aides who were the architect of the obvious criminalization of dissent in Cross River State didn’t do well. The Governor ought to reprimand them to avoid a recurrence of such posture which dents the public image of government. This is important because there had been governors before Otu, some notorious on the same subject while others like Donald Duke left with their names and honours intact. If, however, Bassey Otu prefers to intimidate critics, he is free to follow the footsteps of Ben Ayade who used his office to silence critics instead of being accountable. In his days, Ayade imprisoned journalist Agba Jalingo without telling the world how he handled the funds he was accused of diverting.

The allegation made by Jalingo was that Governor Ayade approved and diverted N500 million meant for Cross River State Microfinance Bank. Rather than explain the circumstance of the fund, the government decided to place the Journalist on trial on charges bordering on conspiracy, terrorism, treasonable felony and attempt to topple the government of Cross River. Following the sham trial it organized, the state was described by Amnesty International as ‘a den of repression.’ Against this backdrop, the case of Denis Odama should not have taken the same shape of leaving the substance to pursue shadows except if the state wants to wear the same repression toga

Irrespective of the provocative diction of the critic, we think Bassey Otu, has a duty to explain the continued darkness in Bekwarra, a community he had promised to restore light to since 2024. What happened to the promise by the governor? Was a budget approved for it? Why has the promise not been redeemed? These are the questions to which the average citizen deserves answers. To claim that the critic was rude or derogatory does not deal with the subject. It is worse that overzealous aides of the governor now laid a complaint to the police leading to the arrest of the critic amidst a no change situation in Bekwarra. So, who ended up bullying the other – the detained citizen or those who decided when to arrest him and when to release him without trial?

The police in Cross river and indeed in many other states must discontinue their posture of an army of occupation whose main goal is to be anti-people. The opposition politicians in the states are quite aware that in any conflict the government party is the one the police would support. Such an approach merely consolidates lack of faith in government. Earlier in the year, the African Democratic Congress (ADC), in the same Bekwarra chapter had petitioned the Inspector General of Police (IGP) over alleged political intimidation by the Area Commander of Ogoja. Although the police denied any partisanship, it is doubtful if the police itself believed its own version. Eyewitnesses confirmed that opposition events were disrupted by official thugs.

It was however worthy of note that during the tensions of last week which coincided with Odama’s case, the new Commissioner of Police in the state, CP Ajo Geoffrey Ordue formally warned officers against unlawful detention, abuse of power, and other forms of misconduct by police officers. The CP insisted that officers who violate the fundamental rights of citizens will no longer be tolerated, stressing that professionalism and respect for human dignity must guide every police operation across the state. CP Ordue spoke during his maiden lecture at the State Police Command headquarters where he addressed senior police officers.

It is hoped that with constant interactions, the police can develop an impartial habit across board that can assist in boosting her image. Most importantly, the police must stop supporting the wealthier or more powerful in society. It is irrational to say a harmless citizen was bullying a governor who has dozens of armed aides. All of us, governors inclusive should always remember that in a democracy, the sovereignty of the people is the first canon. So, let’s stop intimidating our people.

World.title: From tears to laughter, by Funmi Komolafe
World.content:
Beloved, gradually we are moving to the end of the month of a new beginning but it does not mean that the manifestation of new things would cease.

As Christians, we are aware that the mercy of God never ceases.

Lamentations 3 vs.23 ( KJV) “They (mercies) are new every morning: great is thy faithfulness”,

Whatever the situation with a person, for one that knows the Lord, such a person should daily give thanks to God. If not for anything, for the breath of life.

Some say that when a child is born, the reason the child cries is because of uncertainty that awaits that child in the world.

The child coming from a perfect kingdom into a word filled with troubles usually cries because he or she is worried.

Believe it or not, when a child does not cry, the birth attendant and the mother would be concerned.

What this simply means is that there is no human being that is not worried about something. It varies from one person to another.

Isaiah 30 vs. 19: “For the people shall dwell in Zion at Jerusalem: thou shalt weep no more: he will be gracious unto thee at the voice of thy cry; when he shall hear it, he will answer thee”.

God does not want his children to be in a state of tears of pain or sorrow. The Lord detests weeping, he said, “ thou shalt weep no more”.

With this, at the back of our minds, we must know that weeping does not glorify God, it solves no problem. If anything, it could endanger one’s health. So what is expected of a Christian is to cry unto the LORD that in God in his grace will hear and answer.

Note, the emphasis in the Bible passage quoted. You will first cry to God. Crying is not necessarily about shedding tears but about going to God in prayer. Tears may drop while praying but that is not weeping due to delay or non-manifestation of one’s heart’s desires.

The Holy Bible records in the story of Hannah that she was in bitterness of soul.

1st Samuel 1st Samuel 1 vs. 10: “ And she was in bitterness of soul, and prayed unto the LORD, and wept sore”.

Her tears dropped as she poured out her heart to the God in prayer. In other words, she prayed earnestly.

When we pray with total focus on the LORD, the Bible tells us , “he will hear and then answer”.

May the LORD hear our prayers as we cry unto Him in Jesus name.

Hannah after she prayed and made a vow, continued to wait on the LORD and the Bible records that “ God remembered her”.

I may not know what you so desire, as long as it is in line with the word of God, before this month ends, the LORD will remember you in Jesus name.

It is written in Isaiah 64 vs. 4: “ For since the beginning of the world men have not heard, nor perceived by the ear , neither hath the eye seen, O God, beside thee, what he hath prepared for him that waiteth for him”.

This Bible passage simply tells us that amazing miracles await those that wait on the Lord.

You want to experience a new beginning, then you must be ready to wait patiently in the presence of the God.

Brethren, while waiting on the Lord, we must shun provocation and anger as they are tools of the enemy to keep our miracle farther away from us.

You don’t believe, let’s see the story of Hannah and Peninnah in 1st Samuel 1 vs. 6: “ And her adversary also provoked her sore, for to make her fret, because the LORD had shut up her womb”.

Brethren, if Hannah had given in to Peninnah’s provocation, the house would have become a war zone. Her tears of sorrow would have multiplied because, the children of Peninnah would be on the side of their mother and Hannah would be alone.

It would only be a matter of time before Hannah’s husband that loves her switch to the other side.

Whatever you are going through right now, the word of God for you is , you are not alone, God is with you in Jesus name.

Rather than waste her time fighting and quarrelling, she took her tears to the Lord.

Beloved, when last did you have a conversation with the LORD?

I mean when last did you create a quite time to thank God for life and remind him that since He created you, you would move from grass to Grace.?

It sounds simple but believe me, God responds to such swiftly because, you may not get to that level until you are in Christ and Christ is in you.

Provocation and anger are weapons of the enemy to shut the door of God’s mercy against anyone waiting on the Lord.

May God give us the Grace to shun these two evils in Jesus name.

Apostle Paul told us in 1st Corinthians 16 vs. 9 : ( NIV) “ Because a great door for effective work has opened to me, and there are many who oppose me”.

King James Version puts it this way, “ For a great door and effectual is opened unto me, and there are many adversaries”.

If Penninah knew that God would bless Hannah with a Samuel that would be a man of God and a judge over Israel, she probably would not have provoked her .

Peninnah’s provocative attitude led Hannah to make a desperate cry unto the LORD and she got a reward beyond her imagination.

That would be someone’s story very soon in Jesus name.

The just concluded 74th Annual Convention of the Redeemed Christian Church of God, produced amazing testimonies.

I’ll share one to lift up the faith of readers trusting God for one issue or the other.

One of the amazing testimonies was that of a woman who said she attended a programme during which our father in the Lord, Daddy Enoch Adejare Adeboye announced that he wanted the Lord to bless his people with 83,000 babies.

That should be March last year when he turned 83 .

This woman jokingly said, it is the three above the 80 that she would like to have. She must have said this knowing that the blessing that our Daddy G.O. requested isn’t for her alone.

The most important point in her testimony that many of us missed, is that what she had was a conversation with the LORD which she counted as a joke.

Unknown to her, anyone that has a strong relationship with the LORD cannot utter words jokingly because her thoughts and words are anointed and God would honour such words.

While giving her testimony, she had with her a set of triplets.

Beloved, be determined to move from tears to laughter .

Someone in a conversation with the Lord, may appear abnormal to others because, the person is not praying like Hannah on the altar of God but a person that has a conversation with God is a person has total trust in God and has become a friend of Jesus.

Are you his friend already? If not, begin to take steps to improve your relationship with Christ. It isn’t too late.

Brethren, be prepared for the September Holy Ghost night. It is a programme for people trusting God for children and other things.

Be there, it is your turn to laugh. It is well.

World.title: Kwara Distributes 1,755 Computers, Devices to 70 Schools
World.content:
︎ Digital literacy a necessity, not a luxury, says Gov AbdulRazaq

Kwara State Government on Friday flagged off the distribution of about 2,000 computer devices for public senior secondary schools in the state to equip teachers and students with digital literacy skills.

A statement by the Communications Officer, Kwara Adolescent Girls Initiative For Learning said Employment (AGILE), Ayobami Ashaolu, said at least 70 public schools cutting across the 16 local governments of the state will receive 25 gadgets apiece in the first phase of the educational intervention.

The project is being implemented by

the AGILE under the Ministry of Education and Human Capital Development.

Performing the flag-off in Ilorin, the state capital, Governor AbdulRahman AbdulRazaq said digital literacy is no longer a luxury but a necessity in today’s global economy, noting that education remains the bedrock of sustainable development.

The hovernor, who spoke through the Deputy Governor, Elder Kayode Alabi, said the programme further attests to the commitment of the administration to transforming education through innovation, technology, and strategic investment in human capital.

“The future belongs to those who can leverage technology to solve problems, create opportunities and contribute meaningfully to society. It is for this reason our administration continues to prioritize investments that improve learning outcomes and prepare our young people for the demands of a rapidly evolving world,” the governor said.

“We are not merely distributing digital devices, we are equipping our children with the tools they need to compete and excel in an increasingly digital and knowledge-driven world.”

AbdulRazaq implored the affected schools and students to use the instruments for learning, creativity, innovation and self-development.

Commissioner for Education and Human Capital Development, Dr Lawal Olohungbebe, for his part, said the AGILE project is designed to improve girls’ access to quality education, enhance learning outcomes and equip them with relevant skills for their future.

Calling it a substantial investment in the education system, Olohungbebe

said the facilities will enable teachers and students to integrate technology into teaching and learning, develop digital competencies, and acquire creativity and problem-solving skills required in today’s world.

According to him, the gadgets that will be distributed across the selected schools include 1,755 all-in-one desktop computers, 70 printers, 70 projectors, and 70 motorized projector screens.

He said the government has already installed a 10kVA solar power system, internet connectivity, and CCTV cameras in each of these schools, apart from equipping their teachers (three per school) with the necessary skills.

“The Government of Kwara State recognises that digital literacy is now an essential component of quality education. Our children must not only have access to education; they must also acquire the digital skills necessary to thrive in today’s digital world,” he said, declaring, however, that the exercise will be continuous.

Olohungbebe commended Governor AbdulRazaq for his continued investments in human capital development towards the transformation of the education sector.

He called on the beneficiary schools and host communities to take ownership of the equipment and ensure that they are used primarily for the intended educational purposes.

State Coordinator for Kwara AGILE project, Adeshina Azeez Salami, in his remarks, said the office continues to bank on the support of the state government to thrive, commending Governor AbdulRazaq for setting a pace in the sector.

He also thanked the commissioner, Dr. Olohungbebe, and all members of the state project steering committee for the AGILE for supporting them to achieve this far.

“On behalf of the State Project Implementation Unit (SPIU), I thank you all for your presence in today’s event which is a testimony to the good works of the administration of Mallam AbdulRahman AbdulRazaq, our amiable Governor of Kwara State,” Salami said.

Also present at the event were the Commissioner for Communications, Hon. Bolanle Olukoju; Commissioner for Youth Development, Hon Shehu Ndanusa Usman; Permanent Secretary, Ministry of Education, Mrs. Rebecca Bake; Executive Director of the Agency for Mass Education (AME), Mallam Yusuf Saka; Chairman of Kwara State Teaching Service Commission, Mallam Taoheed Abubakar, who was represented by Director of Personnel, Finance and Supply, Issa Abdulrahman.

Highlight of the event was a symbolic presentation of devices to selected schools, such as United Secondary School, Ilorin; Government Girls Day Secondary School, Oke-suna; Government Day Secondary School, Tanke; and St. Anthony Secondary School, Ilorin.

Communications Officer, Kwara AGILE, Ayobami Ashaolu,

World.title: Atiku’s Subsidy Restoration Plan Offers Hope For Nigerians, Says Imansuagbon
World.content:
A chieftain of the African Democratic Congress (ADC) and former Edo State governorship aspirant, Mr Ken Imansuagbon, has thrown his weight behind the presidential candidate of the party, former Vice-President Atiku Abubakar, over his pledge to restore petrol subsidy if elected in 2027, insisting that the policy reversal would provide immediate relief to millions of Nigerians battling economic hardship.

Imansuagbon, in a strongly worded statement issued on Saturday in Benin City, described the criticism that greeted Atiku’s position from the presidency and the ruling APC as “misplaced and politically motivated”.

He argued that the removal of fuel subsidy by the President Bola Tinubu-led administration had further impoverished Nigerians, worsened inflation and inflicted unprecedented hardship on families across the country.

According to him, “The removal of fuel subsidy has not translated into a better life for Nigerians. Instead, it has pauperised millions of citizens, destroyed the purchasing power of workers, increased the cost of transportation, food, healthcare and education, while businesses continue to shut down under the weight of unbearable operating costs.”

The ADC stalwart maintained that Atiku’s promise to restore the subsidy was not a sign of inconsistency but evidence of courageous leadership capable of reviewing policies that had failed to achieve their objectives.

“Atiku should not be attacked simply because he is prepared to reconsider a position he held in 2023. That is the mark of a compassionate and people-oriented leader,” he said.

Imansuagbon further argued that despite claims by the Federal Government that trillions of naira had been saved from subsidy removal, Nigerians had seen little evidence of prudent deployment of the funds.

“Where are the trillions reportedly saved? Nigerians deserve transparent answers. We still have collapsing infrastructure, worsening insecurity, failing hospitals, underfunded schools, mass unemployment and deepening poverty. If these enormous resources were truly invested in the people’s welfare, the ordinary Nigerian should have felt the impact by now,” he stated.

He insisted that the real debate should not be about whether subsidy should remain or be removed, but whether the policy had improved the quality of life of ordinary citizens.

“The important question is simple: Has subsidy removal made life better for Nigerians? The answer is clearly no. The resources released were expected to improve transportation, healthcare, education, employment opportunities and social protection programmes, but Nigerians have only experienced more suffering and economic despair,” Imansuagbon added.

The former governorship aspirant expressed confidence that Atiku possessed the experience, competence and economic understanding required to rescue Nigeria from what he described as the “economic quagmire” created by the APC-led Federal Government.

“Atiku Abubakar remains the only presidential aspirant today with the courage, capacity and economic blueprint to reset Nigeria on the path of recovery. The pains inflicted on Nigerians under President Tinubu’s administration can begin to heal within Atiku’s first 100 days in office through people-centred economic reforms, including the restoration of subsidy where necessary to cushion the suffering of citizens,” he said.

He praised the former vice-president for what he described as his enduring love for humanity and commitment to the welfare of Nigerians, urging citizens to look beyond partisan sentiments and support policies capable of restoring hope to the country.

He maintained that Nigeria’s economic recovery should take precedence over politics, stressing that any policy that failed to improve the living conditions of the people deserved to be reviewed in the national interest.
