World.title: Guadalajara residents turn to citizen science as water crisis deepens
World.content:
On a Saturday morning in Guadalajara’s historic Analco neighborhood, residents arrived at the Casa Bandera community center carrying bottles and jars filled with water from their homes.

At folding tables, researchers from ITESO, Guadalajara’s Jesuit university, showed them how to dip inexpensive reactive strips into the samples, wait for the colors to change and compare the results against a chart measuring pH, chlorine, lead, mercury and other indicators. Samples showing signs of possible bacterial contamination could undergo additional testing for E. coli.

It was the latest workshop in an expanding citizen water-monitoring network that has grown out of Guadalajara’s months-long water crisis — and out of residents’ frustration with what they see as inadequate information and action from the authorities responsible for providing safe water.

“We don’t claim to be scientific specialists or water experts,” Héctor Morales, one of the workshop presenters, told participants. “We are citizens contributing evidence from what we are observing and living through, and that is equally valid.”

“We’re not trying to compete with science,” he continued. “We’re trying to generate knowledge that comes from everyday life. That’s the approach of citizen science.”

Sunday: Mega March + Agua KK Fest

Guadalajara’s water activists will be having some fun with the theme at Sunday’s festival — without losing sight of the very serious problem behind it.

When: Sunday, Aug. 23

10 a.m.: Gather at Parque Rojo

11 a.m.: Mega March for Water departs along Av. Juárez

Noon: Agua KK Fest at Plaza Liberación

The workshops will feature home water filters, rainwater harvesting, dry toilets and water testing, plus children’s activities, music, decorated water jugs, costumes and karaoke. The cheeky Agua KK name is a play on the word caca — a pointed joke about the dirty water that residents say has been coming from their taps.

From complaints to citizen evidence

The network brings together neighborhood residents, scientists from ITESO University, the Mexican Institute for Community Development (IMDEC) and the citizen campaign #ElSiapaQueQueremos, or The SIAPA We Want — SIAPA being the city water utility.

The idea is not simply to tell residents what might be in their water. María González of IMDEC said the testing has two purposes: helping families take care of themselves, and creating a body of evidence that can be used to press authorities for action.

“This helps us protect ourselves. You are going to know what is in the water in your homes,” González told the group. But the results, she said, are also “our citizen evidence for legal action, for institutional action, for mobilization.”

Before Saturday’s workshop, the network had analyzed roughly 184 samples from 90 neighborhoods in five municipalities. Organizers said residual chlorine was found in only 12 of the 184 samples. That’s a problem, they pointed out. Chlorine is added during water treatment, and a small amount should remain as water travels through the distribution network to help protect it from bacterial contamination.

The monitoring also detected lead in 20 samples, fluoride in 52 and mercury in an unspecified number, according to Morales. Four of the 184 samples tested positive for E. coli, a form of fecal coliform bacteria.

The citizen findings are not a statistically representative survey of Guadalajara’s water supply, a limitation organizers repeatedly emphasized. The low-cost tests do not measure all of the dozens of parameters required under Mexico’s drinking-water standard.

“What does this analysis tell us?” Morales asked. “It tells us when the water is not safe. What doesn’t it tell us? It doesn’t tell us when the water is good.”

Certifying water as safe, he said, requires much more extensive laboratory testing.

Still, official testing has now documented some of the same warning signs.

In late July, Jalisco health authorities confirmed that E. coli had been detected in 18 of 297 samples analyzed between March and June in neighborhoods affected by water-quality problems. Officials also acknowledged insufficient chlorination in some areas.

The findings came after months of complaints about yellow, brown or foul-smelling water, as well as sediment and service interruptions across the Guadalajara metropolitan area. González said the #ElSiapaQueQueremos campaign has now received nearly 1,500 complaints, with water quality by far the most common problem, followed by outages and high rates.

A multibillion-peso response

The Jalisco government and SIAPA, the metropolitan water utility, have acknowledged serious problems in the aging system and announced a long-term overhaul requiring more than 20 billion pesos in investment.

Among the major projects are the replacement of the aging Chapala-Guadalajara aqueduct and the modernization and expansion of Potabilizadora No. 1 in Miravalle. Governor Pablo Lemus said this month that the federal government had agreed to support both projects.

But for the citizen coalition, repairing infrastructure is only part of the solution.

The movement is increasingly focusing on who participates in decisions about the water system, how information is shared and whether communities themselves can have a formal role in monitoring and oversight.

That shift will be on display Sunday, when the same groups organizing the monitoring workshops will hold a “Mega March for Water.” Participants will gather at Parque Rojo at 10 a.m. and march along Avenida Juárez to Plaza Liberación, where the deliberately scatological “Agua KK Fest” — a play on caca, or “poop,” in reference to residents’ complaints about dirty water — will begin at noon.

The festival will combine protest with workshops on household filters, rainwater harvesting, dry toilets, urban gardens, community water systems and water-quality monitoring. Organizers describe the event as peaceful, family-oriented and nonpartisan.

Beyond fixing SIAPA

The coalition’s demands now extend beyond cleaner water. Its latest statement calls for greater transparency, citizen participation in decisions over water quality, distribution and infrastructure, formal recognition of community monitoring and protection of the watersheds that supply the metropolitan area.

It also proposes “public-community agreements” that would bring SIAPA, universities, neighborhood organizations, workers and other sectors together to share knowledge and participate in water governance.

The organizers explicitly reject privatization as the answer to SIAPA’s failures.

“The alternative to an inefficient SIAPA is not a privatized SIAPA,” their statement says, calling instead for a public utility that is transparent, efficient and subject to democratic social oversight.

González said the campaign is also pushing for a permanent working group focused specifically on water quality, health and sanitary risks. Authorities have not yet agreed to participate.

But organizers do not intend to wait indefinitely.

The group, González said, “is going to be established with authorities or without authorities,” functioning independently if necessary to prevent health risks.

That determination reflects how far the movement has come since residents first began showing up at public meetings with bottles of discolored water.

Morales said citizen monitoring allows residents to reach places government agencies may not sample and to turn individual experiences into systematic evidence. He has watched workshop participants take what they learn back to their neighborhoods — and then into the streets.

“It’s beautiful to see people who come to the workshops later at demonstrations with signs saying, ‘There are nitrates and nitrites in our water,’” he said.

“The authorities never expected that.”

World.title: The story of Zarzaparilla, an Indigenous root beer from Veracruz
World.content:
Mexico’s truest beauty can often be found in its widely diverse, uniquely regional variations of culture and flavors. No two places in Mexico are exactly alike. Whether it’s the way a certain salsa is prepared, the protein of choice used to stuff a tamal or the techniques that may differ from coast to coast, pueblo to pueblo, the country reflects an endless multiverse of realities inside its kitchens. As a taxi driver in Oaxaca once told me while driving across the desert terrain, you can spend two lifetimes in Mexico and even then, you still wouldn’t uncover all of its secrets and taste all of its idiosyncrasies.

It was a revelation, then, when I learned about zarzaparilla — about its historic origins and regional importance — from one of my uncles who grew up in Veracruz. In the simplest terms, zarzaparilla (referred to simply as zarza by locals) is what modern consumers would likely associate with root beer. But centuries before making its way into European markets via the Spanish — who in the 16th century first encountered the Indigenous remedy in the mountains of what is now Veracruz, and then exported it to Seville, Spain — zarza was a native drink with purported medicinal qualities made from local roots and ingredients that combated syphilis and, according to the American Homebrewers Association, far predates root beer.

A root beer revelation

In an effort to learn more about it, I drove 45 minutes to the source, on a southbound road from my home in Veracruz past two Pueblos Mágicos — first Coatepec, then Xico — until I reached Mexico’s cradle of zarza: Teocelo (or, in Nahuatl, “Tiger God”).

The mountain town of around 11,000 can only be reached through narrow, curving roads that carve through the subtropical terrain at a high elevation — with humid and wet conditions that allow all sorts of vegetation and crops to flourish in the surrounding areas (coffee, in particular, is a notable product from this part of Mexico).

It’s here that zarzaparilla (also confusingly spelled “sarsaparilla”) gained notoriety as a beverage among Spaniards and mestizos, becoming a local commercial industry of sorts that would expand beyond the region. Today, zarzaparilla can be found throughout Mexico, particularly within Veracruz and its neighboring states. But back then, it was — much like jalapeños were until they became commonplace elsewhere — a specialty product known only to those in the greater Xalapa vicinity.

The origins of ‘zarza’

In snooping around the tiny pueblo, it’s easy to find where it all started: Zarzaparilla Flores (a family-owned business that is not to be mistaken for a separate branch of family operations, Zarzaparilla Flores Doña Chabe, which is literally next door, but technically unaffiliated). The original Zarzaparilla Flores is said to have opened in 1920 inside what used to be a storage building for the nearby train yard, which served as a prominent trade route during the Porfiriato era from Xico to the United States. Due to the train, lots of immigrants and outsiders were able to pass through town, bringing a transient mixture of passersby who helped give zarzaparilla its fame beyond Veracruz.

Today, a third-generation family member runs the business — with antique family photos dating back to the Mexican Revolution bedecking the walls (one photo of the original shop owner, Don Manuel Flores, and his wife hangs stoically beneath two old rifles).

Rubén Olivares is the current face of operations. He married into the Flores family and has taken over the zarzaparilla tradition with pride.

A family tradition and recipe

“This region used to be known for cultivating pineapples and oranges, and that created a local exporting economy early on,” Olivares says. “But over time, with climate change and different farming methods, everything shifted, and pineapple exports migrated further south, due to the hotter temperatures down there. And this area, which has always been colder and at higher altitudes, began to grow coffee and other ingredients that were good for making zarzaparilla.”

Without revealing the specifics of their family recipe, he tells me their zarzaparilla is a mix of ginger, cardamom, star anise, cinnamon, lime, jamaica, egg whites and more. They also sell hidromiel (mead) and other liquors made from fermented oranges, arrowhead plants, cherry and crucetillo (a shrub that in the past was used to treat venomous snakebites).

The family’s zarza recipe has remained the same for more than a century and was patented in 1920 by Don Manuel Flores, but according to Olivares, Don Manuel only sold a few liters of it at the time. The family now regularly brews batches of around 1,000 liters and ships it all over Mexico. Predominantly made as a syrupy concentrate, the molasses-like mixture is put into various sizes of plastic bottles and jugs, which consumers can mix with any ratio of filtered or mineral water to their liking.

How the drink conquered the ‘Wild West’

In the 19th and 20th centuries, the beverage was viewed as a medicinal remedy and was brought to the U.S. According to The Seattle Times, “Sarsaparilla was widely consumed all across 19th-century America, easy to find in the local saloon if the one-road town one rode into had no dedicated apothecary or pharmacy, and was supposedly quite popular with cowboys and ranchers looking to tame a rumbling tummy or put a little pep in their step, much as people use kombucha today.” Eventually — and it’s unclear when, why or how — zarzaparilla (made from “dried root bark of several plants in the genus Smilax,” which grew plentifully in Veracruz) was replaced by sassafras, and zarzaparilla became known as root beer. (In 1960, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration banned real sassafras in commercial root beer as safrole in high amounts was found to be carcinogenic.)

Throughout it all, zarza remained the dominant beverage of choice in and around the town of its origin in Veracruz. The Flores family is no longer the only one making it, either: A Google Maps search will reveal no fewer than five other zarzaparilla businesses in the town of about 23 square miles (for comparison’s sake, Mexico City is estimated at 573 square miles, yet according to Google, unfortunately has no official zarzaparilla-dedicated outlets).

Travel attractions in Teocelo

Teocelo has other worthwhile features besides zarza: It’s the site of the Fiesta Patronal, a weekend-long celebration that includes parades, fireworks and religious celebrations in honor of the burial of Jesus after his crucifixion. At the pueblo’s main entrance, there’s a bee sanctuary that produces all kinds of honey products you likely won’t find anywhere else, at least not in abundance — jugs of honey wine, salsa macha made with honey and “honey butter” (akin to peanut butter, with a similarly thick consistency) in variations that range from almond and walnut to berry or garlic.

Note: The honey shop, known as La Mielada, or “The Honeydew,” also has an accompanying restaurant that serves honeyed meats and breads, with an affordable selection of beverages like the aforementioned honey wine or my personal favorite, a mug of locally cultivated coffee with large dollops of organic honey mixed in — a pure delight of sweet and bitter flavors. For outdoor-seeking adventurers, the surrounding area also offers waterfalls, hikes, cabins and whitewater rapids.

To be sure, there’s no shortage of offerings — and mugs of zarza — to enjoy for a weekend in the chilly mountain locale.

Alan Chazaro is the author of “These Spaceships Weren’t Built For Us” (Tia Chucha Press, 2026), “Notes from the Eastern Span of the Bay Bridge” (Ghost City Press, 2021), “Piñata Theory” (Black Lawrence Press, 2020), and “This Is Not a Frank Ocean Cover Album” (Black Lawrence Press, 2019). He is a graduate of June Jordan’s Poetry for the People program at UC Berkeley and was selected as a Lawrence Ferlinghetti Poetry Fellow at the University of San Francisco. His work can be found in NPR, The Guardian, SLAM, GQ, L.A. Times, and more. He is currently based in Veracruz.

World.title: The hottest product on the planet is increasingly made in Mexico: A perspective from our CEO
World.content:
Let’s start today’s column with a quick quiz:

Pop Quiz Question #1: What is currently the top Mexican export to the United States?

If you are like most people, you are thinking of one of three categories: alcoholic beverages (think tequila, mezcal, Corona beer), food (perhaps avocados, jalapenos, tomatoes) or automobiles. All of those answers are incorrect.

Pop Quiz Question #2: Which country sells more AI servers and equipment to the United States, Mexico or Taiwan?

Of course, most people answer Taiwan. That would also be incorrect.

Mexico’s server-related exports to the US have overtaken autos, underscoring how AI data-center demand is reshaping its export base. Source: @financialtimes https://t.co/QtrH6mKZ0I pic.twitter.com/pyRYc40ktb — (((The Daily Shot))) (@SoberLook) August 7, 2026

Sometimes just one picture, or in this case — one chart recently published by the Financial Times — can be incredibly insightful. Above, you’ll see a chart comparing Mexican exports of two product categories from 2010 to the present day. The blue line shows vehicles, which Mexico has been exporting for over 60 years. Last year, nearly 80% of Mexico’s light vehicle exports went to the United States. The red line shows server-related hardware (think AI data centers). The x-axis shows the years from 2010 to 2026. The y-axis shows monthly exports in billions of US dollars.

As can be clearly seen, exports of server-related hardware have absolutely exploded in the past two years, to the point where they are now surpassing vehicles. Last month alone, over US $15 billion of these products were exported. Think about that for a minute. The news is filled on a daily basis with headlines telling us that Trump has decided not to renew the USMCA or that Trump commented that “we don’t need anything that Mexico has.” Other headlines lead us to believe that tariffs are being slapped on most Mexican goods, significantly hurting Mexico in the process. Neither is true.

That being said, much of the conversation often seems to revolve around two categories of products highly influenced by two distinct voting groups in the U.S. The first is union members and more specifically the members of the United Auto Workers, who have an obvious interest in keeping as much vehicle production as possible in the country. The second is U.S. farmers, who naturally want to keep food production domestic. As a result of these two powerful and influential groups, those segments are what we most often hear about — more specifically cars and tomatoes. And in fact, the U.S. currently has a 17% “antidumping” tariff on Mexican tomatoes and a relatively small and extremely complex-to-calculate tariff on Mexican vehicles. Fun fact: One of the final projects my senior year of college was to analyze the impact of U.S. tomato tariff practices and policies on Mexico. (Yes, I am aware of what an exceptionally boring topic that is for a final project!)

Perhaps not surprisingly, server equipment from Mexico has a 0% tariff from the United States. The most in-demand product on the planet right now has firmly established Mexico in its supply chain, and investment, jobs and exports are all booming in this area. Taiwanese companies are investing heavily in Mexico. It’s all happening very fast. It’s quite exciting and going to be very interesting to continue to follow.

So while most headlines would have you believe that the Mexico-U.S. trade relationship is in shambles, the reality is as follows:

1. Mexico moves past Taiwan as the top AI server exporter to the U.S.: https://mexiconewsdaily.com/business/mexico-moves-past-taiwan-as-top-ai-server-exporter-to-united-states/

2. Mexico is now by far the leading exporter to the U.S.: https://mexiconewsdaily.com/business/mexico-in-numbers-mexico-exports-us-china-canada/

3. Inflation is now lower in Mexico than in the U.S. for the first time: https://mexiconewsdaily.com/business/inflation-mexico-lower-united-states-why-thats-such-a-big-deal-a-perspective-from-our-ceo/

4. Mexico’s export revenue is up 25% so far this year: https://mexiconewsdaily.com/news/mexico-export-revenue-this-year/

So what’s the bottom line here? Follow the data, not the noise, and stay tuned to what is the most dynamic segment in the world, growing fast and furious right here in Mexico.

Travis Bembenek is the CEO of Mexico News Daily and has been living, working or playing in Mexico for nearly 30 years.

World.title: Missed the deadline? Here’s how to get your cell phone service back
World.content:
The first enforced deadline for compliance with mandatory cell phone registration came and went on Aug. 15 and approximately 2.6 million phone lines were suspended, prompting chaos and confusion for users whose now-unregistered phone numbers end in “0.”

Mexico’s Telecommunications Regulatory Commission (CRT) announced on Thursday that nearly 9.7 million users whose number ends in “0” successfully registered their cell phones before the deadline.

The CRT also said that just over 2.3 million users whose lines had been suspended managed to reactivate their phone service by Aug. 19. Another 2.6 million mobile phones are expected to be reactivated in the coming days, while the CRT expects 2.5 million “unused” lines to be decommissioned.

Those who failed to register before the deadline faced plenty of online misinformation, but those whose service was suspended can still recover their service because their phone number was not canceled.

To reactivate the service, users must complete the registration process via their phone company. Prepaid lines must also be registered to remain active.

You can register through the phone company’s registration portal and by verifying your identity. Links to all providers’ platforms can be found on the CRT website here.

You can also complete the process in person at one of your company’s customer service centers, where staff is on hand to assist with the registration.

Mexican mobile phone owners must provide a CURP (Unique Population Registry Code) and a valid official ID, such as the INE-issued voter ID.

Foreigners must also register their phone lines (if it is a Mexican provider) by using the corresponding identity or immigration document, such as a resident visa or a passport.

Procedures vary slightly depending on the phone company, but the process is free.

It is important to note that suspended lines can still make calls to emergency numbers, citizen services and their phone company. They will also continue to receive earthquake alerts and they can be used to complete the registration process.

The government mandated cell phone registration procedures in an effort to eliminate anonymous mobile lines, stop criminal extortion and curb the use of untraceable “burner” prepaid SIM cards.

The CRT had originally established a June 30 deadline for all cell phones to be registered, but when it became apparent that a significant number of users would see their lines suspended, the deadline was extended.

The official schedule to register cell phones now depends on the final digit of your phone number. If your phone number ends in “1,” you must register by Aug. 31. If it ends in “2,” your deadline is Sept. 15, and so on through the end of the year as shown in the graphic above.

In its Aug. 20 report, the CRT said a total of 73.2 million lines — or 60.5% of the total lines expected to be connected in the country — were registered. By the end of the registration process, it expects a purge of around 25 million lines.

With reports from El Universal, Wired and LatinUS

— Amount 4.5 billion pesos (4,500 million pesos) in long-term trust-issued exchange certificates.

— Series FONDO 26 (1,337.5 million pesos), FONDO 26-2 (2,234.25 million pesos), and FONDO 26S (928.25 million pesos).

— Tenors About 1.5 years for FONDO 26, 4.5 years for FONDO 26S, and 5.5 years for FONDO 26-2.

— Rating Fitch assigned ‘AAA(mex)’, the highest domestic-scale rating, to all three series.

The Mexico farm credit fund has sold its first long-term bonds on the Mexican Stock Exchange. The trust, known as FONDO, placed 4.5 billion pesos in three series, according to El Cronista.

What Is the Mexico Farm Credit Fund?

In fact, the Mexico farm credit fund is FONDO, the Guarantee and Development Fund for Agriculture, Livestock and Poultry Farming. It is a public trust of the federal government, not a bank or ministry.

FONDO is part of FIRA, a group of four federal trusts whose trustee is the Bank of Mexico, the central bank. FIRA lends and guarantees through commercial banks rather than directly to most borrowers.

FONDO is one of four trusts that form FIRA, alongside FEFA, FEGA, and FOPESCA. However, FONDO’s role is to guarantee and develop agriculture, livestock, and poultry.

The trust’s full name is the Guarantee and Development Fund for Agriculture, Livestock and Poultry Farming. However, it is commonly known by its short name, FONDO.

First Long-Term Bond Sale

In addition, the Mexico farm credit fund placed 4.5 billion pesos in long-term trust-issued exchange certificates, known as certificados bursátiles fiduciarios. This is the standard instrument Mexican public trusts use to borrow on the domestic capital market.

The operation is described as FONDO’s first long-term placement, according to noti. mx.

It was reported on Friday 21 August 2026. The Mexico farm credit fund sold the certificates on the Bolsa Mexicana de Valores, the main Mexican exchange.

However, the exact day of the placement was not confirmed in the research. The certificates are debt securities issued by a trust and listed on a Mexican exchange.

Investors buy the paper and are repaid with interest, as is standard for such instruments.

Three Bond Series With Different Terms

Meanwhile, the bonds were issued in three series, each with its own ticker. FONDO 26 raised 1,337.5 million pesos, FONDO 26-2 raised 2,234.25 million pesos, and FONDO 26S raised 928.25 million pesos.

The tenors vary by series. Overall, FONDO 26 has a term of about 1.5 years; FONDO 26S, about 4.5 years; FONDO 26-2, about 5.5 years.

In addition, this comes from a rating document filed with the exchange. FONDO 26S, the social bond, has a tenor of about 4.5 years.

In addition, FONDO 26-2 has the longest term at about 5.5 years. The three series add up to the 4,500 million peso total.

Meanwhile, the tenors range from about 1.5 years to about 5.5 years.

Fixed and Floating Rates

However, the Mexico farm credit fund structured the rates differently across the series. FONDO 26 pays a floating interest rate, while FONDO 26S and FONDO 26-2 pay fixed rates.

No specific coupon or reference rate was disclosed in the available information. The rate types were confirmed in the rating document.

FONDO 26’s floating rate means its interest payments will vary over time. Meanwhile, FONDO 26S and FONDO 26-2 offer fixed rates, providing predictable payments.

The floating rate for FONDO 26 means its payments will adjust over time. In contrast, the fixed rates for the other two series offer stable payments.

A Social Bond in the Mix

FONDO 26S is labelled a social bond, or bono social in Spanish. For example, social bonds are debt whose proceeds go to projects with a stated social benefit, such as lending to small producers.

The coverage describes it as a social bond, but no issuance framework or external review was found. The label itself was confirmed by El Cronista and noti.

mx. Social bonds are a growing category in Mexico’s capital markets.

Still, FONDO 26S is the only social bond in this placement. The social bond label indicates the proceeds are earmarked for projects with social benefits.

However, no issuance framework or external review was found.

Purpose of the Funds

The stated purpose of the money is to strengthen financing for agricultural and rural projects. Still, the operation is intended to support producers in the sector, according to El Cronista.

In short, the funds will help FONDO continue its mission of facilitating credit access for farming and related activities. The funds will help FONDO support producers in the agricultural and rural sectors.

As a result, the operation aims to strengthen financing for these projects. The funds are intended to strengthen financing for agricultural and rural projects.

As a result, they will support producers in the sector.

FONDO’s Role in FIRA

FONDO is the first and oldest of the four trusts that make up FIRA. FIRA was created in 1954, and the Bank of Mexico records that FONDO was the first trust set up.

The other trusts are FEFA, FEGA, and FOPESCA. In short, FONDO’s original aim was to depoliticise official credit to agriculture and bring commercial banks into that lending.

FIRA’s purpose is to facilitate access to credit through lending and guarantees. In addition, FONDO’s original aim was to root a culture of repayment in Mexico.

FONDO is the first and oldest of the four trusts that make up FIRA. Since its creation in 1954, it has been administered by the Bank of Mexico.

Historical Context

The FIRA system has a long history of reaching producers. The number of producers served rose from 6,678 in 1958 to 34,175 in 1970, according to the Bank of Mexico.

These figures are historical and not related to the current bond sale. They show the scheme’s growth over decades.

The FIRA system was created in 1954, with FONDO as its first trust. Since then, it has grown to include four trusts.

The number of producers reached by the scheme grew from 6,678 in 1958 to 34,175 in 1970. These figures show the system’s early expansion, though they are not current.

Separate FEFA Operations

Meanwhile, another FIRA trust, FEFA, has done its own placements this year. In July, FEFA placed 8,000 million pesos on BIVA, Mexico’s second stock exchange, not the BMV.

That operation is separate from the Mexico farm credit fund’s sale. FEFA also placed 7,017 million pesos in March, including a green bond, but those are not part of this deal.

FEFA’s July placement on BIVA was for 8,000 million pesos, a larger amount than FONDO’s 4,500 million. However, FEFA’s March operation included a green bond, not a social one.

FEFA’s July placement on BIVA was for 8,000 million pesos, larger than FONDO’s 4,500 million. Meanwhile, FEFA also placed 7,017 million pesos in March, including a green bond.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the Mexico farm credit fund?

The Mexico farm credit fund is FONDO, a federal public trust that provides credit guarantees to agriculture. It is part of FIRA and is managed by the Bank of Mexico.

How much did FONDO raise in its first long-term bond sale?

FONDO raised 4.5 billion pesos in three series. The largest series, FONDO 26-2, raised 2,234.25 million pesos.

What is a social bond in this context?

A social bond is debt whose proceeds are used for projects with a social benefit. FONDO 26S is labelled a social bond, but no detailed framework was disclosed.

Who rated the bonds?

Fitch assigned a ‘AAA(mex)’ rating to all three series. This is the highest rating on Fitch’s Mexican national scale, meaning low credit risk relative to other Mexican issuers.

Sources: El Cronista; noti.mx; Bolsa Mexicana de Valores filings; PCR Verum; Diario Oficial de la Federación; Banco de México; FIRA.

The Argentina China technology cluster was launched on Thursday 20 August 2026 at the University of Buenos Aires. The new platform, called CITAC, aims to boost technological cooperation between the two countries.

What Is the Argentina China Technology Cluster?

CITAC is a cluster, platform, and articulation space for universities, companies and public bodies. Its site citac.

ar calls it the Argentina China technology cluster. The launch occurred in the Aula Estela de Carlotto at the Cero+Infinito building.

The Faculty of Exact and Natural Sciences hosted it with free registration. CITAC is not a government body or treaty-created institution.

Instead, it is a flexible collaboration platform, part of the Argentina China technology cluster. The launch was held on Thursday 20 August 2026 at the University of Buenos Aires.

However, CITAC is not a new legal entity but a flexible platform for existing institutions.

Who Led the Launch Event?

Three people led the presentation. They were Sabino Vaca Narvaja, Wang Xiaoxu, and Guillermo Durán.

Vaca Narvaja served as Argentina’s ambassador to China from 2019 to 2023. Wang Xiaoxu spoke about China’s 15th Five-Year Plan, highlighting frontier sectors.

These include artificial intelligence, quantum technology and humanoid robotics. He said Argentina has significant scientific capabilities and enormous potential to deepen cooperation.

Meanwhile, Wang Xiaoxu, as minister counsellor, represented the Chinese embassy, not the ambassador. His remarks underscored the potential for deeper scientific ties between the two nations.

Vaca Narvaja was Argentina’s ambassador to China from 2019 to 2023. Meanwhile, Wang Xiaoxu, as minister counsellor, represented the Chinese embassy at the event.

Why Science and Technology Matter

Vaca Narvaja said the only genuine way to accelerate development is science and technology. He called CITAC a tool born to foster cooperation with China in those fields.

He also warned about digital dependency. If the Global South contributes minerals while others concentrate algorithms, a new dependency could emerge.

His strategy is to raise the standing of science and technology within the bilateral relationship. In addition, Vaca Narvaja emphasized that cooperation should go beyond trade.

He stressed the goal to research, develop, and produce together with China. Vaca Narvaja warned that without cooperation, the Global South could face a new digital dependency.

Therefore, he stressed the need to research, develop, and produce together with China.

What CITAC Is Not

CITAC is not an intergovernmental centre, a binational institute or a body created by treaty. Its founders describe it instead as a new space for coordination.

Instead, it is a platform of existing institutions. Still, it is separate from existing Argentina-China science bodies, such as the MINCyT-MOST policy centre.

Still, no source places CITAC under any existing bilateral science body. Thus, it operates independently, with no hierarchical link to those programs.

CITAC is not an intergovernmental body or a treaty-created institution. Instead, it is a platform for articulation, separate from existing bilateral science bodies.

First Stage Work Lines

In its first stage, CITAC has four lines of work. These include joint projects, academic links, technology missions and trade fairs.

This was reported by Ámbito Financiero and the cluster’s own website. The announced next step is a technology mission to China from 18 to 30 November 2026.

Activities will take place in Shanghai, Beijing and Shenzhen, including participation in the China Hi-Tech Fair. After the launch, the cluster plans a technology mission to China in November 2026.

This mission aims to turn institutional links into concrete projects and financing. The first stage includes four lines: joint projects, academic links, technology missions, and trade fairs.

After the launch, a technology mission to China is planned for November 2026.

Who Is Involved From Argentina

For example, Argentine institutions include CESSI, CABASE, and LIFIA, a computer science lab at the National University of La Plata. Also involved are Polo IT La Plata, the Red Federal de Economía del Conocimiento and Fundación Blockchain Argentina.

The initiative is backed by the Cámara Argentino China, the Cámara de Empresas Chinas en Argentina and the Consejo Argentino Chino. Officials from the Buenos Aires provincial Ministry of Production also attended.

While the named Argentine groups come from tech and internet sectors, the cluster also includes universities. However, no specific Chinese university or company was named as a member.

Argentine participants include CESSI, CABASE, and LIFIA, among others. Meanwhile, the initiative is backed by three Argentine-Chinese chambers and provincial officials.

The Venue and Its Significance

The launch was held at the UBA’s Faculty of Exact and Natural Sciences, where about 10 percent of CONICET researchers work. The faculty graduates about 25 percent of the country’s doctorate holders.

Dean Guillermo Durán said partnering with a giant like China is truly decisive for a country like Argentina. He listed disciplines under way or starting, including computer science, data science, mathematics, physics, biotechnology, chemistry, materials science, geology and climate change.

Since the faculty hosts many researchers and graduates, it offers a strong base for scientific collaboration. Therefore, the venue choice highlights the academic focus of the cluster.

The venue hosts about 10 percent of CONICET researchers and graduates 25 percent of the country’s doctorates. As a result, the choice highlights the academic strength behind the cluster.

Trade Context Behind the Cluster

In 2025, Argentina exported US$9.799 billion to China and imported US$17.954 billion. Therefore, the deficit was US$8.155 billion.

China took 11.3 percent of Argentina’s exports and supplied 23.7 percent of its imports. The Argentine Foreign Ministry called this the highest bilateral deficit with any partner.

In the first half of 2026, the deficit was US$3.578 billion. Meanwhile, China represented 9.9 percent of exports and 22.5 percent of imports.

Although Argentina’s overall trade surplus was US$11.320 billion in 2025, the deficit with China stood out. As a result, the cluster aims to boost technological cooperation to balance trade.

In 2025, the bilateral deficit with China was US$8.155 billion, the highest with any partner. Meanwhile, the deficit in the first half of 2026 was US$3.578 billion.

Broader Bilateral Ties

Argentina and China describe their relationship as a comprehensive strategic partnership. Argentina has also signed a Belt and Road cooperation plan with China’s National Development and Reform Commission.

In addition. The central bank announced on 5 August 2026 that its currency swap line had been renewed for five years at 130 billion yuan.

Argentine media reported this as roughly US$19 billion. While the currency swap renewal signals financial cooperation, the cluster focuses on science and technology.

Nevertheless, both initiatives reflect deepening ties between the two countries. Argentina and China have a comprehensive strategic partnership and a Belt and Road plan.

In addition, the central bank renewed a currency swap line for five years in August 2026.

Frequently Asked Questions

What does CITAC stand for?

CITAC stands for Clúster de Innovación Tecnológica Argentina-China, which translates as the Argentina and China Technology Innovation Cluster. It is a cluster, a platform and a space for articulation between universities, companies and public bodies.

Is CITAC a government agency?

No, CITAC is not a government agency or an intergovernmental body. It is a platform of existing institutions, without its own legal statute or permanent headquarters.

Who attended the launch?

The launch was led by Sabino Vaca Narvaja, president of CITAC; Wang Xiaoxu. Minister counsellor of the Chinese Embassy; and Guillermo Durán, dean of the Faculty of Exact and Natural Sciences.

What is the next step for CITAC?

The next step is a technology mission to China from 18 to 30 November 2026. The mission will include activities in Shanghai, Beijing and Shenzhen, and participation in the China Hi-Tech Fair.

World.title: Ecuador Cocoa Brand Aims at the Premium Chocolate Shelf
World.content:
Ecuador · AGRIBUSINESS

Key Facts — Launch Anecacao unveiled the brand on Wednesday 19 August 2026 at UEES in Samborondón.

— Brand name ‘Cacao ecuatoriano, naturalmente, el mejor del mundo’ means ‘Ecuadorean cocoa, naturally, the best in the world’.

— Fine flavour share Ecuador supplies roughly 60% to 63% of the world’s fine flavour cocoa, all linked to the Nacional variety.

— Export value Cocoa exports fell 63.5% in the first quarter of 2026, from US$1.208 billion to US$441 million.

— Fair tie-in The brand launch accompanied the announcement of the fifth Chokao fair, running 25-27 August 2026 at UEES.

The exporters’ guild hopes a new origin label will lift Ecuador’s premium cocoa from a commodity to a story. Even as prices slide.

A cocoa farm at Machala, Ecuador. Ecuador’s beans are sold as fine flavour cocoa.

The Ecuador cocoa brand aims to move the country from being a raw ingredient supplier to a name on the premium chocolate shelf. The trade association Anecacao launched the origin label on Wednesday 19 August 2026 at a university convention centre near Guayaquil.

A New Origin Brand for Ecuador Cocoa

In fact, the Ecuador cocoa brand is ‘Cacao ecuatoriano, naturalmente, el mejor del mundo’. It means ‘Ecuadorean cocoa, naturally, the best in the world’.

Anecacao, the National Association of Cocoa Exporters and Industrialists of Ecuador, presented it at UEES in Samborondón. Samborondón is the affluent canton across the Daule river from Guayaquil, Ecuador’s main port city.

The launch event took place at the university’s convention centre. The launch took place on Wednesday 19 August 2026, according to El Universo.

Meanwhile, Forbes Ecuador also covered the event at the UEES convention centre. The event took place at the Universidad de Especialidades Espíritu Santo, known as UEES, in Samborondón.

However, the brand is not an official state label, as no government decree was found.

Ecuador Cocoa Brand: Supplier to Symbol

Merlyn Casanova, Anecacao’s executive director, explained the goal at the launch. She said: ‘We want to go from being recognised for what we supply to being recognised for what we represent.

Therefore, the campaign is about identity, not just volume. The association wants the world to see Ecuador as a source of quality, not just a producer of beans.

Casanova’s words reflect a shift from commodity to identity. However, this ambition faces a tough market in 2026.

Casanova’s vision reflects a desire to be valued for what Ecuador represents, not just what it supplies. Meanwhile, the campaign aims to shift global perceptions of Ecuadorean cocoa.

Four Strands of the Campaign

Forbes Ecuador reported that the plan has four parts. These include a country brand with an origin logo, a film, a seal, and a communications strategy.

In addition, the brand was unveiled alongside the announcement of the fifth edition of Chokao, the International Cocoa and Chocolate Fair. That fair runs from Tuesday 25 to Thursday 27 August 2026 at the UEES convention centre, with seminars and master classes.

The film will travel the world to promote the brand. In addition, the seal aims to certify origin nationally and internationally.

The four strands include a country brand with an origin logo, a film, a seal, and a communications strategy. In addition, the film will travel the world to promote the brand.

A Trade Association Effort, Not a Government Decree

This is a trade-association origin brand promoted by the exporters’ guild. Although it was presented at a public event, no official state brand registration was found in Spanish-language sources.

Still, the brand carries weight because Anecacao has represented the cocoa sector for more than 35 years. The association describes itself as a non-profit body looking after the interests of growers and exporters.

No presidential decree or ministerial accord was found in the sources. Still, Anecacao’s long history gives the brand credibility.

Anecacao has represented the cocoa sector for more than 35 years, according to its own description. Still, the brand’s official status remains unclear, as no trademark registration was found.

Ecuador’s Fine Flavour Advantage

The Ecuador cocoa brand builds on a strong natural asset: fine or flavour cocoa, known in Spanish as cacao fino de aroma. Moreover, this premium grade is tied to the Nacional variety, prized for floral and fruity notes.

According to Anecacao, Ecuador produces approximately 60% of the world’s fine flavour cocoa. Sector analyses put the figure closer to 63%; however, the Ministry of Production states 100% of bean exports are fine flavour.

Ecuador supplies roughly 60% to 63% of the world’s fine flavour cocoa. As a result, this premium grade is a key selling point.

Fine or flavour cocoa, known as cacao fino de aroma, is tied to the Nacional variety. In addition, Ecuador produces 60% to 63% of the world’s fine flavour cocoa.

Premium Demand Drives Value

A PUCE study found that demand from premium markets has pushed up the value of fine flavour cocoa exports. These markets prioritise traceability, sustainability and fair trade.

For example, the study, titled ‘Análisis del cacao fino de aroma en el Ecuador’, was published on 12 January 2026. It confirms that the shift towards quality is already happening.

The PUCE study was published on 12 January 2026. Since then, it has highlighted the value of traceability and sustainability.

The PUCE study highlights that premium markets value traceability and sustainability. As a result, these factors have increased the value of fine flavour cocoa exports.

A Global Export Powerhouse

Ecuador was the world’s third largest cocoa exporter in 2025, behind Ivory Coast and Ghana. However, Anecacao expects the country to ship more than 623,000 tonnes in 2026 and to overtake Ghana as the second largest exporter.

In a March 2026 radio interview, Anecacao put the target at 625,000 to 630,000 tonnes, calling that conservative. The association says more than 600,000 tonnes were placed abroad in 2025.

In 2023, Ecuador exported 396,042 tonnes of cocoa worth US$1.320 billion. However, by 2024, exports reached US$3.617 billion on 460,000 tonnes, according to the central bank.

Ecuador was the third largest cocoa exporter in 2025, behind Ivory Coast and Ghana. However, Anecacao expects to overtake Ghana in 2026 with more than 623,000 tonnes.

A Challenging Price Year

The Ecuador cocoa brand arrives in a difficult market. Primicias reported that Ecuadorean cocoa closed January 2026 with the lowest export figure in 22 months.

This was because of the fall in the international price. As a result, the value of Ecuador’s cocoa exports fell 63.5% in the first quarter of 2026.

It dropped from US$1.208 billion to US$441 million. This drop makes the branding push even more urgent.

The first quarter of 2026 saw exports fall to US$441 million. This drop follows a record 2024, when cocoa was Ecuador’s third largest non-oil export.

The brand arrives as cocoa export values have fallen sharply in 2026. Meanwhile, the first quarter saw a 63.5% drop, making the branding push more urgent.

Looking Ahead to Chokao and Beyond

The brand launch and the Chokao fair are part of a broader strategy to strengthen Ecuador’s position. The fair will bring together industry players for seminars, business round tables and master classes.

In short, the Ecuador cocoa brand is a bet on identity over commodity. Whether it can lift prices remains to be seen, but the sector is clearly aiming for the premium shelf.

Chokao runs from Tuesday 25 to Thursday 27 August 2026. Meanwhile, the fair offers a platform for the new brand to gain traction.

Chokao, the International Cocoa and Chocolate Fair, runs from 25 to 27 August 2026. Meanwhile, the fair offers a platform for the new brand to gain traction.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the Ecuador cocoa brand?

The Ecuador cocoa brand is a new origin label launched by Anecacao, the exporters’ association. Its name in English is ‘Ecuadorean cocoa, naturally, the best in the world’.

Who launched the brand?

Anecacao, the National Association of Cocoa Exporters and Industrialists of Ecuador, launched it on Wednesday 19 August 2026. The executive director, Merlyn Casanova, is the main voice of the campaign.

Why is Ecuador’s cocoa considered premium?

Ecuador supplies roughly 60% to 63% of the world’s fine flavour cocoa, all linked to the Nacional variety. This cocoa is prized for its floral and fruity notes, unlike bulk cocoa.

How is the brand being promoted?

The campaign has four strands: a country brand with an origin logo. A film, a national and international seal, and a communications strategy.

Sources: El Universo; Forbes Ecuador; Primicias; El Productor; Diario Extra; Anecacao; Ministry of Agriculture and Livestock (SIPA).

World.title: Colombia Factoring Decree Loses Six Articles in Court
World.content:
Colombia · FINANCE

Key Facts — Court Colombia’s Consejo de Estado annulled six articles of Decreto 2669 de 2012 on 4 June 2026.

— Articles The annulled articles are 2, 3, 4, 5, 12 and 13.

— Ground The court found the Executive exceeded its regulatory power under Ley 1231 de 2008.

— Survives Articles 1, 6, 8, 9, 10, 11 and 14 of the decree remain in force.

— Effect Factoring by unsupervised commercial companies now falls back on the law and general commercial rules.

Colombia’s top administrative court has struck down six articles of a 2012 decree that regulated factoring, saying the government overstepped its authority.

The Palacio de Justicia on Bogotá’s Plaza de Bolívar, home to Colombia’s high courts.

Colombia factoring decree has lost six articles after the Consejo de Estado. The country’s highest administrative court, annulled them for exceeding the government’s regulatory authority.

The ruling, dated 4 June 2026, struck down articles 2, 3, 4, 5. 12 and 13 of Decreto 2669 de 2012, which regulated the factoring business of commercial companies.

What the Court Annulled

However, the Consejo de Estado, sitting as its Sección Primera, annulled six articles of the decree. The judgment, dated 4 June 2026, became public news in August 2026, according to Valora Analitik and La República.

The annulled articles include article 2, which defined factoring and related operations, and article 3, which allowed parties to insure against non-payment. Article 4 let parties agree freely on discount rates for past-due instruments, and article 5 governed assignment clauses.

Article 12 limited how factors could fund themselves, and article 13 listed prohibited operations. Therefore, articles 1, 6, 8, 9, 10, 11 and 14 remain in force.

Why the Court Struck Them Down

The ground for annulment was exceso en la potestad reglamentaria, meaning the Executive exceeded its regulatory power. The court concluded that the government went beyond what Ley 1231 de 2008 allowed.

Ley 1231 de 2008 turned commercial invoices into negotiable instruments to help small businesses access financing. The court said the law did not authorize the government to issue a comprehensive regulation of factoring as an economic activity.

For example, the court listed narrow areas the law allowed the Executive to regulate, such as verifying origins. In addition, the annulled articles went further, adding definitions and restrictions.

What Is Factoring

Factoring is short-term finance where a supplier sells unpaid invoices to a third party at a discount. This gives the supplier cash immediately instead of waiting for the customer to pay.

In Colombia, factoring is also called compra de cartera, literally the purchase of a receivables book. In fact, it comes in two forms: sin recurso and con recurso, with different responsibilities.

The decree applied only to factoring companies set up as ordinary commercial companies, not supervised by the financial or solidarity regulators. The Superintendencia de Sociedades oversees these companies and maintains a register of factors.

The Decree’s Background

Decreto 2669 de 2012 was issued on 21 December 2012 by the Ministry of Commerce, Industry and Tourism. It took effect six months later, on 21 June 2013.

The decree’s stated purpose was to ease invoice circulation and help factoring grow for SMEs. The court’s ruling did not change that purpose, but it removed the detailed regulatory frame.

The six annulled articles had also been incorporated into Colombia’s consolidated commerce regulation, Decreto Único Reglamentario 1074 de 2015. They are now flagged as void in the official Normograma compilation.

What Survives the Ruling

Still, the rest of the decree stands, including article 8, which created the Registro Único Nacional de Factores. Article 9, which imposes anti-money-laundering duties on factors, also remains in force.

Despite this, the court did not annul article 6 on assignments or article 10 on corporate governance. Article 7 had already been repealed in 2014 and was not part of this ruling.

Anti-money-laundering duties survive because they rest on the statute rather than on the annulled articles. Factors’ directors remain responsible for compliance with article 8 of Ley 1231 de 2008.

The Court’s Reasoning

Even so, the court held that the Executive exceeded its regulatory power by setting essential rules. Meanwhile, the press note said the government could not issue a comprehensive regulation of this activity.

Moreover, the court explained that decrees may develop laws but cannot create new regulations for Congress. The annulled articles incorporated definitions, contract rules and restrictions that went beyond the law.

The plaintiff’s argument was that Ley 1231 de 2008 only sought to unify the invoice and give anti-money-laundering tools. It did not delegate the power to set the substantive regime for factoring.

Practical Effect on Factoring

As a result, factoring by these unsupervised companies falls back on Ley 1231 de 2008 and ordinary commercial law. This means freedom of contract will govern many aspects of factoring deals.

In short, the ruling eliminates a regulatory framework that exceeded the law, according to Póngase al Día. Firms should review their contract templates and compliance procedures.

Overall, factoring companies will operate with more flexibility but must still comply with surviving articles. The court did not examine other grounds raised in the suit, as it found the excess of regulatory power proven.

Background on the Consejo de Estado

The Consejo de Estado is Colombia’s highest administrative court, separate from the Constitutional Court. Its Sección Primera handles cases seeking to void government decrees for exceeding legal authority.

The court’s role is to ensure that regulations stay within the limits set by Congress. This ruling is an example of that oversight, as it struck down parts of a decree that went beyond the law.

The judgment is dated 4 June 2026, and the news was reported in August 2026 by Valora Analitik and La República. The court’s own press note was reproduced by El Correo.

What This Means for Colombia Factoring Decree

The Colombia factoring decree has been partially annulled, but the core regulatory framework for factoring companies remains. The annulment affects only six articles, not the entire decree.

Factoring companies are still supervised by the Superintendencia de Sociedades, and the register of factors remains in place. The ruling clarifies the limits of executive power in regulating this financial activity.

In short, the court has reaffirmed that the government cannot expand a law beyond its original scope. The Colombia factoring decree now stands with fewer rules, but the legal basis for factoring remains intact.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did the Consejo de Estado annul?

The court annulled six articles of Decreto 2669 de 2012: articles 2, 3, 4, 5, 12 and 13. These covered definitions, contract rules, funding sources and prohibited operations.

Why were the articles annulled?

The court found that the Executive exceeded its regulatory power, known as exceso en la potestad reglamentaria. The government added rules not authorized by Ley 1231 de 2008.

Does the ruling affect all of the decree?

No, only six articles were annulled. Articles 1, 6, 8, 9, 10, 11 and 14 remain in force, including the register of factors and anti-money-laundering duties.

What happens to factoring companies now?

Factoring by these commercial companies falls back on Ley 1231 de 2008 and ordinary commercial law. They are still supervised by the Superintendencia de Sociedades and must comply with anti-money-laundering rules.

Sources: Consejo de Estado press note; Valora Analitik; La República; El Correo; Póngase al Día; Régimen Legal de Bogotá, Secretaría Jurídica Distrital; Secretaría del Senado; official Normograma compilation.

World.title: Oil Industry Asks Brazil Crude Export Tax Be Left to Expire
World.content:
Brazil · ENERGY

Key Facts — Rate The Brazil crude export tax is 12 percent on the total value of crude petroleum exports.

— Legal basis The rate was set by Medida Provisória nº 1.340/2026 and is now in force under Resolução Gecex nº 938/2026.

— Validity The current tax is valid for 60 days from 10 July 2026, which calculates to 7 September 2026.

— Revenue estimate The government estimated the tax could raise R$ 15.6 billion in reais over four months.

— Impact Brazilian crude shipments fell 28.3 percent in May 2026 compared to April 2026, according to the IBP.

Brazil’s oil industry fears the tax will hurt competitiveness, but the finance ministry wants it kept until its current window ends.

An oil production platform off Brazil’s coast. The 12 percent tax applies to crude sold abroad.

The oil industry is asking that the Brazil crude export tax be left to expire. On Friday 21 August 2026, the Instituto Brasileiro de Petróleo, Gás e Biocombustíveis (IBP), the sector’s main trade body.

Sent a formal request to a minister asking that the tax’s validity not be extended.

What Is the Brazil Crude Export Tax?

In short, the Brazil crude export tax is a 12 percent levy on the total value of crude petroleum exports. In short, it was created by Medida Provisória nº 1.340/2026, signed by the federal government on 12 March 2026.

A Medida Provisória, or MP, is a presidential decree that has the force of law immediately. It must be approved by Congress within 60 days, extendable once by another 60 days, or it lapses.

The IBP, Brazil’s main oil and gas trade body, has formally asked a minister not to extend this tax. Meanwhile, the association represents over 200 member companies in the sector.

Why the Tax Was Introduced

The government said the tax was part of a package to mitigate the impact of higher oil prices. The explanatory memorandum stated the goal was to ‘capture and transfer to society part of the gain’ from higher oil prices.

In addition, the MP authorises the federal government to subsidise the sale of diesel used in transport. The finance ministry estimated the tax could raise about R$ 15.6 billion in reais over four months.

The government estimated potential revenue between R$ 13.9 billion and R$ 17.4 billion, depending on Brent prices. However, these are estimates, not actual amounts collected.

The Current Legal Framework

The original MP ran for 60 days and was automatically extended by another 60 days. That window ended in early July 2026, so the government issued Resolução Gecex nº 938/2026 to keep the tax in force.

The resolution, dated 9 July 2026, set the rate at 12 percent on crude petroleum oils under heading 2709. Therefore, it follows the Mercosur Common Nomenclature.

It entered into force on 10 July 2026 and is valid for 60 days from that date. The resolution’s Article 2 states the tax is valid for 60 days from its entry into force.

Therefore, it replaced the expired MP window, keeping the rate continuous since 10 July 2026.

When Does the Tax Expire?

Counting 60 days from Friday 10 July 2026, the sixtieth day falls on Monday 7 September 2026. This date is calculated from the text of Article 2 of the resolution, not printed in the document itself.

Therefore, the Brazil crude export tax is set to expire on that date unless the government decides to extend it. The Gecex resolution states the measure would be reassessed after 30 days.

The Gecex approved the measure on 9 July 2026, stating it would last up to 60 days and be reassessed after 30. As a result, the reassessment likely occurred around 9 August 2026.

The Industry’s Objection

The IBP argues the tax is ‘redundant and damaging to the country’s competitiveness’. It says the sector’s production-sharing model already captures price upcycles efficiently.

As evidence, the IBP noted that Brazilian crude shipments fell 28.3 percent in May 2026 compared to April 2026. The volume dropped from 62.8 million to 45 million barrels, with revenue down 23.3 percent.

The IBP’s evidence shows a sharp drop in May 2026 exports, highlighting the tax’s impact. Consequently, the association argues the measure is redundant given existing revenue mechanisms.

The Government’s Position

The Ministério da Fazenda, Brazil’s finance ministry, wants the tax kept. A technical note issued on 13 August 2026 recommends maintaining the 12 percent tax until the end of its validity.

The ministry’s secretary argues the tax should be kept until at least the end of the validity of Resolução Gecex 938. Therefore, the tax would remain in force until 7 September 2026, but not necessarily beyond.

The finance ministry’s technical note recommends keeping the tax until the end of its validity, not beyond. However, the secretary’s specific name has not been published in reports.

The Industry’s Earlier Request

This was not the IBP’s first such request. On 21 July 2026, the association objected and reiterated its request that the tax not be extended.

In addition, the IBP highlighted that Brazil distributed R$ 36.5 billion in oil royalties in the first half of 2026. Of that, R$ 9.6 billion, or 26.3 percent, was attributed to the surge in crude prices.

The IBP’s July request preceded the formal August pedido to the minister. Meanwhile, the association has consistently argued against extending the tax since its inception.

What Happens Next?

The decision on extending the Brazil crude export tax lies with Gecex-Camex, the executive management committee of Brazil’s Foreign Trade Chamber. This body sets and can reduce export tax rates.

As of 21 August 2026, the MP 1.340/2026 was still in tramitação, meaning it was still being processed by Congress. No definitive outcome has been confirmed, and the tax remains in force until its current window ends.

The Gecex-Camex, within the development ministry, will decide on any extension. Although the tax is set to expire on 7 September 2026, the government may act before then.

The Broader Context

The Brazil crude export tax is part of a broader debate about how the country captures windfall gains from oil. The IBP argues that the state already benefits through royalties and production-sharing agreements.

In short, the industry wants the tax to expire as scheduled. The finance ministry, by contrast, prefers to keep it until the end of its current validity.

The final decision will shape Brazil’s oil export competitiveness in the coming months. The IBP notes the production-sharing model already captures price upcycles efficiently.

Therefore, the tax may be seen as an unnecessary burden on the country’s competitiveness.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the Brazil crude export tax rate?

The Brazil crude export tax is set at 12 percent on the total value of crude petroleum exports. This rate was established by Medida Provisória nº 1.340/2026 and is currently in force under Resolução Gecex nº 938/2026.

When does the Brazil crude export tax expire?

The tax is valid for 60 days from 10 July 2026, which calculates to 7 September 2026. This date is derived from the text of the resolution, not printed in the document itself.

Why does the oil industry oppose the tax?

The IBP says the tax is redundant because the production-sharing model already captures price upcycles. It also points to a 28.3 percent drop in crude shipments in May 2026 as evidence of the tax’s negative impact.

What is the government’s position on the tax?

The finance ministry recommends keeping the 12 percent tax until the end of its validity. This means the tax would remain in force until 7 September 2026.

Sources: Agência Infra; Poder360; Agência Brasil; Valor Econômico; Instituto Brasileiro de Petróleo, Gás e Biocombustíveis; Ministério do Desenvolvimento, Indústria, Comércio e Serviços; Diário Oficial da União.

World.content:
Brazil · HEALTH

Key Facts — Investment R$ 8 million for the new linear accelerator, as reported by Estadão.

— Timeline The machine should begin operating between September and October, per Estadão.

— Treatment days Breast cancer courses may drop from 25 days to 15 or even 5 for some patients, says Dr. Heloísa de Andrade Carvalho.

— Prostate cancer The number of treatment days can be cut to almost half, depending on the case, says Carvalho.

— SUS context Brazil has 370 radiotherapy machines for the public system, according to the health ministry.

The new device could shorten treatment courses for some cancer patients, but it is not yet operating.

São Paulo radiotherapy is getting a boost with a new linear accelerator at a major public hospital, according to an Estadão column. The equipment, purchased by the Instituto de Radiologia do Hospital das Clínicas (InRad), could reduce treatment time for some cancer patients.

New Accelerator for São Paulo Radiotherapy

However, São Paulo radiotherapy is set to improve with a new linear accelerator acquired by InRad. As Estadão reported on 18 August 2026.

The machine, costing R$ 8 million, is part of the institute’s equipment renewal. The accelerator should begin operating between September and October, according to the column.

It is not yet treating patients, as the start date was still in the future when reported. The investment was R$ 8 million, according to Estadão.

However, the funder was not identified in any source. The equipment report rests solely on the Estadão column of 18 August 2026.

No official confirmation from the hospital or government has been found.

What the Estadão Column Says

The report comes from a single column by Alice Ferraz in Estadão, not from an official hospital announcement. Neither Hospital das Clínicas nor the state government has announced the purchase.

The column states that the new linear accelerator will allow the treatment time of some cancer patients to be reduced. This is a key development for São Paulo radiotherapy, though it is not yet operational.

The column quoted Dr. Heloísa de Andrade Carvalho, coordinator of the radiotherapy service. She described the benefits for some patients, but the machine is not yet operational.

The column states the machine will allow treatment time to be reduced for some cancer patients. However, it is not yet operational, as the start is scheduled for later.

Shorter Courses for Some Cancers

Dr. For example, Heloísa de Andrade Carvalho told Estadão that breast cancer patients who used to receive 25 days of treatment have moved to 15 days. Or as few as 5.

This refers to the number of treatment days in a course, not the length of each session. For prostate cancer, Carvalho said the number of days is cut to almost half, depending on the case.

However, these reductions apply only to some patients and some cancers, not universally. Carvalho’s comments were reported by Estadão on 18 August 2026.

These reductions, however, are not universal and depend on the case. These reductions are limited to certain patients and cancers, as the doctor noted.

Meanwhile, the exact number of days depends on the case.

Understanding Radiotherapy Courses

A radiotherapy course is the full series of appointments a patient attends, counted in days. A session is one single appointment, measured in minutes, but no source reports session lengths.

Therefore, newer linear accelerators can deliver doses more precisely, allowing fewer, larger daily doses for some cancers. This is the standard machine used in external-beam radiotherapy.

A linear accelerator generates high-energy beams directed at a tumour. Newer machines can deliver doses more precisely, enabling shorter courses for some cancers.

A course is the full series of appointments, counted in days, while a session is one appointment. However, no source reports the length in minutes of any session.

InRad and Hospital das Clínicas Context

InRad is the diagnostic imaging and radiotherapy institute inside the Hospital das Clínicas complex of the University of São Paulo medical school. The hospital, known as HC-FMUSP, is a public university teaching hospital and one of the largest in Latin America.

Still, in 2016, the São Paulo state government described the complex as the largest public radiotherapy centre in Latin America. But that claim is from an earlier project.

The complex is tied to the São Paulo state government and the University of São Paulo. In addition, it is widely described as one of the largest hospital complexes in Latin America.

InRad is part of the Hospital das Clínicas complex, tied to the University of São Paulo. In addition, the complex is described as one of the largest in Latin America.

SUS Waits and the 60-Day Law

The SUS, Brazil’s public health system, is free at the point of use. In addition, a 2012 law gives patients with malignant tumours the right to begin first treatment within 60 days of diagnosis.

However, waiting times are long. By contrast, according to Todos Juntos Contra o Câncer, reported by g1.

An SUS patient waits 50 days for diagnosis confirmation and another 75 days for first session. The 60-day law was passed in 2012, according to the fact sheet.

Still, waiting times remain long, as reported by g1. The 60-day law guarantees treatment start within that period after diagnosis.

However, the g1 report cites long waits for confirmation and first session.

Radiotherapy Equipment in Brazil

In fact, Brazil’s health ministry technical note from 2025 says the country has 370 radiotherapy machines for the SUS. Counting all legal categories.

Of these, public and non-profit establishments hold 318 linear accelerators, with 94 being over 15 years old and becoming obsolete. A separate 2026 health ministry presentation counts 365 accelerators in use in the SUS and 200 exclusively private ones.

These are different counts on different bases and should not be merged. The health ministry’s 2026 presentation counts 365 accelerators in the SUS.

Meanwhile, a separate 2025 note reports 318 in public and non-profit facilities. The health ministry’s 2025 note counts 370 machines for the SUS, while a 2026 presentation counts 365.

These are separate counts, so they must be reported distinctly.

Other Hospital Deliveries

Meanwhile, in June 2026, the federal government announced a linear accelerator for Hospital Santa Marcelina in São Paulo. With capacity for up to 1,000 treatments a year.

Uruguay wool prices held firm in early August 2026, with active demand moving the local market, according to Blasina y Asociados. The market note, dated 3 August, reported certified Merino lots trading at US$10.30 per kilo greasy for 18-micron wool.

Active Demand in the Local Market

However, Uruguay wool prices remained firm and actively traded in the week to 3 August 2026, according to Blasina y Asociados. The firm’s headline read “Active demand is moving wool business in the local market.

Certified Merino, greasy basis, saw 18-micron wool at US$10.30 per kilo. Lots around 19.5 microns fetched US$9.50, while 20-micron wool reached US$8.50.

Wool above 21 microns traded at US$7.15 per kilo. Coarser crossbred and Corriedale lots of 24 to 25 microns were referenced at US$4.00 to US$4.50.

In addition, the SUL reported a dozen wool deals in that week, though no total tonnage was published. Meanwhile, the market remained active, with certified Merino lots trading at firm prices.

Steady Prices Ten Days Later

By 13 August, Uruguay wool prices were still paying similar money, reported Actualidad Agropecuaria. Merino lots of 17.5, 18.5 and 19.2 microns changed hands between US$9.50 and US$11.00 per kilo greasy.

One meat-breed crossbred lot sold at US$2.00 per kilo for the fleece plus US$0.50 for the belly wool. The lots were small: 5,000 kg, 2,000 kg and 4,000 kg of Merino and 4,000 kg of crossbred wool.

In addition, the Secretariado Uruguayo de la Lana (SUL), the Uruguayan Wool Secretariat, reported a dozen wool deals in that week. It did not publish a total tonnage.

However, these small lots show that demand remained steady, even for coarser wool. As a result, the market held firm without any price slump.

New Season Opens With High Prices

The new zafra, the annual Uruguayan wool season, opened at high prices in July 2026. El Observador Agro reported references above US$11.00 per kilo greasy for certified 17- and 18-micron wool.

Corriedale lots around 28 microns started at US$2.00 to US$2.25 per kilo. The 2026/27 season began with expectations of holding record prices, according to El Observador Agro.

For the season just ended, prices rose between 36% and 81% depending on fineness. Superfine wool, below 16.5 microns, closed averaging US$9.74 per kilogram.

Meanwhile, the season just ended saw prices rise between 36% and 81% depending on fineness. In addition, superfine wool below 16.5 microns averaged US$9.74 per kilogram.

Exports Jump 32% in Value

Wool exports in 2026 to date reached 24.6 million kilos, up 3.4%, worth US$125 million, up 32%. China took 58% of the value and Italy 12%, according to El Observador Agro, citing the SUL.

The breakdown shows greasy wool exports of 9.5 million kilos, down 15%, but worth US$51.2 million, up 39%. Scoured wool exports rose 31% in volume and 79% in value to US$26.3 million.

Meanwhile, tops, combed and scoured wool sliver, reached 8.1 million kilos, up 11%, for US$47.4 million, up 45%. Italy took 30% of tops value and Germany 15%.

In addition, the sheep sector as a whole saw export earnings grow almost 40%, covering wool and sheepmeat. However, the 2026 export figures are partial, running to August only.

Global Benchmark Points Higher

The Eastern Market Indicator, published by the Australian Wool Exchange (AWEX), closed at AU$18.73, equivalent to US$13.11 per kilo clean. That was 61% above the same week of 2025, reported Todo El Campo.

However, the average price after four weeks of 2026/27 selling stood at US$13.11 per kilo clean. Because the Australian auction calendar is in its winter recess.

The recess found Australia at its best prices in five seasons. Australian clean-basis references included 16.5 microns at US$18.15 per kilo and 18 microns at US$17.31.

The rally began in January 2026, when the indicator closed at US$11.04 per kilo clean. Meanwhile, the Eastern Market Indicator closed at US$13.11 per kilo clean, 61% above the same week of 2025.

As a result, Australian wool was at its best prices in five seasons.

Understanding the Zafra

The zafra is the annual Uruguayan wool season, covering the yearly cycle of shearing, classing and selling the clip. Uruguay’s main shearing runs through spring and summer, roughly September to February.

This cycle is central to how Uruguay wool prices are set each year. The new season’s opening references set the tone for the months ahead.

In addition, the SUL reported growth of almost 40% in export earnings from the sheep sector as a whole. This covers wool and sheepmeat.

In addition, the zafra’s opening references set the tone for the months ahead. However, the market has been trading continuously, with no suspension or reopening.

What Microns Mean for Price

A micron is one millionth of a metre and measures a wool fibre’s diameter. Finer wool, with fewer microns, is worth more because it is softer against the skin.

In fact, it can be spun into light, high-value cloth. Merino sheep grow the finest wool, while Corriedale, a dual-purpose breed, grows coarser wool.

This explains why 18-micron Merino fetches US$10.30 per kilo greasy, while 28-micron Corriedale is around US$2.50. So, Uruguay wool prices vary widely by fineness.

The grifa verde, or green tag, is the SUL’s classing and certification system that confirms a lot’s quality. Meanwhile, the grifa verde classing system confirms a lot’s quality and origin.

As a result, certified lots can command premium prices.

Greasy vs Clean Basis

Greasy or fleece basis means wool weighed as shorn, still carrying grease, dirt and vegetable matter. Clean basis means the weight after scouring, and prices on the two bases are not comparable.

Uruguayan lot prices in this article are greasy, while the Australian indicator figures are clean. Therefore, do not compare them directly.

Tops are combed, scoured wool sliver, a semi-processed product one step below yarn. They are Uruguay’s highest-value wool export line.

In addition, tops are a semi-processed product and Uruguay’s highest-value wool export line. However, clean-basis prices are much higher per kilo than greasy.

Uruguay wool prices are holding firm as the new season progresses, with active demand and high opening references. The export value jump of 32% reflects strong global demand, especially from China.

However, the 2026 export figures are partial, running to August only, and not comparable to the full-year 2025 total. In 2025, Uruguay exported 42.3 million kilos worth US$159.3 million.

Overall, the market remains robust, with the SUL reporting a dozen deals in a single week. The sheep flock stands at 4,752,400 held by 21,597 registered holders in 2025.

However, the 2026 export figures are partial and not comparable to the full-year 2025 total. Meanwhile, the market remains robust with active demand and high prices.

Export value rose to US$125 million in 2026 to date, up 32%, driven by higher prices. Volume only grew 3.4%, so the jump came from price gains, especially in greasy and scoured wool.

The zafra is the annual Uruguayan wool season, covering shearing, classing and selling the clip. It runs roughly from September to February, with the new season opening in July with high price references.

How does micron affect wool price?

Micron measures wool fibre diameter; finer wool has fewer microns and is worth more. For example, 18-micron Merino fetches US$10.30 per kilo greasy, while 28-micron Corriedale is around US$2.50.
