World.title: COP17 in Mongolia: Finding solutions to land degradation
World.content:
Geography says that 70% of land mass on our planet is suitable for human life. The rest is an extreme environment where people can hardly survive. But that proportion is rapidly changing. 40% of the soil humanity uses to sustain itself is already degraded and is becoming barren. Brought about by climate change, drought, misuse of agricultural land and other human activity, much of the habitable land is turning into a desert with natural, known deserts expanding every day.

 

This crisis was detected and its effects scientifically described already in the 20th century. The United Nations appealed to the member states saying that every community needs land to sustain life. Without land there is no food and it triggers poverty, migration and conflict. That is why the United Nations Convention to Combat Desertification (UNCCD) was approved in 1994 and came into force in 1996. It has 197 signatories. They meet regularly to find mechanisms to fight desertification and land degradation.

This year the United Nations entrusted Mongolia with organising the conference of parties, COP17. It opened in the capital of Ulaanbaatar on August 17 with participation of most UNCCD member states and over 400 different organisations and community representatives.

One of more than 400 sessions at the COP17 Euronews

State representatives are elaborating on the plans and funding of the UNCCD. This is the only legally binding mechanism that tackles land degradation. In addition to them, hundreds of experts from academic community, NGOs and government institutions gathered to exchange their experience with loss of soil and share thoughts and plans how to stop desertification and land degradation.

Why they need to do something urgently can be expressed in figures. Almost 3 and a half billion people on the planet are affected by land degradation. According to some estimates, it costs their states and local communities 900 million dollars every year to do something about it and save people from loss of income and food sources.

Droughts have increased by two thirds since the year 2000.

Water is becoming a scarce resource and the demand for it will surpass the sources by 40% by 2030.

85% of the affected people live in medium and low-income countries and much of the mass migration has to do with food and income being unavailable due to land degradation.

Our languages, cultures, ethnic backgrounds and religions may differ, but we share a common determination to safeguard the future in which we can all continue to live in harmony with Mother Earth. Nyam-Osoryn Uchral Prime Minister of Mongolia

The story of the host country, Mongolia where cost to produce a loaf of bread has tripled over just one past decade was repeated by all other participating regions. From the very opening, the leaders were eager to stress that the COP17 is not about some distant environmental worry, but about the problem that is already here and getting worse by the month.

“This summer we saw across different parts of the world, also in Europe, how drought disrupted river transport and strained energy production. It reduced agricultural yield and induced wildfire with losses of lives. Similar stories are there around different parts of the world that we never thought would be affected. The message is clear, droughts are no longer just an environmental issue, they are not just absence of rain or a geographic environmental issue. They are a systemic risk to food and water security, to international commerce, energy supply, livelihood and , simply to stability and prosperity,” said dr Yasmin Foudh, Executive Secretary of the UNCCD at the opening ceremony.

Prime Minister of host country Mongolia, Nyam-Osoryn Uchral TenGer TV, Mongolia

Mongolia has been chosen as the venue for the COP17 for three reasons. First, it wanted to be the host and applied 4 years ago. Second, it is among the countries that feel effects of land degradation. Over the last 8 decades the average temperature in Mongolia rose by 2 degrees Celsius and precipitation dropped significantly. Winds started carrying sand from the Gobi desert over the Mongolian flatlands all the way to South Korean and even Japan. Last but not least, it has been on the forefront of global efforts to combat the spread of deserts.

“Mongolia, our vast country, is among the most affected by the challenges facing the world today. On this vast territory, where there are only two people per every square kilometre, 77% of the country, or in another words, eight out of every ten steps of the land, are affected by desertification and is increasingly being covered by the encroaching sands,” said Mongolian Prime Minister, reminding that since his country joined the UN Convention on Combating Desertification, it has implemented many measures in its development plans.

Assuming the role of the COP17 president, Mongolia’s Foreign Minister Battsetseg Batmunkh pledged her country’s full commitment to combating the degradation of the land that the fabric of her nomadic nation is made of. Pledge supported by action taken so far.

“Today, Mongolia is contributing to global efforts through national initiatives aimed at protecting ecosystems, combating desertification, restoring degraded land, strengthening food security and increasing the resilience of our people and communities. The Billion Trees National Movement, the Food Revolution, White Gold and Unlock initiatives launched by the President and the Prime Minister of Mongolia, together with the recently adopted law on climate change, are tangible expressions of this national commitment. At the multilateral level, Mongolia initiated the United Nations General Assembly resolution proclaiming 2026 as the International Year of Rangelands and Pastoralists,” said Foreign Minister Batmunkh.

What are the solutions and what can COP17 achieve?

There is no one solution to the problem of desertification as each region has its own specific problems with drought, land degradation and their consequences. The sheer scale of the expense needed to combat the problem, estimated at almost 6,500 billion dollars a year sounds like unsustainable lost cause. But it is not so.

Experts have calculated and business people proved, that in many projects aimed at saving soil from turning into Mars-like surface, for every 1 dollar invested you can get 7 to 30 back. Because it is the investment into sustainable food production and green projects, all of which is profitable.

This is fortunate because it allows for the private money to flow into the desperately needed solutions. Since the establishment of UNCCD many countries have implemented measures and added them to their development programmes. Public-private cooperation have been established.

“Countries have already committed to the one billion hectare by 2030 and more than 70 countries had submitted already their drought management plans. So we are not starting from scratch. More than 100 countries would like to translate the land plans into actual projects, investable projects with the potential of 2 billion US dollars. More than 300 businesses are already engaging with us here,” says executive secretary Foudh.

There are many corporate parties involved in the conference as it seeks to utilize private funds and only the host country expects more than 1.5 billion dollars of funds to be directed at its programmes of re-forestation, green energy and sustainable agriculture.

But equally important impact of COP conferences is the interaction between all the stakeholders in the battle against losing soil. In this particular one, more than 500 representatives of indigenous communities, from Amazonia, through Africa to the Asian steppes, were able to speak and relate their problems and proposed solutions.

With 60 organisations exhibiting their solutions and over 400 cultural and scientific events, COP17 also promises to be the of the busiest and liveliest ones during the 12 days of gathering.

Organisers expect more than 30,000 people to visit the event before it closes on August 28.

World.title: German Chancellor Merz visits Hürtgen Forest fire site amid boos and whistles
World.content:
It was his first public engagement after the summer break: Two days after the complete extinguishing of the forest fire in the Hürtgen Forest, Federal Chancellor Friedrich Merz (CDU) visited the affected area today to thank the emergency services.

 

Merz was met with boos and whistles. Numerous onlookers gathered on the village square where Merz arrived. At times the chancellor was barely audible, as his words were drowned out.

A member of the Hürtgenwald volunteer fire brigade expressed anger at the loud reactions. "Those who are shouting and whistling should turn that negative energy into positive energy and become members of the fire brigade or of the THW," said the firefighter.

Merz said he had deliberately chosen to travel to Hürtgenwald-Gey only today. He had wanted to ensure that the emergency crews could work undisturbed. At the same time, he said, he had been continuously briefed on the situation and had asked the local authorities what support was needed to bring the fire under control as quickly as possible.

Merz was thus responding to criticism that he had arrived at the scene too late. "I am not impressed by those who stand there shouting," Merz said. "I talk to the people who are not shouting, but who are working. I talk to those who help and to those who act in the interests of the community."

The chancellor described the large-scale forest fire in Hürtgenwald and the High Fens as a consequence of climate change. However, he did not spell out which concrete measures should be derived from this. He said he had come to Gey above all to thank the emergency services for their efforts and commitment.

Earlier, during a visit to the forest, Merz had seen the scale of the damage for himself.

Largest forest fire in North Rhine-Westphalia's history

The blaze broke out during the recent heatwave and spread rapidly because of the dry soils and woodland. According to North Rhine-Westphalia's agriculture ministry, around 300 to 400 hectares of forest – equivalent to roughly 420 to 560 football pitches – were damaged or destroyed. The authorities described the fire as the largest forest fire in the history of North Rhine-Westphalia.

At the height of the operation, around 1,400 emergency personnel and about ten firefighting helicopters were deployed. Four armoured vehicles were also used to cut firebreaks and support the firefighting efforts.

The nearby village of Gey had to be evacuated at times. Around 1,800 people were affected. After about a week, the fire was finally extinguished completely.

Criticism of Merz's late visit

Politically, the visit has sparked debate. While the forest fire was still raging, no member of the federal government was on the ground. Merz was on his summer holiday at the time, but said he was being regularly briefed on the situation.

By contrast, North Rhine-Westphalia's state premier Hendrik Wüst (CDU) interrupted his holiday and visited the affected area. Opposition politicians, especially from the Greens, criticised Merz's decision not to travel to the region earlier.

The federal government defended the chancellor, pointing out that he had been kept informed of developments during his holiday and could have intervened if needed.

The issue is likely to remain relevant beyond the current forest fire. At next week's cabinet retreat, topics will include heat protection, climate adaptation and how to deal with increasingly frequent extreme weather events.

The cabinet retreat at Neuhardenberg Castle is scheduled for Tuesday, 25 August, on the federal government's official calendar.

World.title: Poland: Man who ordered 300 pizzas in food-delivery pranks faces up to eight years in prison
World.content:
Polish authorities have launched mesaures to deal with malicious food-delivery pranks after persistent harassment and threats issued via bogus orders for meals to be paid for on delivery began to resurface.

 

Officers from the Central Bureau for Combating Cybercrime (CBZC), under the supervision of the District Prosecutor's Office in Szczecin, say they have detained a man suspected of organising the scheme.

The 23 year old suspect faces up to eight years in prison for stalking, identity fraud, and causing massive financial harm to local restaurants by ordering hundreds of unpaid meals (including 300 pizzas) to random, unsuspecting residents.

Authorities say the man has been remanded in custody for two months.

Threats issued in the orders

Some of the descriptions of the orders repeatedly included detailed information about the victims, which could only have been known to them or those closest to them according to local authorities.

These actions left them feeling threatened and tormented, and also constituted an intrusion into their privacy, CBZC said.

The orders themselves also contained threats, including references to abducting a minor, setting fire to a notary's office and causing a road accident, the agency added.

Local media reports the man also used the personal details of well-known figures from politics and the media, listing them as the recipients of the meals. One of the orders was for an amount exceeding 37,000 zlotys, the equivalent of _€_8.572.

The deliveries were primarily meant to go to addresses in Szczecin, but orders were also placed to other cities, including Wrocław, Kraków and Warsaw, where more than a dozen such incidents were recorded.

However, the people indicated as recipients were not informed about the orders placed in their name.

Not all of the orders were fulfilled. In some cases, restaurants refused to accept them for technical reasons, especially where the number of meals ordered made efficient preparation impossible, as in the case of an order for 300 pizzas.

Joint operations by officers from the Central Bureau for Combating Cybercrime and the Investigative Department of the Municipal Police Headquarters in Szczecin led to the suspect being detained at his home.

During the search, police seized devices and data carriers that may have been used to place the fake orders.

World.title: France to give new interceptor missiles to Ukraine, Macron says
World.content:
French President Emmanuel Macron announced on Saturday that France would deliver new interceptor missiles to Kyiv following a major Russian attack on a shopping centre in Kryvyi Rih in central Ukraine.

 

Ukrainian authorities said Russia launched two waves of drone attacks on the city on Friday, killing at least 16 people and injuring 130 others, including 23 children.

The attack on Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's hometown has prompted condemnation from leading figures across Europe, with Kaja Kallas, the EU's top diplomat, calling it "terror by design."

In a post on X, Macron said he had spoken with Zelenskyy following the daylight "double strike" on Kryvyi Rih and that he had expressed his "horror" and "deep concern" over the incident.

"It is crucial to provide Ukraine with all the necessary means to defend its airspace and thwart this aggression," he wrote, adding that he had informed Zelenskyy of Paris' "increased support, including the deployment of interceptors."

"We must also continue to increase the pressure on Russia as long as it chooses to refuse to halt the fighting and make peace," he added.

Zelenskyy said in a separate post that the pair had spoken for close to two hours, touching on Ukraine's air defence needs, funding, and communications with Washington, among other things.

"We agreed to accelerate the delivery of the latest French equipment and missiles. Thank you for confirming your readiness to provide licenses for the production of missiles," Zelenskyy wrote.

Kyiv has long been pleading with allies for more interceptor missiles as it continues to fend off Russian missile and drone attacks.

Ukraine strikes back

Ukraine launched its own strikes against Russia over the last 24 hours, hitting the Novokuybyshevsk oil refinery, a logistics hub in the Samara region, and targets in the Black Sea, per Zelenskyy.

Kyiv has been ramping up its so-called "long-range sanctions" on Russia in recent months as it seeks to hamper the Russian economy and grind down Vladimir Putin's war machine.

It has particularly targeted energy infrastructure sites such as oil refineries, depots, and terminals as part of this strategy.

World.title: Health ministry mobilises vaccines to Ceuta after tuberculosis and scabies cases detected
World.content:
The Ministry of Health has called an emergency meeting with Spain's autonomous communities to address the supply of vaccines for migrants who remain in Ceuta after the mass arrivals from Morocco recorded at the end of July.

 

The extraordinary meeting of the Public Health Commission will take place this Monday 24 August at 12:00 by videoconference, according to several Spanish media outlets, and will be attended by Public Health representatives from the autonomous communities and cities.

According to information first reported by 'El Mundo', the meeting will have a single item on the agenda: the launch of a "solidarity mechanism for vaccines in relation to the situation in Ceuta".

The aim of the meeting is to ensure that the autonomous city has the doses it needs to immunise the migrants who are still there and to strengthen protection against various infectious diseases.

Vaccines against polio, diphtheria and chickenpox

Among the vaccines the Health Ministry plans to administer is the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) jab, which protects against measles, mumps and rubella. Immunisation is also being considered against diseases such as chickenpox, poliomyelitis, tetanus and diphtheria.

The migration crisis has also increased pressure on the city's health services. Between 31 July and 14 August, the National Institute of Health Management (Ingesa) recorded 5,801 medical attendances linked to the crisis, while the Red Cross operation set up on Trampolín beach provided more than 2,500 additional consultations. The peak came on 31 July, with 1,149 attendances in a single day.

The Health Ministry has also reported 18 minors with a positive Mantoux test and two confirmed cases of tuberculosis. Healthcare professionals have also reported consultations related to gastroenteritis, scabies and impetigo. The Spanish Army has logged at least 24 cases of scabies among its personnel at the General Command in Ceuta.

The Spanish Society of Epidemiology warns, however, that these diseases should not be directly linked to migrant status and stresses that the health problems are mainly related to the overcrowding, poor sanitary conditions and lack of resources in which some of these people are living.

World.title: Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan strengthen ties as Israel tensions rise
World.content:
Tensions between Turkey and Israel have intensified after an Israeli airstrike targeted a Syrian military airbase near the Turkish border. The strike came days after Turkey’s new military pact with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan.

Advertising

Ankara swiftly condemned Tuesday's Israeli airstrike on Syria’s Abu Duhur military airbase, 70 kilometres from its border, calling it illegal and a breach of Syrian sovereignty.

Ankara is a key ally of Syria's new authorities. Israel justified its actions, accusing Turkey of seeking to expand its military footprint in Syria, which it sees as a serious threat.

“Israel is uneasy about the Turkish presence in Syria, and Turkish ambitions to play a major role in Syria’s future are unsettling from an Israeli perspective,” explains Turkey expert Gallia Lindenstrauss of Israel's Institute for National Security Studies.

“There's concern that Turkey will establish its own bases in Syria,” she added.

Israeli-Turkish tensions have risen over Israel’s war in Gaza and Lebanon, and Ankara’s support of Hamas, evolving into a broader regional rivalry.

“In general, there's uneasiness [in Israel] about Turkey's assertiveness, both in Syria and in the Mediterranean and other parts of the Middle East and the greater regional arena," said Lindenstrauss.

Landmark agreement

Earlier this month, Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan made headlines by signing a landmark military accord in the Saudi city of Mecca. Known as the Mecca Accord, this alliance pledges mutual defence if any member is attacked, akin to NATO’s Article 5.

Turkish international relations expert Soli Ozel claims the impetus for the agreement is uncertainty around Washington’s willingness or ability to protect its regional allies amid ongoing tensions involving Iran.

“Undoubtedly, the United States is proving to be an increasingly unreliable partner. Countries worldwide, especially in the larger Middle East region, are looking for other ways to provide security for themselves,” said Ozel.

Iran says ‘Muslim Nato’ pact reflects retreat from US security umbrella

The Mecca Accord members view each other as bringing complementary strengths to deal with shared concerns.

"Pakistan brings military capabilities and is a nuclear power. The Saudis have the money. Turkey has a budding defence industry and a large army. It claims not to be against any country, but I think those three parties agree that Iran is a destabilising actor, as is Israel,” explained Ozel.

The Mecca Accord is set to boost defence and intelligence ties, with Saudi Arabia expected to bolster Turkey’s expanding defence sector.

But many analysts see Iran and Israel as the accord’s principal focus.

“The deal is meant to signal both to Iran and Israel that they will be isolated in the region if they continue with assertive, belligerent policies,” said Asli Aydintasbas of the United States-based Brookings Institution.

Turkey steps up as Europe's indispensable and uncomfortable defence partner

'Two axes in the Middle East'

Despite Iran’s recent attacks on Saudi Arabia, Aydintasbas argues that while the Mecca Accord has a mutual defence clause – meaning an attack on one member is an attack on all – Turkey and Pakistan will not be drawn into a conflict with Iran.

“We know that they have no desire to get involved. But it does mean there will be greater military cooperation,” said Aydintasbas.

Countering Houthi rebel attacks in the Red Sea on Saudi tankers could be the first real test of the alliance.

But Aydintasbas cautions that the Mecca Accord will not replace the US as the “ultimate security provider” for the region. Instead, it's more about burden sharing, a move that fits well with Washington’s wider agenda.

Washington has given its blessing to the accord, and expansion talks are already under way.

European Union slams 'inflammatory' Houthi Red Sea tanker attack

Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan hinted that Egypt could be the next member, with Turkish media reporting that Egypt’s foreign minister will join his Saudi, Turkish and Pakistani counterparts for a meeting in Istanbul later this month.

“Developments in Egypt are of major concern to Israel,” said Lindenstrauss. But she believes the Mecca Accord is an opportunity for Israel, given there are mutual concerns among its allies over the Accord.

“Israel already has very close relations with Greece, Cyprus, the United Arab Emirates and India,” she noted. "And I do envision a deepening of this relationship. And so we have the formation of two loose axes in the Greater Middle East."

World.title: Iran warns countries against joining US 'economic war'
World.content:
Iran has said nations joining US economic sanctions against it would be considered enemies. Earlier this week, President Trump had announced what he called the "most crushing economic operation" against Tehran.

Iran on Saturday warned countries against joining the United States' campaign to isolate the Iranian economy.

"We declare to all countries... do not join the economic war waged by the United States," said Mohsen Rezaei, the head of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, on state television.

"Any country participating in the imposition of economic restrictions against us is considered an enemy," he added.

As the war nears its six-month anniversary, US President Donald Trump announced earlier this week what he called the "most crushing economic operation" against Tehran.

Should Trump "take action, our confrontation will be like an earthquake," said Rezaei.

US urges others to back Iran sanctions

Washington has also called on other governments to join its efforts to ramp up economic pressure against Iran.

But China, one of Iran's top strategic partners, has criticized the new campaign, arguing that "sanctions and pressure will not help resolve the issue."

"China calls on all relevant parties to take responsible measures and resolve the problem through political and diplomatic means," Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Lin Jian told reporters on Friday.

The United Arab Emirates, a major trading partner for sanctioned Iran, already announced on Wednesday that it was cutting all financial and economic ties with Tehran until further notice.

The decision was made in "light of escalations that undermine peace and security in the region," the UAE said in a statement .

US-Iran war: Will it ever end? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

US tells allies: 'With us or against us'

Talks between Washington and Tehran remain on hold after nearly six months of war since the US and Israel launched airstrikes against Iran on February 28.

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent is expected to hold a press conference at 2 p.m. EDT (1800 GMT) on Monday to give further details of the economic measures against Iran.

"This is going to be the greatest coordinated economic isolation in the history of the world. And we are going to them and saying you are either with us or against us,” Bessent said.

Since the 1979 Islamic Revolution, Iran has faced almost 50 years of near-continuous economic sanctions.

World.title: Canada to hit back with retaliatory tariffs after US trade talks fail
World.content:
The trade standoff between Ottawa and Washington has escalated as Canada announced tariffs on US products. The move comes in response to the US saying that tariffs would follow the collapse of talks.

In an ongoing trade dispute with the United States, Canada said on Saturday that it would introduce tariffs on several US products starting September 8.

The announcement comes in retaliation to the US imposing 50% tariffs earlier on Saturday on a broad range of Canadian products after the two sides failed to reach a trade deal on Friday.

"Canada will match Washington's new ⁠tariffs ​dollar for dollar in order to protect ​Canadian workers, farmers, families, and businesses," Prime Minister Mark Carney told reporters in Ottawa.

"In the coming days, we will release the details of these new tariff measures, which will come into force the Tuesday after Labor Day," he said.

While the US had blamed Canada for declining to finalize the trade pact with Washington on Friday, Carney defended Ottawa's position, explaining, "We cannot accept what they have offered, and we will not give what they have asked."

He later on Saturday met virtually with provincial and territorial premiers to discuss the suspension of the trade talks with the US.

What products are affected by the tariffs?

The US tariffs will affect a broad range of products, including wine, furniture, dairy products, cement, clothing, fishing ‌rods, and hockey ​equipment, and cover some $20 billion (€17 billion) worth of Canadian exports to its southern neighbor.

Canada's retaliatory tariffs would, in turn, target steel, dairy, appliances, agricultural equipment, pulp and paper and electronics, Carney said.

The US currently accounts for roughly 70% of Canadian exports, making Ottawa potentially more vulnerable in the standoff Carney explicitly described as a trade "war."

"You're at war when you get attacked. We got attacked," he said, adding that Canada had the reserves, resilience and plan to respond.

How have Canadian and US politicians reacted?

Doug Ford, the premier of Canada's most populous province Ontario and one of the most vocal opponents of Trump's tariffs, slammed the proposed trade deal and backed Carney's decision to retaliate.

"I'm glad he didn't sign that deal because it was a bad deal. It was a bad deal for Ontario. It was a bad deal for the auto sector, the steel sector and ​manufacturing sector," Ford said on Saturday.

In the US, Democratic lawmakers and governors have blamed Trump for the escalating trade conflict.

"Needlessly picking fights with our allies and raising prices here at home. That's Trump's economic policy in a nutshell," New York Governor Kathy Hochul posted on X.

During a 2025 Washington trip, Carney was still all smiles — but tensions appear to have worsened Image: Evelyn Hockstein/REUTERS

Friendly ties turned sour

The fresh tariffs are the culmination of long and tense trade negotiations between the two sides and mark a sharp reversal from just two days earlier, when officials from Washington and Ottawa appeared optimistic that a compromise was in the making.

According to the AP news agency, no further talks were planned to resolve the situation.

The US administration's approach to Canada is a major change from the friendly ties the two countries have traditionally had.

US President Donald Trump has often said he wants tariffs on Canadian goods to encourage companies to move manufacturing back to the US.

He has also made controversial comments about making Canada the 51st US state. Carney said Canada understood that "America has changed" and that the two countries would "not return to their old relationship."

World.title: Cargo vessel sinks off Indian coast
World.content:
The Panama‑flagged Ocean Winner reportedly had a crew of 24, at least two of whom appear to have been rescued. The ship is thought to have been carrying iron ore from India to Singapore.

A cargo ship has sunk off the eastern coast of India, the country's coast guard said. The Panama-flagged vessel Ocean Winner had 24 crew on board, at least two of whom were reportedly rescued.

The crew included 20 Chinese nationals, three seamen from Myanmar and one from Bangladesh, Indian officials said.

Why the ship sank remains unclear.

According to officials cited in the Indian Express, the ship was about 240 nautical miles (444 kilometers, 276 miles) off the coast of Odisha. A joint operation by the Indian Coast Guard and the country's navy was underway to find more survivors.

The Hindustan Times reported local Paradip police official Sanjay Negi saying that rescue teams would reach the site "by tomorrow morning" and that other vessels in the vicinity had been alerted to help with the rescue effort.

According to ship-tracking app MarineTraffic, the Ocean Winner was carrying iron ore from Paradip port in Odisha to Singapore.

World.title: Nigeria: Jihadis kidnap dozens during Friday prayers
World.content:
Witnesses said men carrying guns and machetes set upon two villages in Niger State. Many details about the attack have yet to be confirmed by police.

Extremists attacked and abducted a number of worshipers in Nigeria's Niger State, authorities said on Saturday.

Police said the armed men attacked a number of villages in the Borgu Local Government Area before storming mosque in the village Kpenya during Friday prayers.

"People were abducted while praying at a Juma’at mosque on Friday," Borgu area council chair Abdullahi Mohammed Nasir told the Associated Press.

"That was when the bad people came and surrounded the mosque and took them away."

Some witnesses recounted extreme violence.

"Soon after finishing the normal Friday prayer, the armed group [...] in their hundreds, wielding guns, knives and machetes, began to attack us," one survivor told the AFP news agency. "They slaughtered some of our people, saying we are not practicing the true teachings of Islam."

Local residents told the AFP and Reuters news agencies that dozens of people — as many as 60 — were kidnapped.

Witnesses also told AFP that the armed men killed several people, although according to police, "the developing report indicated that no life ‌was ​lost."

Who was responsible for the attack?

No group claimed responsibilityfor the attack in the day that followed and police have not identified the culprits.

One witness told AFP that the gunmen belonged to Lakurawa — an increasingly radical outfit that researchers link to the "Islamic State Sahel Province" group.

Another resident told AFP that the attackers were Ansaru, which split from Boko Haram and is now aligned with al-Qaeda.

Witnesses also said that a third, rival jihadi group known as Mahmuda clashed with the attackers and allowed some of the abductees to escape.

Nigeria develops drone tech to fight insurgents To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Although jihadi attacks have declined in Nigeria since the height of Boko Haram's insurgency last decade, the military and police remain overstretched as they face multiple, sometimes overlapping conflicts.

In addition to jihadist insurgency in the north, parts of Nigeria also face violence and kidnappings from non-ideological gangs known locally as "bandits."

World.title: Germany news: Friedrich Merz visits area struck by fires
World.content:
08/22/2026 August 22, 2026 Merz says forest fires 'a consequence of climate change'

Merz thanks firefighters for battling the blaze, and came in for criticism for not ending his vacation to meet them earlier Image: Christoph Reichwein/dpa/picture alliance

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz thanked local firefighters for their efforts battling last week's dramatic forest fire in western Germany's Eifel region and stressed that such fires are a consequence of climate change.

"We have to expect such events more often," he said during a visit to the communities affected by the fires. "This is climate change."

"I want to tell all those climate change deniers: Look at what's happening here," he added.

Merz said he would do everything possible to combat climate change but stressed that "we also have to live with climate change."

When it comes to climate policy, Merz's CDU has stressed the importance of market-based strategies rather than bans to protect the environment.

He was met with whistles and boos from people holding signs and saying Merz's government has not adequately addressed the climate crisis.

The chancellor thanked the firefighters and all other local groups that helped fight the Hürtgenwald fire that raged for a week, forcing the evacuation of entire villages before it was finally extinguished late last week.

It was Merz's first public appearance since July 29, when he left for his summer vacation. He previously thanked emergency workers for their "tireless effort" on X.

Opposition parties criticized his prolonged absence while the country was grappling with heat waves and forest fires and suggested he was not taking climate change seriously.

World.title: Kazakhstan's future after the elections: Russia, EU or China
World.content:
Kazakhstan, where power is being continuously consolidated in the president's hands, will have to continue its tough balancing act between the EU, Russia and China following the parliamentary elections this Sunday.

On August 23, Kazakhstan, a former Soviet country that has recently adopted a new constitution, will hold elections to its parliament.

The legislative body will be transformed from a two-chamber to a single-chamber system. Citizens will elect 145 members of parliament via party lists. All seven registered parties have been admitted to the election, including the ruling party, Adilet (which translates to "Justice").

But the election result is the least of the campaign's intrigues. Experts DW interviewed agree that no party other than President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev's Adilet stands a chance of winning.

Consolidation of power in the president's hands

Luca Anceschi, Professor of Eurasian Studies at the University of Glasgow, Scotland, suggests that the new parliament will do the same as the previous one, "which is pretty much to represent whatever the regime wants them to do."

In his view, one should not expect representatives of the genuine opposition to be elected to parliament.

Stefan Meister, Head of the Center for Order and Governance in Eastern Europe, Russia and Central Asia at the German Council on Foreign Relations (DGAP), shares this assessment. He says the ruling party is likely to win the election, a scenario also reflected in recent opinion polls.

Both experts agree that these elections are intended to consolidate Tokayev's power and further weaken the bloc led by Nursultan Nazarbayev, the country's president from 1991-2019.

Constitutional amendments approved earlier allow Tokayev to seek another seven-year presidential term in 2029 and replace the two-chamber parliament with a single-chamber assembly called the Kurultai.

Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev voted in the referendum on a new constitution for his country on March 15, 2026 Image: Kazakh Presidential Press Service/REUTERS

According to former Kazakhstani senator Zauresh Battalova, who now heads the NGO Foundation for the Development of Parliamentarism in Kazakhstan, what matters is not the number of chambers in parliament, but "the scope of its powers, its autonomy and its ability to oversee the executive branch of government."

The new constitution has changed not only the structure of parliament but also the way its members are elected. Independent candidates are no longer allowed to run under the current electoral system. Zauresh Battalova sees this as one of the factors limiting voters' political choice.

"The election will be held exclusively on the basis of party lists, in the absence of a political opposition and with limited party competition. The scope for genuine political choice remains extremely narrow," she told DW.

Kazakhstan's democratic backlash: Will Europe react?

Meister and Anceschi both say that one should not expect any reaction from European Union members or the European Commission to the deterioration in political freedoms in Kazakhstan.

Meister points out that, since the start of the war in Ukraine, the EU has adopted a more pragmatic approach towards Central Asian states. Europe is now interested in developing trade routes as an alternative to those via Russia, as well as in the region's abundant resources. In his view, the only bodies likely to react to the current situation in Kazakhstan are civil society organizations, the European Parliament or the Council of Europe.

The election campaign ahead of Kazakhstan's parliamentary elections involves more than just posters and info flyers Image: Anatolij Weißkopf/DW

"The days when the European Union and individual EU member states were more critical of the rule of law and governance in Central Asia are gone, unfortunately," Anceschi says.

The University of Glasgow professor notes that an authoritarian backslide is taking place not only in Kazakhstan but also in other EU partner countries.

As for Kazakhstan itself, says Meister, it remains the least repressive authoritarian country in the region, with at least some space for civil society, albeit one that is narrowing.

"Wherever you buy your oil and gas from, you are never going to buy it from a democracy ― unless it is Norway. So, in that sense, there is not much of a choice," Anceschi says.

In 2025, Kazakhstan became the second-largest oil exporter to the EU, with a total share of 12.8%, amounting to 55.8 million tons of crude oil, surpassed only by the United States, according to the European Council of the EU .

The future of Kazakhstan's foreign policy

Experts acknowledge that Kazakhstan has managed to remain neutral in the standoff between Russia and Europe against the backdrop of the war in Ukraine. Maintaining this course may prove difficult.

"They are affected by the conflict, but they are not participating," says Anceschi, describing the country's current position as a "geopolitical comfort zone."

How can Kazakhstan navigate ties with Russia and China? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Kazakhstan has not officially opposed the European sanctions against Russia, nor has it joined them.

"Of course, it is a task with only one ultimate goal, which is the preservation of authoritarian rule," Anceschi says. "So even in this case, foreign policy is becoming an instrument for achieving internal stability."

Meister, in turn, draws attention to the increasing level of cooperation between the Central Asian states, which, facing significant external pressure, tend to act as a single bloc while actively seeking to reduce tensions among themselves. He suggests that Kazakhstan is interested in diversifying its external relations not only with the EU, Russia and China, but also with other world powers, such as Arab or East Asian states.

According to Meister, Kazakhstan "does not want to be too dependent on Russia ― it has seen what Russia is doing in Ukraine ― and it does not want to be dependent on China."

So, the country is looking for alternatives, and Europe could be one of them, both as a market for its resources and as a potential investor in Kazakhstan's economy.

This article was adapted from Russian.

World.title: Spain battles forest fire a short drive from flash flood
World.content:
The blaze, near Valencia, forced more than 1,000 people from their homes. In nearby Catalonia, civil defense teams carried out 200 rescue operations after floods trapped residents in cars and homes.

A forest fire in eastern Spain sparked the evacuation of around 1,000 people on Saturday, authorities said.

The blaze is one of hundreds that firefighters across Europe have been battling this summer amid record high temperatures along the Mediterranean and elsewhere.

Barely 150 kilometers (93 miles) away on the Costa Dorada, flash floods trapped people in cars, toppled walls and forced the evacuation of a campsite.

What do we know about the fire?

The fire is burning close to Gatova, an inland village with a population of 450, northwest of Valencia.

TV footage showed the flames were moving close to built-up areas.

Spain's Military Emergency Unit UME posted a video to X showing its firefighters working in the darkness to douse the flames.

Several firefighting helicopters and aircraft were also deployed.

Local media reported that the blaze is thought to have been started by a lightning strike late Thursday.

By Friday evening, more than 400 hectares of land had been burnt.

Juan Carlos Valderrama, Valencia autonomous community's civil protection minister, said buses were on standby to help residents without their own vehicles to leave their homes.

Can Germany teach Europe how to prevent wildfires? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

What's the latest on the floods?

Further north, along Spain's Costa Dorada, heavy rain overnight flooded streets and caused the collapse of two walls, injuring at least seven people, officials said.

According to local media, roads in the coastal towns El Vendrell, Coma-ruga and Torredembarra in the Cataloniaregion were partially submerged.

The Meteorological Service of Catalonia said several towns recorded nearly 200 liters per square meter in just a few hours.

On Saturday morning, the agency warned of more heavy rainfall for the coastal region.

Local media reported that several people got trapped in their vehicles during the flooding.

A regional emergency official said firefighters had carried out more than 200 missions to rescue people from vehicles and flooded buildings.

Three people were injured when a wall collapsed at the port of Roda de Bera, about 75 kilometers (45 miles) southwest of Barcelona, emergency services said.

Another wall collapse at a nearby campsite injured two others.

Around 300 people staying at the campsite were evacuated, with many sheltering at a nearby sports center, officials said.

World.title: Chinese robot beats Usain Bolt's 100m world record
World.content:
A Chinese humanoid robot finished a 100-meter practice race in just 9.32 seconds, beating the human world record, Chinese media reported on Saturday.

That put the robot, called Lightning, at the finish line 0.26 seconds faster than Jamaican Usain Bolt, who set a world record at the World Athletics Championships in Berlin in 2009 with a 100m time of 9.58 seconds.

Lightning's preparatory run was for the second World Humanoid Robot Games that opened in Beijing on Saturday.

The sporting event is one of a kind where technology companies — mostly Chinese — and university groups gather to show off the many tasks their robots can do.

Lightning's extraordinary race to the finish line is a big marker of progress in the field of artificial intelligence because the best of humanoid robots were struggling to complete a race just last year.

China progressing fast at humanoid robotics

Lightning, developed by Chinese smartphone maker Honor, also won the Beijing half-marathon (21 kilometers) earlier this April in 50 minutes and 26 seconds.

That was several minutes faster than the human world record holder, Uganda's Jacob Kiplimo, who ran the same distance in 57 minutes, 20 seconds, in Lisbon this March.

Lightning stood 169 centimeters tall and had 95-centimeter ​legs at ⁠the half marathon.

Jacob Kiplimo of Uganda holds the men's half-marathon record with a time of 57 minutes and 20 seconds. Ethiopia's Letesenbet Gidey holds the women's record, having finished in 1 hour, 2 minutes, 52 seconds.

In a feat its human competitors would have a difficult time replicating, Lightning's legs were lengthened by ⁠10 cm ​to 1.05 meters ahead of the World Humanoid Robot Games, China Central Television reported.
