World.title: Starc strikes early again as Bangladesh chase Australian lead on day two
World.content:
SportCricketTest cricket Starc strikes early again as Bangladesh chase Australian lead on day two Nick Wright August 23, 2026 — 11:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Mackay: Australia will look to level the two-Test series with Bangladesh as early as Sunday, after a slice of Bangladeshi history ended the hosts’ first innings in the first session of day two with a commanding 146-run lead. It took a toe-crushing yorker from Shoriful Islam to end Cameron Green’s valiant lone hand with the bat, trapped in front on 67 as the left-arm seam bowler became Bangladesh’s first quick to claim seven wickets in a Test innings (7-48). Cameron Green was out leg before wicket in Australia’s first innings. Getty Images That milestone followed his nation’s first Test win on Australian soil in the first clash in Darwin. Green had looked composed throughout his innings until receiving the Shoriful peach, playing fluently until stumps on day one as wickets fell around him during a dramatic collapse of 5-30 from Steve Smith’s dismissal for 42.



The 27-year-old all-rounder appeared on track to back up his second innings 104 in the first Test in Darwin with a fourth career ton, playing one powerful cut shot and another elegant off-drive for boundaries inside the first three overs of day two at Great Barrier Reef Arena. When Green fell, Nathan Lyon ensured Australia moved beyond 200 – a well-timed on drive to the fence, and pull shot over it, featuring in his unbeaten 32 before Josh Hazlewood was out caught for six attempting to take on spinner Taijul Islam, ending Australia’s stand at 210. Bangladesh bowler Shoriful Islam celebrates his seven-wicket haul against Australia. Getty Images But Bangladesh were in early disarray when they came out to bat for the second time. While there were no repeats of Starc’s first-ball scalp on day one, Tanzid Hasan driving him down the ground to the boundary, the veteran quick did cause carnage in his second over. First, he caught Shadman Islam high on the bat with a sharp, straightening delivery, with Marnus Labuschagne diving forward from point for the catch. Next ball, the left-arm spearhead was on a hat-trick for the second time this Test, as Mominul Haque shouldered arms to a ball that nipped back and knocked out his off stump, to leave Bangladesh reeling at 2-5.



There were 18 wickets to fall on day one, Starc setting the tone by sealing his five-wicket haul after just 43-minutes, finishing with figures of 6-12 as the visitors struggled to contend with the extra bounce and lively green pitch. Despite the carnage, Starc said he had no issues with the pitch on Saturday. “People will sit there and go ’18 wickets, it’s a bad wicket’. I think it’s a very good day one wicket, I think it’s probably played very similar to a Gabba wicket – you see a little bit of tennis ball bounce early at the Gabba, and likewise today,” Starc said. “It was a pretty helter-skelter day of cricket, but I’d say some good bowling led to 18 wickets, as opposed to the wicket.” Should Starc and his fellow quicks roll Bangladesh in similar fashion, there will be no further chances for Labuschagne, Beau Webster and Matt Renshaw to push their case for inclusion in the forthcoming series in South Africa.



While Renshaw (eight) would be expected to be given a reprieve, having only just been brought into the side to replace axed opener Jake Weatherald, both Labuschagne and Webster have struggled for a more prolonged period. Webster, to his credit, had not put a foot wrong in his career until this two-Test series. However, he has managed just 17 runs across three knocks – including a first innings duck in Mackay. Labuschagne’s long-term struggles, meanwhile, have been well-documented – failing to score a century since July 2023, while averaging just 29.69 since the start of that year following his cheap dismissal for four on Saturday.

World.title: Meghan’s acting role ‘in doubt’ in shocking about-turn
World.content:
CultureCelebrityMeghan, Duchess of Sussex Meghan’s acting role ‘in doubt’ in shocking about-turn India McTaggart and Hannah Furness August 23, 2026 — 11:21am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The Duchess of Sussex’s acting role in Guy Ritchie’s Netflix series has been thrown into doubt, The Telegraph understands. In an about-turn less than 24 hours after the news was revealed, the duchess’s role in the third series of The Gentlemen is reportedly uncertain following a public backlash. On Friday, it was revealed that she was in advanced discussions to star in the UK-based production after her relocation to Britain with Prince Harry and their two children, Prince Archie, 7, and Princess Lilibet, 5, at the end of this month. But Tina Brown, a former editor of Vanity Fair, reported the offer “has been withdrawn due to a public backlash”. Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, has reportedly been dropped from Netflix’s The Gentleman less than 24 hours after her role was announced. Getty Images



The Telegraph also understands the deal could collapse after public reaction to the revelation, which would have marked a return to acting for the duchess after 10 years. It is understood that the cold feet are not coming from the team behind The Gentlemen, who anticipated a large public response to the news, but from either Netflix – which declined to comment – or the Sussexes, who have not yet commented. Editor's pick Royal family Harry and Meghan’s California neighbours shrug as their idyll ends Sources said the offer of the role, which was only made recently, formed part of the decision-making process in the family relocating to the UK, but was not the sole reason. After having lived in the US for more than six years, the couple intend to relocate to a private, non-royal residence, thought to be outside London, later this month. The duke and duchess’s status as non-working royals and private individuals will remain unchanged.



In Ritchie’s action series, Theo James, the lead actor, “transitions from duke to drug baron” after inheriting his family’s estate and discovering it is home to an underground cannabis empire. The action-comedy originally aired in 2024, and was Ritchie’s first TV show. The duchess worked as an actor before meeting Prince Harry, and was best known for her role as lawyer Rachel Zane in seven seasons of the US legal drama Suits. She went on an acting hiatus in 2017 and told the BBC she viewed her career break as “a new chapter” after meeting the duke the year before. However, she recently returned to the profession with a cameo as herself in forthcoming comedy Close Personal Friends, starring Lily Collins and Brie Larson. Loading On Friday, it was understood that the duchess was poised to accept the role in The Gentlemen, although it remained unclear how many episodes she would be appearing in the unannounced third series.



A part was believed to be being written for her specifically to enter the series, which starts its second season next month. Editor's pick Royal family Harry and Meghan are returning to the UK. Who will keep them safe? If she were to take on a role in the series, it would mark the latest project in long-standing ties between the duchess and Netflix. The streaming giant was a commercial partner for her US-based lifestyle brand As Ever, which she plans to continue running from the UK, and was the host of the unscripted show promoting the brand called With Love, Meghan. After stepping down as working royals in 2020, the duke and duchess initially had a five-year deal with Netflix, worth a reported $US100 million ($140 million).



However, the deal collapsed last year amid reports published in Variety that the relationship between key executives in the company and the couple had soured. During their initial deal, the couple produced a six-part documentary on their life after leaving the royal family, titled Harry & Meghan, and a polo documentary as well as the duchess’s lifestyle show, which was critically panned and failed to make the top 1000 most-watched programs on the streaming platform. Their production company, Archewell Productions, now maintains a “first look” deal with the streaming giant, and in April the duchess was pictured holding hands with the wife of Ted Sarandos at a party hosted by the Netflix boss. Representatives of the duchess have been contacted for comment. The Telegraph, London Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: ‘Fundamentally dishonest’: Mark Ruffalo fires back at Paramount anti-Semitism claims
World.content:
CultureCelebrityCelebrity relationships ‘Fundamentally dishonest’: Mark Ruffalo fires back at Paramount anti-Semitism claims Benedict Smith August 23, 2026 — 10:31am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Mark Ruffalo has become embroiled in an anti-Semitism row with Paramount. The Hollywood actor, who plays the Hulk in the Marvel films, was accused of pushing “anti-Semitic tropes” while arguing against the US$111 billion ($155 billion) merger between the entertainment giant and Warner Bros. Actor Mark Ruffalo has criticised a proposed merger between Warner Bros and Paramount. Getty Images In a post on social media, Ruffalo told his followers the acquisition meant the technology behind what he described as Israel’s genocide in Gaza would be turned against them. He noted that Larry Ellison, the Jewish founder of the data giant Oracle, had guaranteed more than US$40 billion ($56 billion) for the proposed merger, which is being spearheaded by his son David Ellison, the Paramount chief executive.



At the same time, he posted a 2024 clip of Safra Catz, Oracle’s former chief executive, talking about the “profoundly scary technologies” the company provided to the Israeli military in the wake of the October 7 attacks. Editor's pick Israeli-Palestinian conflict Hollywood’s biggest names split over the Israel-Hamas war “These ‘really profoundly scary technologies’ will most likely be merged into one of the largest media conglomerates in the world and one day be used on you,” Ruffalo wrote on Instagram. “Look how she [Catz] revels in what we now have come to see as a genocide, which was built on an apartheid system of oppression powered by Oracle.” Accusing Oracle of “powering some of the most destructive and inhuman forces in the world”, he asked why Donald Trump, the US president, had “pushed this illegal merger through”.



Trump’s administration approved the acquisition in June, deciding it was “not likely to result in harm to competition or American consumers”, without requiring Paramount to make concessions such as selling off assets. View post on X Larry Ellison, who is worth around US$189 billion ($264 billion), was a “classic oligarch” who was “crushing workers and consolidating the wealth of the world”, Ruffalo went on to claim. A Paramount spokesman told The Hollywood Reporter: “We are, as always, troubled when anti-Semitic tropes are invoked in purported service of a business dispute. “Words like ‘genocide’ and ‘apartheid’, applied to a corporate transaction, aren’t just wrong – they’re a bridge too far, and they cheapen the very real suffering those words are meant to describe.”



Paramount’s David Ellison is spearheading the merger with Warner Bros. The bid was financially backed by his father, Oracle chief Larry Ellison. AP The spokesman claimed Ruffalo’s intervention “simply exposes the true motivation of some who have advocated opposition to this transaction”. He added: “This brings us to a moment to lower the temperature, not raise it. We’d rather build than further engage in such rhetoric.” Editor's pick Updated

Mergers & acquisitions Warner Bros takes aim at billionaire family as it rejects ‘misleading’ takeover bid Among the channels Paramount would acquire is CNN, the news channel, raising alarms among press freedom campaigners who note the Ellison family’s ties to Trump. Paramount and Warner Bros are delaying their merger until next year, amid a legal challenge by 12 Democratic state attorneys general, led by California’s Rob Bonta, who argue the media behemoth would “extinguish competition” in Hollywood.



Last month, Bonta called the proposal “illegal” and vowed that it would “never see the light of day”. “Our argument against this illegal merger is straightforward: when too few corporations have too much power in markets central to American life, it makes things more expensive, and it makes things worse,” he said. On July 20, a US district judge granted a temporary restraining order on the acquisition, saying the states had raised “serious questions” and made a strong case that it could “substantially lessen competition”. Ruffalo, in his social media post, said the resulting media empire would “flatten out competition”, push up the cost of cable TV and cause the loss of thousands of film jobs. “It also concentrates an enormous amount of creative control to companies that say and do things like this strange woman from Oracle,” he added, referring to Catz.



Editor's pick Updated

Media & marketing Trump’s son-in-law part of Paramount’s hostile takeover bid for Warner Bros The Paramount spokesman said it hoped the merger would “be judged based on the legal merits, not underlying bias”, adding: “We’re asking for the same good faith we’re extending: less rhetoric, more understanding.” Ruffalo’s spokesman said: “This merger has real consequences for real people, and for the entire country. Scrutinising the Ellisons, including Oracle’s business built on data, surveillance technology and government contracts, and the serious threat to editorial freedom and the loss of a livelihood for thousands of families, is fair and necessary. Ruffalo called the anti-Semitism allegation “appalling and fundamentally dishonest”. “Criticising the actions of the Israeli prime minister, a military technology contract, or the executives who supply it is not the same as criticising Jewish people,” he said.



“This critical and necessary dialogue is then dishonestly framed as being anti-Israel. To be clear, my views come from my own political convictions and should never be interpreted as hostility toward Jewish people, for whom I have deep love and respect.” The Telegraph, London

World.title: One Nation MP concedes migration target ‘not too different’ from Labor’s
World.content:
Breaking PoliticsFederalImmigration One Nation MP concedes migration target ‘not too different’ from Labor’s Matthew Knott August 23, 2026 — 10:17am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

One Nation MP David Farley has conceded the party’s net overseas migration target would be scarcely different to the Albanese government’s once at least 100,000 foreign workers are taken into account. Farley sought to redefine the meaning of net overseas migration (NOM) in an interview on Sunday, arguing there was a “true form” of the figure that differs to the way it has long been officially calculated. One Nation MP David Farley has sought to clarify the party’s migration targets. Janie Barrett “Well, the raw number is not too different [to the government’s], but the reality is, where do we need them?” Farley told the ABC’s Insiders on Sunday, a concession likely to be seized upon by One Nation’s political opponents. “We don’t need them in the great urban metroplex. We need them out to be productive, working in agriculture, engineering, mining, etc.”



He continued: “I think the big difference is we’re focusing on what are the skills we need as a nation, where do we need these migrants to be? But the raw number is not too different.” Related Article Immigration One Nation flip-flops on migration policy, announces tobacco excise cut Amid confusion over its migration policy, One Nation last week clarified that its plan to cap visas was based on a net overseas migration target of 130,000 a year. In his Insiders interview, Farley said this figure did not include a raft of key migrant categories and that these workers would add at least 100,000 people to the target. “Well, what we’re doing is we’re focusing on the NOM in its true form, he said.



“Now, on top of the NOM, of course, we’ve got all the other programs that we run, the PALM program, which is important to my electorate of Farrer, the skilled registered aged care nurses etc are all very important,” he said. The Pacific Australia Labour Mobility (PALM) scheme includes around 40,000 workers a year, he said, adding that aged care nurses would add around 70,000 a year - plus more in the engineering and mechanical fields. Migrants are included in the official NOM figure if they stay in the country for a total of 12 months within a 16-month window regardless of their visa category. Farley, elected in a byelection in May, said that “at a minimum” there would be 100,000 extra migrants on top of the 130,000 target “but the 130,000 is what we call the ‘true NOM’”. The federal government’s net overseas migration target is 245,000 for 2026-27 and 225,000 for each of the following two years, around the same as Farely’s total estimate.



Liberal housing spokesman Andrew Bragg has nominated under 180,000 as the size of net overseas migration under a Coalition government. During this year’s byelection, Farley broke with party policy during a candidate forum by suggesting it was “probably not” an issue if Australia’s net migration reached 306,000. “If we’re successful in One Nation’s water policies, we’re going to need more labour, and we’re going to need more labour quickly, skilled labour,” he said. World.title: ‘Don’t abandon the club’: Swans fans ready to show support after week of turmoil
World.content:
SportAFLSydney Swans ‘Don’t abandon the club’: Swans fans ready to show support after week of turmoil Billie Eder August 23, 2026 — 9:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A desire to support the players not caught up in the Sydney Swans scandal looks set to ensure a large number of fans attend Sunday’s double-header at the SCG. While disappointment remains among Swans fans at what captain Callum Mills said was the “actions of a few within our group”, sentiment has shifted from anger to a desire to back the club – and especially the women’s team. Robert Sharp and partner Kate Bennett will be at the SCG on Sunday to support the men’s and women’s Swans teams. George Chan Five Swans players – Isaac Heeney, Chad Warner, Nick Blakey, James Jordon and Riley Bice – have been suspended for their part in the events that unfolded in a hotel room in East Melbourne in the early hours of last Monday. A woman who visited the room has alleged she was sexually assaulted by one of the players. A police investigation is under way. Heeney is at the centre of the investigation.



Kate Bennett and her partner Robert Sharp have been going to Swans games for the 28 years they’ve been together. Sharp is a Swans supporter, while Bennett switched her allegiance to the Giants 13 years ago. They will be there tomorrow for the first match day since the storm broke; first for the AFLW team’s clash against Essendon, then when the men’s team takes on North Melbourne. Bennett has been a Giants fan for 13 years but also supports the Swans, Sharp’s team. George Chan “I go with Robert to the Swans, and he comes with me to the Giants – we see a lot of football over the season,” Bennett said. “I’m going tomorrow because I really do feel sorry for the men, because they just look devastated. And I just think, you’ve done nothing wrong ... these kids, and the older players like Dane Rampe and Jake Lloyd who have been foot soldiers for them, and have played really well, they don’t deserve to not have fans there.”



Initially, Bennett didn’t think she would attend the match. However, she decided she wanted to support the players who weren’t involved in the scandal. “I spoke to my daughter who said it’s not the boys who are left behind’s fault, and if nobody goes, then that would be devastating,” Bennett said. Swans AFLW captain Lucy McEvoy encourages fans to support the women’s team at the SCG on Sunday. Sitthixay Ditthavong “And I thought, ‘You know what, you’re right’, and it would be devastating for the girls – how exciting [for them] to play on the SCG.” However, Bennett’s sentiment is not universally shared by Swans fans. Many, such as Emma Gray and her daughter, Esther, are only planning on attending the women’s match, from 12.30pm, before leaving ahead of the men’s game at 3.20pm.



Gray has been a Swans supporter for about 20 years, while her daughter backs Essendon, and was frustrated she couldn’t buy a ticket solely for the women’s match. “It’s a women’s match at a big venue which is definitely worth supporting for the promotion of the game,” Gray said. Emma Gray and her daughter Esther will be at the Swans AFLW match on Sunday. “We’re not staying for the men’s game because I don’t condone the misogynist culture which is clearly prevalent at the club. Why men, particularly in positions of privilege, think that celebrating with the ‘boys’ needs to involve demeaning women is absolutely beyond me.” Fans of rival clubs will also attend the SCG on Sunday, after the GWS Giants women’s team urged their supporters to turn up in solidarity.



“As we will be playing the Demons away from home in Melbourne, we would like to encourage our Sydney based and non-travelling fans, to continue supporting the spectacle of women’s football in Sydney by attending the match, before watching us play in Melbourne,” the Giants’ AFLW leadership team said in a statement. “This is a moment to put rivalries aside and bolster the women’s game in NSW by showing up and supporting the league and women in football.” ‘I’m going tomorrow because I really do feel sorry for the men, because they just look devastated. And I just think, you’ve done nothing wrong.’ Swans fan Kate Bennett The Swans’ AFLW team will play for points at the historic ground for just the second time since the team’s inception in 2022. Nat Zil, a Swans fan who became a Giants supporter through clinics and community events, said she would be going to both matches tomorrow with her family.



“I’m both a Swans and Giants supporter,” Zil said. “I typically haven’t been to a lot of the AFLW games, but I will be going to support the girls. I saw the Giants message on social media, and I was so proud of them.” Meanwhile, Carolyn Cummins – a former employee of The Sydney Morning Herald who remains an occasional contributor – has been a Swans member for almost 30 years and sponsors the locker for AFLW player Ash Van Loon. Her grandfather played for South Melbourne – the Swans’ origin club – in 1918. Carolyn Cummins has been a Swans supporter since she moved to Sydney in 1988. Cummins, a committee member for Ladies @ Sydney Swans – a fan group supported by the club that hosts events for female supporters, said both the men’s and women’s team needed their fans now more than ever. “I am a very proud Swans ambassador and I will certainly be there to support the AFLW team – I can’t wait to see how we perform throughout the season,” Cummins said.

World.title: Sydney Swans LIVE updates: Women’s and men’s team play first matches following week of scandal
World.content:
More than an hour before the AFLW’s Sydney Swans are set to take on Essendon, dozens of die-hard fans queued up at the members’ gate.

“Go the Swannies, all of the Swans,” one woman is heard yelling.

Owen Moynahan has been a Swans member for 12 years and has attended most of their games for more than three decades. He said today was “very exciting”.

“It’s not very often we get the ladies here, and so we’ve brought the family out to come and support the women’s team and the men’s team today. It should be a really good day,” he said.

“I’m proudly red and white until the day I’m in a box”.

World.title: Paul McManus was killed five years ago. His family is still waiting for justice
World.content:
NationalVictoriaCourts Paul McManus was killed five years ago. His family is still waiting for justice Eleanor Campbell August 23, 2026 — 11:39am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Every time she passes a green light at an intersection, Jennifer McManus thinks of her 40-year-old son Paul. In October 2021, the Melbourne-born tech engineer was riding home on his motorcycle from a James Taylor concert when a driver allegedly ran a red light and struck him at a busy intersection in San Francisco’s Mission District. Paul McManus’ family (from left): father Brian, sister Sarah, mother Jennifer and brother Dave. Eddie Jim He was taken to hospital with critical injuries after 11pm and died before midnight. The woman allegedly driving the grey Jeep Compass, Breanna Gordon, then aged 32, was charged with misdemeanour vehicular manslaughter and released from police custody.



The man in Gordon’s passenger seat – identified as her boyfriend at the time – fled the scene before police arrived due to having two active warrants out for his arrest, according to police allegations. Thousands of kilometres away in the Victorian town of Aireys Inlet, Jennifer McManus was in the shower after spending the day at the beach with her family when her daughter, Sarah, took a call from Paul’s wife, Fern, in California. Paul and Fern during their wedding in 2020. “I knew it was midnight there, and Fern wouldn’t usually ever call us, it was always Paul’s phone, so I instantly thought something was wrong,” Sarah recalls. “She was upset, and she said, ‘There’s been an accident’, and she was like, ‘Well, Paul’s dead’. Mum was in the shower, and we were just in shock.”



In San Francisco, Fern remembers going out to search for Paul when he didn’t return home that night. She recalls remaining oddly calm after arriving at the scene of the crash when she went out to look for him, a habit she picked up from her husband, whom she describes as “devastatingly funny” and one of the “most brilliant people I’ll ever know”. “He had this sort of code of behaviour where he would not freak out about anything before he had all the facts,” Fern says. “I remember when the worst imaginable happened, I found myself grateful that he had helped equip me with this toolkit of how to deal with horrible things.” Paul and his beloved dog, Huxley. The pair met in Mexico while travelling with friends a decade earlier and bonded over a conversation about the famous oceanographer Sylvia Earle. They were married for more than a year when he died. Six weeks after the crash, Gordon failed to appear for a court arraignment hearing and for three years the case lingered in pre-trial status due to a backlog of pending cases caused by COVID-19.



When the case was finally set for trial in June 2024, Gordon again failed to show in court and a bench warrant was issued for her arrest. Despite ongoing pleas to US authorities to track her down, family members say they were told there were not enough police resources to locate her. “She [Gordon] hasn’t had a period of not driving, that we know of,” Jennifer says. “She got her car back before Fern got Paul’s motorbike back from the insurance company.” A spokesperson for Gordon was contacted for comment. Frustrated, the McManus family considered hiring a private investigator for thousands of dollars but ultimately decided against it. After contacting the Australian Department of Foreign Affairs, they were told that nothing could be done to help them except lodging an overseas death certificate.



It was not until two years later, in May 2026, that Gordon was re-arrested on a bench warrant and brought back to San Francisco. Paul’s family says they learnt of the development from a journalist at The San Francisco Standard. “You would have thought the government would do more in the circumstances, but we haven’t heard anything since that,” Paul’s brother, Dave, says. Paul McManus’ family is still waiting for the case to go to the trial. Eddie Jim After almost five years in limbo, the family is now preparing for Paul’s case to go to trial by the end of October. Although they have since established regular contact with California’s district attorney, they remain deeply sceptical about the prospect of a swift resolution. Paul, who grew up in the Melbourne suburb of Eltham, is described by his loved ones as an adventurous, humble and fiercely unique spirit. He spent much of his childhood diving and spearfishing with siblings Dave, Sarah and older brother Luke.



“He should have been born with gills,” Dave says. “Paul did a lot for ocean conservation and a lot of his friends and network in San Francisco were a part of that.” A photo of Paul McManus in the water. His family says he was an adventurous, humble and free spirit who loved the ocean. The Age At the time of his death, he and his brother Dave were working on launching a seaweed farm to regenerate ocean habitats, a business his brother has since launched in his honour. Hundreds of people, including police officers who were at the scene of the crash, attended a funeral paddle-out ceremony in his honour at Dillon Beach, north of San Francisco, and at Point Roadknight on Victoria’s Surf Coast. Paul’s parents are clear about what justice looks like for their son.



“We just want simple justice and whatever it is – it needs be done in a fair way,” his father Brian says. Jennifer adds: “There should be some sort of rehabilitation program, that’s what Paul would have wanted. Just something worthwhile and putting something good back into the world.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Starc strikes early again as Bangladesh chase Australian lead on day two
World.content:
SportCricketTest cricket Starc strikes early again as Bangladesh chase Australian lead on day two Nick Wright August 23, 2026 — 11:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Mackay: Australia will look to level the two-Test series with Bangladesh as early as Sunday, after a slice of Bangladeshi history ended the hosts’ first innings in the first session of day two with a commanding 146-run lead. It took a toe-crushing yorker from Shoriful Islam to end Cameron Green’s valiant lone hand with the bat, trapped in front on 67 as the left-arm seam bowler became Bangladesh’s first quick to claim seven wickets in a Test innings (7-48). Cameron Green was out leg before wicket in Australia’s first innings. Getty Images That milestone followed his nation’s first Test win on Australian soil in the first clash in Darwin. Green had looked composed throughout his innings until receiving the Shoriful peach, playing fluently until stumps on day one as wickets fell around him during a dramatic collapse of 5-30 from Steve Smith’s dismissal for 42.



The 27-year-old all-rounder appeared on track to back up his second innings 104 in the first Test in Darwin with a fourth career ton, playing one powerful cut shot and another elegant off-drive for boundaries inside the first three overs of day two at Great Barrier Reef Arena. When Green fell, Nathan Lyon ensured Australia moved beyond 200 – a well-timed on drive to the fence, and pull shot over it, featuring in his unbeaten 32 before Josh Hazlewood was out caught for six attempting to take on spinner Taijul Islam, ending Australia’s stand at 210. Bangladesh bowler Shoriful Islam celebrates his seven-wicket haul against Australia. Getty Images But Bangladesh were in early disarray when they came out to bat for the second time. While there were no repeats of Starc’s first-ball scalp on day one, Tanzid Hasan driving him down the ground to the boundary, the veteran quick did cause carnage in his second over. First, he caught Shadman Islam high on the bat with a sharp, straightening delivery, with Marnus Labuschagne diving forward from point for the catch. Next ball, the left-arm spearhead was on a hat-trick for the second time this Test, as Mominul Haque shouldered arms to a ball that nipped back and knocked out his off stump, to leave Bangladesh reeling at 2-5.



There were 18 wickets to fall on day one, Starc setting the tone by sealing his five-wicket haul after just 43-minutes, finishing with figures of 6-12 as the visitors struggled to contend with the extra bounce and lively green pitch. Despite the carnage, Starc said he had no issues with the pitch on Saturday. “People will sit there and go ’18 wickets, it’s a bad wicket’. I think it’s a very good day one wicket, I think it’s probably played very similar to a Gabba wicket – you see a little bit of tennis ball bounce early at the Gabba, and likewise today,” Starc said. “It was a pretty helter-skelter day of cricket, but I’d say some good bowling led to 18 wickets, as opposed to the wicket.” Should Starc and his fellow quicks roll Bangladesh in similar fashion, there will be no further chances for Labuschagne, Beau Webster and Matt Renshaw to push their case for inclusion in the forthcoming series in South Africa.



While Renshaw (eight) would be expected to be given a reprieve, having only just been brought into the side to replace axed opener Jake Weatherald, both Labuschagne and Webster have struggled for a more prolonged period. Webster, to his credit, had not put a foot wrong in his career until this two-Test series. However, he has managed just 17 runs across three knocks – including a first innings duck in Mackay. Labuschagne’s long-term struggles, meanwhile, have been well-documented – failing to score a century since July 2023, while averaging just 29.69 since the start of that year following his cheap dismissal for four on Saturday.

World.title: Meghan’s acting role ‘in doubt’ in shocking about-turn
World.content:
CultureCelebrityMeghan, Duchess of Sussex Meghan’s acting role ‘in doubt’ in shocking about-turn India McTaggart and Hannah Furness August 23, 2026 — 11:21am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The Duchess of Sussex’s acting role in Guy Ritchie’s Netflix series has been thrown into doubt, The Telegraph understands. In an about-turn less than 24 hours after the news was revealed, the duchess’s role in the third series of The Gentlemen is reportedly uncertain following a public backlash. On Friday, it was revealed that she was in advanced discussions to star in the UK-based production after her relocation to Britain with Prince Harry and their two children, Prince Archie, 7, and Princess Lilibet, 5, at the end of this month. But Tina Brown, a former editor of Vanity Fair, reported the offer “has been withdrawn due to a public backlash”. Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, has reportedly been dropped from Netflix’s The Gentleman less than 24 hours after her role was announced. Getty Images



The Telegraph also understands the deal could collapse after public reaction to the revelation, which would have marked a return to acting for the duchess after 10 years. It is understood that the cold feet are not coming from the team behind The Gentlemen, who anticipated a large public response to the news, but from either Netflix – which declined to comment – or the Sussexes, who have not yet commented. Editor's pick Royal family Harry and Meghan’s California neighbours shrug as their idyll ends Sources said the offer of the role, which was only made recently, formed part of the decision-making process in the family relocating to the UK, but was not the sole reason. After having lived in the US for more than six years, the couple intend to relocate to a private, non-royal residence, thought to be outside London, later this month. The duke and duchess’s status as non-working royals and private individuals will remain unchanged.



In Ritchie’s action series, Theo James, the lead actor, “transitions from duke to drug baron” after inheriting his family’s estate and discovering it is home to an underground cannabis empire. The action-comedy originally aired in 2024, and was Ritchie’s first TV show. The duchess worked as an actor before meeting Prince Harry, and was best known for her role as lawyer Rachel Zane in seven seasons of the US legal drama Suits. She went on an acting hiatus in 2017 and told the BBC she viewed her career break as “a new chapter” after meeting the duke the year before. However, she recently returned to the profession with a cameo as herself in forthcoming comedy Close Personal Friends, starring Lily Collins and Brie Larson. Loading On Friday, it was understood that the duchess was poised to accept the role in The Gentlemen, although it remained unclear how many episodes she would be appearing in the unannounced third series.



A part was believed to be being written for her specifically to enter the series, which starts its second season next month. Editor's pick Royal family Harry and Meghan are returning to the UK. Who will keep them safe? If she were to take on a role in the series, it would mark the latest project in long-standing ties between the duchess and Netflix. The streaming giant was a commercial partner for her US-based lifestyle brand As Ever, which she plans to continue running from the UK, and was the host of the unscripted show promoting the brand called With Love, Meghan. After stepping down as working royals in 2020, the duke and duchess initially had a five-year deal with Netflix, worth a reported $US100 million ($140 million).



However, the deal collapsed last year amid reports published in Variety that the relationship between key executives in the company and the couple had soured. During their initial deal, the couple produced a six-part documentary on their life after leaving the royal family, titled Harry & Meghan, and a polo documentary as well as the duchess’s lifestyle show, which was critically panned and failed to make the top 1000 most-watched programs on the streaming platform. Their production company, Archewell Productions, now maintains a “first look” deal with the streaming giant, and in April the duchess was pictured holding hands with the wife of Ted Sarandos at a party hosted by the Netflix boss. Representatives of the duchess have been contacted for comment. The Telegraph, London Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: ‘Fundamentally dishonest’: Mark Ruffalo fires back at Paramount anti-Semitism claims
World.content:
CultureCelebrityCelebrity relationships ‘Fundamentally dishonest’: Mark Ruffalo fires back at Paramount anti-Semitism claims Benedict Smith August 23, 2026 — 10:31am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Mark Ruffalo has become embroiled in an anti-Semitism row with Paramount. The Hollywood actor, who plays the Hulk in the Marvel films, was accused of pushing “anti-Semitic tropes” while arguing against the US$111 billion ($155 billion) merger between the entertainment giant and Warner Bros. Actor Mark Ruffalo has criticised a proposed merger between Warner Bros and Paramount. Getty Images In a post on social media, Ruffalo told his followers the acquisition meant the technology behind what he described as Israel’s genocide in Gaza would be turned against them. He noted that Larry Ellison, the Jewish founder of the data giant Oracle, had guaranteed more than US$40 billion ($56 billion) for the proposed merger, which is being spearheaded by his son David Ellison, the Paramount chief executive.



At the same time, he posted a 2024 clip of Safra Catz, Oracle’s former chief executive, talking about the “profoundly scary technologies” the company provided to the Israeli military in the wake of the October 7 attacks. Editor's pick Israeli-Palestinian conflict Hollywood’s biggest names split over the Israel-Hamas war “These ‘really profoundly scary technologies’ will most likely be merged into one of the largest media conglomerates in the world and one day be used on you,” Ruffalo wrote on Instagram. “Look how she [Catz] revels in what we now have come to see as a genocide, which was built on an apartheid system of oppression powered by Oracle.” Accusing Oracle of “powering some of the most destructive and inhuman forces in the world”, he asked why Donald Trump, the US president, had “pushed this illegal merger through”.



Trump’s administration approved the acquisition in June, deciding it was “not likely to result in harm to competition or American consumers”, without requiring Paramount to make concessions such as selling off assets. View post on X Larry Ellison, who is worth around US$189 billion ($264 billion), was a “classic oligarch” who was “crushing workers and consolidating the wealth of the world”, Ruffalo went on to claim. A Paramount spokesman told The Hollywood Reporter: “We are, as always, troubled when anti-Semitic tropes are invoked in purported service of a business dispute. “Words like ‘genocide’ and ‘apartheid’, applied to a corporate transaction, aren’t just wrong – they’re a bridge too far, and they cheapen the very real suffering those words are meant to describe.”



Paramount’s David Ellison is spearheading the merger with Warner Bros. The bid was financially backed by his father, Oracle chief Larry Ellison. AP The spokesman claimed Ruffalo’s intervention “simply exposes the true motivation of some who have advocated opposition to this transaction”. He added: “This brings us to a moment to lower the temperature, not raise it. We’d rather build than further engage in such rhetoric.” Editor's pick Updated

Mergers & acquisitions Warner Bros takes aim at billionaire family as it rejects ‘misleading’ takeover bid Among the channels Paramount would acquire is CNN, the news channel, raising alarms among press freedom campaigners who note the Ellison family’s ties to Trump. Paramount and Warner Bros are delaying their merger until next year, amid a legal challenge by 12 Democratic state attorneys general, led by California’s Rob Bonta, who argue the media behemoth would “extinguish competition” in Hollywood.



Last month, Bonta called the proposal “illegal” and vowed that it would “never see the light of day”. “Our argument against this illegal merger is straightforward: when too few corporations have too much power in markets central to American life, it makes things more expensive, and it makes things worse,” he said. On July 20, a US district judge granted a temporary restraining order on the acquisition, saying the states had raised “serious questions” and made a strong case that it could “substantially lessen competition”. Ruffalo, in his social media post, said the resulting media empire would “flatten out competition”, push up the cost of cable TV and cause the loss of thousands of film jobs. “It also concentrates an enormous amount of creative control to companies that say and do things like this strange woman from Oracle,” he added, referring to Catz.



Editor's pick Updated

Media & marketing Trump’s son-in-law part of Paramount’s hostile takeover bid for Warner Bros The Paramount spokesman said it hoped the merger would “be judged based on the legal merits, not underlying bias”, adding: “We’re asking for the same good faith we’re extending: less rhetoric, more understanding.” Ruffalo’s spokesman said: “This merger has real consequences for real people, and for the entire country. Scrutinising the Ellisons, including Oracle’s business built on data, surveillance technology and government contracts, and the serious threat to editorial freedom and the loss of a livelihood for thousands of families, is fair and necessary. Ruffalo called the anti-Semitism allegation “appalling and fundamentally dishonest”. “Criticising the actions of the Israeli prime minister, a military technology contract, or the executives who supply it is not the same as criticising Jewish people,” he said.



“This critical and necessary dialogue is then dishonestly framed as being anti-Israel. To be clear, my views come from my own political convictions and should never be interpreted as hostility toward Jewish people, for whom I have deep love and respect.” The Telegraph, London

SportAFLSydney Swans ‘Don’t abandon the club’: Swans fans ready to show support after week of turmoil Billie Eder August 23, 2026 — 9:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A desire to support the players not caught up in the Sydney Swans scandal looks set to ensure a large number of fans attend Sunday’s double-header at the SCG. While disappointment remains among Swans fans at what captain Callum Mills said was the “actions of a few within our group”, sentiment has shifted from anger to a desire to back the club – and especially the women’s team. Robert Sharp and partner Kate Bennett will be at the SCG on Sunday to support the men’s and women’s Swans teams. George Chan Five Swans players – Isaac Heeney, Chad Warner, Nick Blakey, James Jordon and Riley Bice – have been suspended for their part in the events that unfolded in a hotel room in East Melbourne in the early hours of last Monday. A woman who visited the room has alleged she was sexually assaulted by one of the players. A police investigation is under way. Heeney is at the centre of the investigation.



Kate Bennett and her partner Robert Sharp have been going to Swans games for the 28 years they’ve been together. Sharp is a Swans supporter, while Bennett switched her allegiance to the Giants 13 years ago. They will be there tomorrow for the first match day since the storm broke; first for the AFLW team’s clash against Essendon, then when the men’s team takes on North Melbourne. Bennett has been a Giants fan for 13 years but also supports the Swans, Sharp’s team. George Chan “I go with Robert to the Swans, and he comes with me to the Giants – we see a lot of football over the season,” Bennett said. “I’m going tomorrow because I really do feel sorry for the men, because they just look devastated. And I just think, you’ve done nothing wrong ... these kids, and the older players like Dane Rampe and Jake Lloyd who have been foot soldiers for them, and have played really well, they don’t deserve to not have fans there.”



Initially, Bennett didn’t think she would attend the match. However, she decided she wanted to support the players who weren’t involved in the scandal. “I spoke to my daughter who said it’s not the boys who are left behind’s fault, and if nobody goes, then that would be devastating,” Bennett said. Swans AFLW captain Lucy McEvoy encourages fans to support the women’s team at the SCG on Sunday. Sitthixay Ditthavong “And I thought, ‘You know what, you’re right’, and it would be devastating for the girls – how exciting [for them] to play on the SCG.” However, Bennett’s sentiment is not universally shared by Swans fans. Many, such as Emma Gray and her daughter, Esther, are only planning on attending the women’s match, from 12.30pm, before leaving ahead of the men’s game at 3.20pm.



Gray has been a Swans supporter for about 20 years, while her daughter backs Essendon, and was frustrated she couldn’t buy a ticket solely for the women’s match. “It’s a women’s match at a big venue which is definitely worth supporting for the promotion of the game,” Gray said. Emma Gray and her daughter Esther will be at the Swans AFLW match on Sunday. “We’re not staying for the men’s game because I don’t condone the misogynist culture which is clearly prevalent at the club. Why men, particularly in positions of privilege, think that celebrating with the ‘boys’ needs to involve demeaning women is absolutely beyond me.” Fans of rival clubs will also attend the SCG on Sunday, after the GWS Giants women’s team urged their supporters to turn up in solidarity.



“As we will be playing the Demons away from home in Melbourne, we would like to encourage our Sydney based and non-travelling fans, to continue supporting the spectacle of women’s football in Sydney by attending the match, before watching us play in Melbourne,” the Giants’ AFLW leadership team said in a statement. “This is a moment to put rivalries aside and bolster the women’s game in NSW by showing up and supporting the league and women in football.” ‘I’m going tomorrow because I really do feel sorry for the men, because they just look devastated. And I just think, you’ve done nothing wrong.’ Swans fan Kate Bennett The Swans’ AFLW team will play for points at the historic ground for just the second time since the team’s inception in 2022. Nat Zil, a Swans fan who became a Giants supporter through clinics and community events, said she would be going to both matches tomorrow with her family.



“I’m both a Swans and Giants supporter,” Zil said. “I typically haven’t been to a lot of the AFLW games, but I will be going to support the girls. I saw the Giants message on social media, and I was so proud of them.” Meanwhile, Carolyn Cummins – a former employee of The Sydney Morning Herald who remains an occasional contributor – has been a Swans member for almost 30 years and sponsors the locker for AFLW player Ash Van Loon. Her grandfather played for South Melbourne – the Swans’ origin club – in 1918. Carolyn Cummins has been a Swans supporter since she moved to Sydney in 1988. Cummins, a committee member for Ladies @ Sydney Swans – a fan group supported by the club that hosts events for female supporters, said both the men’s and women’s team needed their fans now more than ever. “I am a very proud Swans ambassador and I will certainly be there to support the AFLW team – I can’t wait to see how we perform throughout the season,” Cummins said.

World.title: Labour releases fiscal strategy, promises to slash debt
World.content:
Labour has released their fiscal strategy for the election, promising to get back to surplus by 2029/30, slash debt and set up an independent Parliamentary Budget Office, if elected.

Leader Chris Hipkins said his party would "get the books back into shape", but would not do it by "making life harder" and cutting services.

"New Zealand should be a country where hard work gets you somewhere. Where you can get ahead, put down roots and know your kids will have opportunities here.

"We'll invest in the things that make New Zealand stronger - our hospitals and schools, infrastructure, skills and the businesses that create jobs" Hipkins said.

Labour's fiscal strategy has six policies:

Achieve a surplus by 2029/30 and keep a sustainable fiscal position over the forecast period. Labour return to using the original OBEGAL (Operating Balance Before Gains and Losses) indicator and ditch the OBEGALx measure introduced by Finance Minister Nicola Willis.

Aim to reduce net debt down to 20 percent of GDP over time and investment in initiatives that support a growing economy.

Keep core Crown Expenditure and revenue at around 33 percent of GDP when their capital gains tax is fully implemented.

Set up an independent Parliamentary Budget Office to scrutinise government finances and election commitments.

Give the Reserve Bank it's dual mandate back, making so it must consider price stability and maximum sustainable employment.

And, bring back wellbeing reporting to so decisions take into account the impact on New Zealanders.

Finance and economy spokesperson Barbara Edmonds said the plan would balance the books and bring down debt, while giving New Zealand the "capacity to invest in its future".

"Labour will return the books to surplus by 2029/30 and reduce net debt over time but we won't do that by cutting the foundations of our economy."

Finance and economy spokesperson Barbara Edmonds and Labour leader Chris Hipkins. Baz Macdonald/RNZ

"Under National unemployment is at an 11-year high, business liquidations are up 71 percent, homelessness and KiwiSaver hardship withdrawals are at record levels, and public services are under pressure - that isn't economic success," Edmonds said.

Edmonds told media at the policy announcement in Wellington that a more detailed fiscal plan would be laid out once the Pre-election Economic and Fiscal Update (PREFU) was outlined.

"The pre-election fiscal update is really important for us to show our debt trajectory as part of our fiscal plan... [that's] the reason why we want it [debt] at 20 percent, around a prudent level. It allows for buffers for economic shocks. "

"We saw that in previous years when Labour brought back the books into surplus. We had to put the umbrella up when we were faced with a 1-in-100-year pandemic. That's why debt levels can change because of extra conditions that the government has no control over." she said.

Edmonds said expenditure would be "be a little bit higher" under her party's plan because of the investments they planned to make in areas like healthcare.

"With the CGT, revenue increases over time, that's what you see in overseas jurisdictions."

"So for us, we bring the legislation, and then obviously as the years progress... it does increase over time." she said.

Hipkins said Labour was "always" looking for better ways to spend taxpayer money.

"There are some changes in the medium to longer term we're seeing in education, for example, [where] we have the opposite trajectory to the one we're seeing in aged care."

"There's actually going to be fewer kids coming through the education system. [and] that's going to open up some choices about what we do there."

The government has recently signed a public-private partnership (PPP) agreement to build the first section of the Northland Expressway between Warkworth and Te Hana.

Asked what Labour would do to fund infrastructure projects, Hipkins said that was a "subject of considerable debate across the house".

"We do need more stability in the infrastructure pipeline, and that includes a more mature conversation about how we fund that over the medium to longer term."

"A lot of the projects that the National Party have been announcing around the country, they haven't identified how they're going to pay for them yet." he said.

Hipkins had a message for his potential coalition partners.

"Voters should get the sort of government that they vote for, and if New Zealanders vote for Labour to lead the next government, this is the sort of economic management approach that we're going to be taking." he said.

Speaking on introducing an independent Parliamentary Budget Office, Edmonds said she wanted the position to be an "officer of Parliament", meaning the position agreed to unanimously and with bipartisan support.

"However, Treasury also looked at other particular options where it becomes like a unit of treasury, for example. But the ideal option is to try to get that bipartisanship because it benefits all New Zealanders."

Edmonds said the Australian model was something she "looked at closely" and she had a members bill that sought to replicate that model.

On well-being reporting, Edmonds said they would be introduced through an amendment to the Public Finance Act and would provide a "fuller understanding" of how fiscal decision impacted on the wellbeing of New Zealanders.

Asked about giving the Reserve Bank a dual mandate to consider price stability and employment, Hipkins said it was "hardly radical".

"The Australians have one, the Americans have one. Many other countries around the world have the same objective." he said.

Edmonds said using the OBEGAL, as opposed to OBEGALx, would provide "certainty".

"OBEGAL is quite an internationally well-used measure, used by credit reporting agencies and other governments. We're providing that certainty that we want to keep Obi-Gal and not just make up a new measure to exclude ACC."

'Exploding debt and economic vandalism' - National

In a statement, National's finance spokesperson Nicola Willis said Labour's strategy amounted to nothing more than "spending more, borrowing more and taxing more".

National's finance spokesperson Nicola Willis RNZ / Baz Macdonald

"[It's] the same approach that led New Zealand into the sky-high inflation, exploding debt and economic vandalism Labour imposed on Kiwis last time."

"Targeting revenue at 33 percent of GDP means that by 2031, Labour would need to be collecting an additional $10.3 billion in revenue every year - far more than the $1.35 billion they say their capital gains tax will raise in that same year."

She said the proposal to "water down" the Reserve Bank's inflation targets risked "rising prices for every Kiwi".

"Tellingly, Labour has not made clear in their fiscal rules announcement that their new Capital Gains Tax is the only tax change they would implement, leaving the door open to a suite of further tax changes."

"Before the 2020 election, Labour ruled out the Ute Tax, changes to the bright-line tax and changes to interest deductibility - then implemented all three after the election. And it's growing clearer by the day that Labour is planning the same thing if elected on 7 November." she said.

Around two weeks ago the National Party released its own so-called Budget Responsibility Rules which Finance spokesperson Nicola Willis described as "fiscal guard-rails" and leader Christopher Luxon said would protect the country against economic shocks.

National said it would return to surplus in 2028/29 - under its OBEGALx formula - but would hit surplus the same year as Labour is projecting under the OBEGAL measure.

National would also keep Crown expenditure down towards 30 percent of GDP and get debt down to below 40 percent of GDP.

ACT Leader David Seymour said Hipkins was "going back to the future".

ACT Leader David Seymour RNZ / Nathan McKinnon

"Higher taxes, higher spending, more complicated monetary policy, and another empty promise that somehow it will all add up."

"He has promised billions of spending to tickle every electoral itch, but today is promising to spend less with no explanation how other than more taxes that don't come close to paying for his promises."

He said restoring the Reserve Ba k's dual mandate was an "Ardern-era" policy.

"The Reserve Bank is meant to be laser-focused on reining in inflation. Adding a second "jobs" target, totally at odds with the inflation target, will mean a higher cost of living for New Zealanders."

World.title: ACT Party takes aim at 'activist judges', Treaty of Waitangi clauses
World.content:
The ACT Party has released a policy designed to protect core democratic values and property rights, reign in "activist judges" and stop Parliament creating "divisive" Treaty of Waitangi clauses.

"Today's policy is about ensuring New Zealanders can move forward under one law for all with one future together," party leader David Seymour said.

"ACT will add three principles to the Constitution Act, affirming the basic values that Parliament is sovereign, the rule of law is fundamental and all New Zealanders are equal before the law."

Key to the policy is restraining courts from considering Māori tikanga (custom) in decisions.

"Recent Supreme Court decisions have pushed the line further than Parliament ever legislated," Seymour said.

"Parliament has pushed back in some instances, such as Smith v Fonterra and the Marine and Coastal Area cases, but others, such as Ellis, where the Supreme Court widely expanded the use of tikanga in the law, have not been responded to.

"Parliament is elected, judges are not. We cannot allow tikanga to become a separate source of law applying to broad areas of unrelated law without Parliament ever deciding that it should.

"ACT will make clear that tikanga cannot be used to influence court decisions, except where Parliament has expressly allowed for it."

The party would also amend the Legislation Act 2019 to ensure statutes are enacted in the context of the time they were passed. Judges could resolve ambiguity, but not override statutory language.

"Courts are often responding to unclear legislation or Parliament's silence, when they make decisions that substantially change how the law is understood.

"ACT will stop governments writing vague treaty clauses into law that create uncertainty, and leave courts and officials to decide what they mean through divisive interpretations."

Any bill referring to the Waitangi Treaty would require cabinet to agree which interests were engaged, who they apply to and what obligations they created, restoring "clear lines of democratic accountability".

"We won't unlock New Zealand's potential while the political and judicial classes experiment on our basic rights," Seymour said.

"Inventing new legal concepts, dividing us according to some people's version of history and trampling our property rights might be fun for wig wearers in court and lanyard wearers in the public service, but all it does for the ordinary person is created uncertainty and frustration."

World.title: Meat sector unclear what Trump's tariff's mean for New Zealand
World.content:
The export meat sector says it's not clear what the implications will be for New Zealand, from Donald Trump's latest tariff announcement.

In an effort to control soaring grocery prices in America, the US has decided that countries can send up to 300 thousand metric tonnes of ground beef product to the US for 90 days, without triggering expensive out-of-quota tariffs.

Usually, countries which exceed their usual import levels face a heavy tariff of just over 26 percent. It has not yet been announced which countries will be included in the deal.

Trump said on a post to Truth Social, that his administration has secured a commitment that imported beef will be sold at 25 percent below current US market prices.

Kate Acland from Beef and Lamb, said New Zealand already has excellent meat access into the US and is currently tariff-free.

"We sell a lot of lean beef trim into there, so it's an important market for what could otherwise be a lower value product but it's also a really important market for some of our competitors like Brazil and Australia who don't enjoy quite the same same access into the US."

Kate Acland from Beef and Lamb. Beef & Lamb

Acland sad it's too soon to judge whether the announcement will lower beef prices, but she says if Brazil benefited from the tariff change, it would have the potential to have a slight downward impact on prices.

World.title: 'The astounding thing was the speed': Residents survey aftermath of Albert Town fire
World.content:
Residents have been examining the scorched remnants of a park near Wānaka, where a fierce, fast-moving fire came within metres of homes on Saturday night.

The blaze in Albert Town prompted the evacuation of 22 people and has been described by locals as a sobering reminder of the region's wildfire risk.

Eight fire crews battled for two-and-a-half hours in windy conditions to bring it under control, before rain began to fall at about 10pm.

The cause remains under investigation.

After witnessing the tall, wind-fanned flames tearing through the patch of kānuka, local resident Estelle said there was no doubt the community was lucky.

"Just the astounding thing was the speed with which it moved, because it was so gusty last night," she said.

"We were watching an orange silhouette up into the sky with all of the ducks and the birds as they were leaving. It was just the power, the raw energy and how quickly it moved."

Estelle, who was taking a walk through the burnt trees on Sunday morning, said it was sad to see the devastation to the local reserve, and all its resident bugs and insects.

"I'm just so thankful, as well, that for all of our local residents that actually it was back under control so quickly, so that devastation was limited," she said.

Terry Terry, whose home overlooked the flames, said a minor shift in the wind could have been a catastrophe.

Burnt vegetation overlooks nearby houses at Albert Town. RNZ/Katie Todd

Embers flew through the air and some of the trees exploded from the force of the fire, he said.

"If it had been blowing from the south, we could have been in jeopardy... there were a lot of people quite terrified," he said.

The blaze was a warning of the region's wildfire risk, particularly given the number of homes surrounded by dry shrubbery, he said.

Lagoon Avenue resident Mario said, when he was alerted to the fire by a barrage of sirens, the 2020 Lake Ōhau fire came to mind and he feared the worst.

"The whole thing seemed to move so bloody quick... and we're all surrounded by shrubbery everwhere," he said.

Residents praised the quick response of emergency services, which travelled from as far as Tarras and Cromwell.

Earlier, Fire and Emergency assistant district ommander Nic McQuillan said the incident highlighted the danger of dry, windy weather, even during winter months.

World.title: Severe Wellington winds of 168 km/h bring unseasonal warm weather
World.content:
A meteorologist says severe gusts hit 168 km/h on Sunday morning at Wellington's Mt Kaukau, but as the wind coming from the Tasman Sea eases, the country is being treated to unusually warm weather during winter.

MetService meteorologist Gerard Bellham said "strong, blustery winds" have hit central parts of the country.

An orange strong wind warning is in place for Wairarapa until 3pm and Tararua District until 8pm.

Meanwhile, down south, the same warning is in place for Southland, Fiordland and Stewart Island until 2pm, and Dunedin and Clutha until 3pm.

Bellham said the front was coming from the Tasman Sea, bringing a lot of warm air over from Australia.

He said Hawke's Bay and Napier would be the first to see high temperatures this week, getting to 21 degrees on Sunday - well above the 15-degree maximum the areas usually see at this time of year.

Bellham said Kiwis would see "spring-like" weather this week, with temperatures in the low 20s.

MetService wind watches and warnings for Sunday, 23 August. MetService

Wellington Airport said two flights were unable to land this morning, due to high winds, and were diverted.

The airport said two more flights were cancelled before takeoff today, but normal operations had resumed for now.

Widespread power outages

Bellham said widespread power outages were wind related.

Wellington Electricity reported outages for more than 650 customers across the region, with restoration times of up to five hours.

The wind brought down a powerline across Treadwell Street in Lower Hutt, with police blocking off the hazard.

Power Co reported almost 400 homes were without power in the Wairarapa region and 200 in Manawatū.

More than 700 homes had unplanned outages in the Marlborough area, according to provider Marlborough Lines' outage map.

More than 300 homes in Tasman had been out since early Sunday morning, Network Tasman advised.

Westpower said almost 400 homes along the West Coast in places like Hokitika and Wahapo were out.

World.title: Teens charged after fleeing driver crash left cop critically injured in Palmerston North
World.content:
Police have filed charges against two teenage boys after a fleeing driver crash that left a Palmerston North officer critically injured.

The officer, a constable based in Palmerston North, was deploying road spikes on Kairanga Bunnythorpe Road about 2am on Saturday, when the vehicle hit him, throwing him several metres. He was airlifted

to Wellington Hospital in a critical condition, while a second officer was treated for minor injuries.

Central District Commander Superintendent Dion Bennett said the officer is being well looked after in hospital.

"He's got talented doctors and nurses looking after him, but his recovery will take some time. He is in a stable condition and remains on a ventilator, but the hospital staff are doing everything they can for him.

"He is a great family man. In his mum's words, he's a good bloke - and we think so too.

"There is no shortage of love and support pouring in for him; his family are by his side and staying incredibly strong for him, and we're also doing everything we can to support them as they navigate this awful situation."

The investigation into the crash is ongoing, however the alleged driver, the older of the two teenagers, now faces charges relating to theft, failing to stop, dangerous driving and reckless driving causing injury. A second teenager has been charged with unlawfully getting into a motor vehicle.

Both are due to appear in the Palmerston North Youth Court on 27 August.

World.title: Hundreds across Wellington, South Island without power
World.content:
Hundreds of homes across Wellington and the South Island are without power this morning.

Wellington electricity reported outages for more than 1300 customers in the Naenae, Plimmerton, and Kaitoke areas.

Power Co said over 200 homes are without power in Carterton, and 150 in Taihape.

Network Tasman has recorded 1300 unplanned outages across the region.

About 80 homes in the Wahapo Area on the West Coast are without power, according to provider Westpower.

Orion says about 20 homes just out of Christchurch in the Little River area also have no power.

Meanwhile, a powerline has fallen and is hanging low across Treadwell Street in Lower Hutt.

World.title: How world media reacted to All Blacks win over South Africa
World.content:
The All Blacks have beaten the Springboks 33-16 in the opening Test of their tour of South Africa in Johannesburg.

New Zealand's win - by a rather significant margin of 17 points - was dubbed "surprising" and "comfortable", with world media highlighting the All Blacks dominating performance.

Meanwhile, the Springboks were left to reflect on a disappointing performance, as noted by media.

The victory gives the All Blacks an early advantage in the four-match series and will give the team a boost of confidence heading into the second Test.

Here's how world media reacted to the All Blacks vs Springboks series opener.

The Telegraph

The Telegraph's post-match article describes the All Blacks victory as a "statement win".

"Rugby's Greatest Rivalry did not begin with the year's greatest game, but a New Zealand victory against the odds, at high altitude in Johannesburg, has poured intrigue and interest on to a series which was already brimming with them," the article reads.

It said the All Blacks win was almost as "comfortable as it was surprising".

Rugby 365

"Wasteful" is how the online outlet Rugby 365 has described the Springboks performance.

The Boks wasted several scoring opportunities throughout the game, which couldn't be ignored.

The article said that "proved costly as New Zealand took their chances to outscore the hosts by five tries to one".

Will Jordan scores a try. Photosport NZ Ltd / www.photosport.nz

RugbyPass

Online outlet RugbyPass' post-match article angles in on All Black Will Jordan, who said the victory "means everything".

"Serious shift of 80 minutes, love the way our boys just dug deep. Some guys playing here against the Springboks for the first time, got a taste of what it's like.

"Extremely proud of our whole group. We realise it's just one of four, but an awesome start to us for the series."

The article highlights that despite the win, the group understood it was the first Test of a four-match series.

The South African

"All Blacks punish Springboks" - a line from The South African newspaper.

The paper's post-match article focuses on the Springboks losing their World Rugby No 1 ranking.

"The result not only gives the All Blacks the early advantage in the four-Test Rugby's Greatest Rivalry series, but also sees them move above South Africa at the summit of the world rankings," the online paper wrote.

It noted that the 17-point victory was New Zealand's biggest-ever win over the Springboks at Ellis Park in South Africa.

World.title: Pogačar hails rival after 'unimaginable' week following brother's death
World.content:
Tadej Pogačar has delivered an ominous and stunning start to the Vuelta a España, edging British rider Ethan Hayter by just 0.09 seconds in the opening stage time trial.

However, the world number one said after the race that he had hoped Britain's Josh Tarling would come out on top.

Tarling was competing in the Vuelta just days after his brother Finlay Tarling was killed when he was hit by a non-accredited car on the course during the Volta a Portugal.

Competing despite his brother's death, Tarling delivered a blistering time of his own to be well in contention for stage honours.

As it happened, Soudal Quick-Step's Hayter finished four seconds faster than his grieving compatriot, with Pogačar pipping them both, before saying it would have been fitting had Tarling claimed victory.

"When I was going to the start line, I saw that Josh has the best time and, I really wish he wins today," Pogačar said at the finish.

"For sure I would do my best, but it was also this kind of strange moment. I was really rooting, myself, for Josh.

"Then I came to the intermediate [time check] and I hear a different name [over the radio], I hear Ethan Hayter was ahead of me by three seconds and I say, 'OK, I give it my all but no risks' and then we'll see what happens.

"I would really like to see Josh do well at this Vuelta."

Tarling's Netcompany INEOS director sportif Geraint Thomas was also full of praise for Tarling.

"It's been great to have him here. He was really keen to ride and wanted to get back to the day job and find comfort in the process and be around the team to be a normal as possible," fellow Welshman Thomas said.

"It's been unimaginable what he's gone through this last week or so.

Josh Tarling was awarded the white jersey as the race's Most Combative Rider after the first stage. (Getty Images: Tim de Waele)

"To put in a performance like that at the end of the week or so is just fantastic and shows the class of him as person and an athlete, so [we] couldn't be prouder.

"I think the course suited him technically. He's one of the best and yesterday was probably the first time he's ridden a bike properly in a while, so to still put that in is insane, really.

"We'll just continue to be normal around him now and support as best we can."

Tarling's parents, Michael and Dawn, had both given their eldest son their blessing to compete at the Vuelta, saying it was what his brother would have wanted.

"Finlay was so incredibly proud of his big brother, and would be watching, nose to the TV and shouting as he competed," they wrote in a post on social media.

"So it is right that Josh honours that love."

Pogačar, who's bidding to become just the ninth men's rider to win all three Grand Tours in their career, put himself in position from the offset by completing the highly technical 9.5-kilometre course through the streets of Monaco — where he resides — in 10 minutes, 57 seconds.

Pogačar is competing at the Vuelta for the first time since making his Grand Tour debut as a 20-year-old in the 2019 race. He won three stages and finished third, which incredibly is his worst overall result in the three-week events.

This year is going much better, though.

Why these people believe in 'freak' Pogačar's victories As Tadej Pogačar continues to mop up cycling's biggest accolades and most controversial record, one former doper believes he's found the answer to his success: he is just a "freak".

Pogačar won the Tour de France for the third-straight time to claim his fifth overall title in July, equalling the record for the most overall wins at the race.

The two-time reigning world champion also won the Tour de Suisse and Tour de Romandie stage races as well as celebrating victories at three of the year's one-day monument races — Liège-Bastogne-Liège, the Ronde van Vlaanderen and Milano-Sanremo — while finishing second in the other, Paris-Roubaix.

He also claimed victory in Strade Bianche and has now finished first in 17 of the 38 race days he has completed in 2026.

Pogačar won the Giro d'Italia at the first attempt in 2024, so the Vuelta is the only Grand Tour race he is yet to conquer.

The only other men to have won all three are Eddy Merckx, Bernard Hinault, Jacques Anquetil, Alberto Contador, Chris Froome, Felice Gimondi, Vincenzo Nibali and his long-time rival, Jonas Vingegaard.

The win was Pogačar's first in the opening stage of a Grand Tour, and it's also the first time he took the red jersey as the Vuelta leader. It's his 36th Grand Tour stage win altogether.

No man has led the Vuelta from start to finish since Swiss legend Tony Rominger did so during the 1994 race.

Such a feat has only happened eight times in men's grand tour history, three times at the Vuelta.

Merckx, the man to whom Pogačar is so often compared, managed the feat once too, at the 1973 Giro d'Italia.

Pogačar's main rival, Vingegaard, is not racing at the 81st edition of the Vuelta as he recovers from a broken collarbone sustained in a crash the day after he was woken at 2am for a doping test at the Tour de France.

Remco Evenepoel, who finished second behind Pogačar at the Tour, is also not competing. The Belgian rider has opted for rest and specific training for the Road World Championships in Montréal next month.

Monaco became the first city to host the start of all three Grand Tours. The Giro d'Italia started in the principality in 1966 and it staged the start of the Tour de France in 2009.

Much of the time trial route on Saturday covered the same course as the annual Formula 1 Grand Prix.

The second stage will also start in Monaco before a 214.3km hilly trek through Provence to Manosque. It will be the longest stage of the race, which finishes in the southern Spanish city of Granada on September 13.
